papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
authors: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu, Yiqing Hu, Caifeng Shan
bullets: Addresses the linear GPU-memory growth and quadratic computation of Transformer KV caches, while preserving more detail than fixed-size state compression.
Uses a memory encoder-decoder to store selected final-layer hidden states and dynamically reconstruct attention KV caches.
Applies sparse attention that retrieves relevant memories once per input and shares the sparse indices across layers.
Reports substantial efficiency gains, including 1313× lower memory-state cache, 6.9× lower prefill latency, and 3.5× higher throughput at 1M context in one adaptation setting.
Generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks with competitive performance against specialized models.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces scalable memory architecture for LLMs with KV-cache reduction and long-context efficiency.
papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MemOnce enables LLMs to retain long-term, fine-grained memories with compact states, reducing memory and computation costs for long-context continual inference.

papers.abstract: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.
authors: Haoyang Wang, Weibo Gao, Zhengxiong Li, Lingfeng Tao
bullets: Addresses the repetitive, expert-heavy workflow spanning geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training.
Each candidate passes cost-ordered gates with status and evidence records; failures trigger bounded parameter revisions and cheaper reruns, while unresolved trade-offs escalate to a human.
The resulting SAGE Hand has four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb.
Under matched training, SAGE Hand achieves 45.6% success on a hexagonal prism and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder; tactile input more than halves cylinder drop rate.
The Skill preserves capture in 164/165 controlled iterations versus 14/165 without it, supporting its role as a regression guard.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the Task2Hand design loop. A human provides a functional manipulation brief and design guidance, and an AI coding agent equipped with the Task2Hand Skill generates parameterized hand-model candidates. Physics-based and learning verification gates evaluate each candidate, and failure evidence guides bounded parameter refinement and morphology revision. The design history depicts the resulting evolution toward the final design and a fabricated prototype.

Fig. 2: The Task2Hand Skill. (1) The user writes a functional brief and exposes the parameter set θ the agent may change; the contract, evaluator, and success rules are frozen before any comparison. (2) The Skill proposes one bounded edit, regenerates the whole model from θ, and runs the cost-ordered gates G1–G7. Every gate returns a status and an evidence record, so the earliest blocker k∗ names a failing mechanism and the ledger identifies a parameter group for targeted revision. One group is revised, and every cheaper gate is rerun. Where the evidence poses a choice it cannot settle, the Skill escalates with at most three costed options; the decision returns to the ledger and the search resumes inside the approved scope. (3) An accepted candidate carries its artifacts and provenance. In the iteration shown k∗ = G4, so G5–G7 never ran and no training budget was spent.

Fig. 6: Training-time success (top) and drop (bottom) rates for SAGE Hand, SAGE Hand-T4, LEAP, and Shadow on (a) the hexagonal prism, (b) the colored cube, and (c) the bicolor cylinder, under the same nominal 400-epoch budget and one frozen learning protocol. Lines are seed means, bands ±1 s.d.; seed counts appear in each panel (n = 1 for Shadow on the cube; n = 3 → 2 after epoch 375 for Shadow on the cylinder). Each point reports a teacher-free evaluation of the checkpoint saved at that epoch. The primary summary statistic is the mean over the final ten available evaluation points.

Fig. 7: Summary of the frozen-protocol evaluation. (a) Last-available-10 success for four hands on three objects; markers are seed means, bars ±1 s.d., n = 3 except where annotated (n = 1 for Shadow on the cube, n = 3∗ for Shadow on the cylinder). (b) The same pairwise differences were recomputed on two evaluation packages. Both cylinder comparisons hold their sign across packages; the cube comparison reverses (+0.8 vs −6.5 pp) and is left undetermined.

Fig. 4: Fully automatic iteration from V74 with and without the Skill. (a) Frozen functional endpoints (Wilson 95 % CI). The Skill path preserves capture (164/165) and static retention (164/165); the path without the Skill degrades both to 14/165 and 4/165. Neither path reaches held-out RL success under a 50-epoch budget. (b) Front and side views of the two resulting morphologies at qopen, unified camera and scale. The Skill-iterated hand retains flat finger geometry; the No-Skill hand introduces distal finger droop consistent with the capture-rate gap in (a).

Fig. 5: Design history of SAGE Hand. (a) Gray circles show historical best success from seed-992 400-epoch runs; orange squares show uniform 50-epoch final success (mean±s.d., n = 3); blue diamonds show E400 late-10 success, the primary late-training metric. Bars denote between-seed s.d.; labels mark n = 1 where applicable. (b) Green squares show 50-epoch drop rate and gray circles show available E400 late-10 drop records. The abscissa follows design-version order.

papers.title: Task2Hand: A Contact-Grounded Skill for Parametric Dexterous-Hand Morphology Design
papers.tldr: Task2Hand automates evidence-driven dexterous-hand design by generating, validating, and training bounded morphology candidates through staged contact, dynamics, and learning gates.

papers.abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .
authors: Yuhang Dai, Yinwei Wu, Ziyue Lin, Han Ji, Xingyi Yang
bullets: Introduces NoPeBench to evaluate obstacle interactions in interactive video world models.
Finds that existing open-source models frequently allow object penetration, despite encoding information predictive of such violations.
Trains a lightweight safety head on frozen DiT hidden states to classify candidate actions as safe or unsafe.
Replaces unsafe actions with safe alternatives that preserve the original intent.
Generalizes zero-shot to open-domain imagery, third-person views, and moving obstacles; code, benchmark, and weights are released.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses a critical failure mode in interactive world models (object penetration) by detecting violations via hidden states and preventing them. This fits 'Interactive World Models' and has direct implications for embodied AI safety.
papers.title: Non-penetrating World Models
papers.tldr: NoPeWorld uses hidden states from frozen diffusion transformers to detect and replace obstacle-penetrating actions, reducing physical violations from 74% to 16% across six video world models.

papers.abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.
authors: Kaden Zheng, Pratyusha Sharma
bullets: Fixed, uniform Transformer architectures may be inefficient for individual tasks.
Learnable scalar gates remove attention or MLP sublayers during training, creating a heterogeneous subnetwork in one run.
Evaluated on standard and looped Transformers ranging from 140M to 2.7B parameters.
Carved models achieve lower validation loss at equal compute and outperform size-matched pruning or distillation models.
Removing sublayers reduces inference cost by up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and up to 1.6× faster decoding, with quality preserved.

Figure 1: Model Carving trains the weights and the topology of a Transformer in one run. (Left) Training starts from an overparameterized Transformer: every sublayer writes through a gate (dot), and learned connections (arcs) join each pair of layers. papers.abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.
authors: Mamoona Tasadduq, Maryam Bashir
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly training candidate configurations on large datasets.
Selects a compact coreset by maximizing Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based rankings while penalizing subset size.
Evaluates the coreset with GA, CHC, and PSO across tabular, text, and image benchmarks.
Reports HPO-stage speedups of approximately 1.14×–8.80×, with comparable test accuracy to full-dataset HPO.
Outperforms same-size random sampling in ranking correlation on held-out configurations for 8 of 11 datasets; construction cost can be amortized through reuse.

papers.selection_reason: Ranking-preserving coreset selection reduces HPO computation by shrinking training data, fitting the broad efficient-AI computation-reduction interest.

papers.abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($\alpha=0$) and 98.83% at $\alpha=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $\alpha=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $\alpha=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
authors: Dylan Forde
bullets: Addresses long-context retrieval degradation caused by attention normalization mass spreading across distractors.
Builds a linear-size local-window-plus-hub transport graph with sparsemax or thresholded-ReLU gating to eliminate excess distractor mass.
Adds annealed Sinkhorn updates, an exact low-rank adjoint, fused Triton kernels, and a causal chunked variant with zero future leakage.
At 262K tokens, sparsemax THOT achieves 97.40% or 98.83% fixed-binding recall depending on loss regularization, while softmax-gated hub OT reaches 3.52%.
Reports 100% multi-needle retrieval on 65K-token WikiText-103 queries and faster operator benchmarks than the compared baselines; broader multi-layer LM runs use an unfused path.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces hub optimal transport with sparse gating for long-context attention, directly targeting long-context models and efficient attention.
papers.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
papers.tldr: THOT uses sparse capacity-gated hub optimal transport and optimized kernels to preserve relevant facts in extremely long contexts while reducing attention overhead.

papers.abstract: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
authors: Hassan Iqbal, Krishna Kumar
bullets: Robot damage changes which routes are feasible and how much risk is acceptable per mission.
The study compares decision policies, fixed-penalty policies, generic outcome models, and capability contracts that compose terrain-level success and travel-time predictions.
Capability contracts rank hazardous terrains using two low-risk probes, avoiding the need for four new trials per hazard.
At a calibrated 5% infeasibility limit, outcome models reduce declined missions from about 32% to 7–8% on Go2 and 57% to 35–36% on H1.
Fixed penalties help but require retuning as the target risk changes; scope is simulated damaged quadruped and humanoid robots.

papers.selection_reason: Compares decision policies and outcome models for risk-aware route planning after robot damage, directly relevant to world models and robot navigation.
papers.title: What Must a Model Tell a Planner? Outcome Interfaces for Risk-Aware Planning After Robot Damage
papers.tldr: Outcome-based interfaces, especially capability contracts, help damaged robots choose safer routes while declining fewer missions than fixed decision policies.

papers.abstract: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.
authors: Jungbin Kim, Youngim Nam, Cheolhyeon Kwon
bullets: Addresses mismatch between nominal and actual vehicle dynamics during on-track racing.
Jointly learns physical parameters and residuals under one shared prediction-error objective.
Recursively alternates updates, accepting only changes that do not increase the objective.
The objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion.
Simulations and hardware experiments show large reductions in lateral-velocity and yaw-rate one-step prediction errors versus the nominal model.

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval asks a system to find, in a large collection of untrimmed videos with subtitles, the video and the time interval that a natural-language query describes. We find that most top-ranked errors of a strong corpus-level scorer come from choosing the wrong video, not from imprecise boundaries, and that re-weighting the evidence the scorer already uses does not fix them. We present DiTraR, which addresses video selection from two complementary directions. A witness-interval scorer decomposes the query into probes and scores every candidate interval of every corpus video exactly; a multi-scorer energy ensemble averages the energies of independently trained scorers before one exhaustive search; and a transcript verifier, a frozen language model that reads the time-stamped dialogue of the highest-ranked videos, re-orders the moments without changing their boundaries. With all settings frozen on development data and a single evaluation, DiTraR reaches 24.36 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 on the TVR validation split. The ensemble improves queries about visual content, the verifier improves queries about dialogue, and their gains largely add up.
authors: Mohammad Alijanpour Shalmani, Alale Rezvani Boroujeni, Ali Amini
bullets: Most top-ranked errors arise from selecting the wrong video rather than inaccurate temporal boundaries.
A witness-interval scorer evaluates query probes against every candidate interval across the corpus.
A multi-scorer energy ensemble combines independently trained scorers before exhaustive search.
A frozen language-model transcript verifier re-ranks top moments using time-stamped dialogue without changing boundaries.
On TVR validation, DiTraR achieves 24.36 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.7; visual and dialogue-query gains are complementary.

papers.abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.
authors: Huaze Tang, Runqing Miao, Tianren Peng, Lam Nguyen, Chao Wang, Jairong Li, Wenbo Ding
bullets: Frames representation learning around which action–future-state dependencies matter for policy improvement and what is lost through compression.

papers.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.
authors: Fabio Guglietta, Tianyi Li, Francesco Viola, Luca Biferale
bullets: Cardiovascular imaging provides noisy, incomplete, and resolution-limited observations, making flow reconstruction inherently ambiguous.
Using a controlled digital twin of a healthy human left heart, the study evaluates unconditional generation and conditional reconstruction.
Repeated conditional samples produce plausible completions rather than a single deterministic estimate; their mean preserves key reference-flow features.
Compared with Gaussian process regression, diffusion-model ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations and better encompass ground-truth features.
The work is a quantitative proof of concept, with scope demonstrated on simulated healthy-heart data and potential application to in-vivo imaging augmentation.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based probabilistic reconstruction of temporally structured flow; transferable to video and world-model generation.
papers.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
papers.tldr: Generative diffusion models can probabilistically reconstruct incomplete cardiovascular flow measurements while capturing diverse, physically plausible flow patterns.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
authors: Chi Yan, Guoyang Zhao, Wentao Yuan, Yixiao Ge, Yanning Zhou, Dan Xu
bullets: Existing VLMs struggle with metric 3D inference because uncalibrated views leave geometry ambiguous.
StereoVLM learns from binocular observations through correspondence, disparity, calibration-conditioned depth, and semantic spatial reasoning.
The authors introduce Stereo3D-Bench, evaluating point-, object-, and spatial-reasoning capabilities.
Disparity supervision generalizes better to unseen environments than direct binocular depth supervision.
Interventions show performance relies on cross-view geometry, while hierarchical supervision improves broader spatial and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component, i.e., the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model-order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth.
authors: JaeSeong Kim, KyungTae Lim
bullets: Introduces an exact inclusion–exclusion measure of connected computation produced only by specified layers acting together under identity ablation.
Across Pythia, OLMo, and Amber checkpoints, write-relative connected coordination strengthens during pretraining across measured interaction orders.
Removing these connected components harms perplexity more than removing norm-matched random directions in all 35 tested model-order cells.
Pairwise representation similarity is negatively correlated with connected coordination, but the two measures can recommend different layers for removal.
The findings indicate that pretraining organizes sequential cross-layer dependencies within the computational opportunities provided by depth.

papers.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.
authors: Zunhai Su, Keyu Fan, Ruishan Guo, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jingzehua Xu, Bohan Sun, Hansen Feng, Ruihan Hu, Yik-Chung Wu, Ngai Wong
bullets: Streaming geometry transformers face growing KV caches and sensitivity to quantization across cache locations, causing cache–geometry mismatch.
Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization preserves sensitive cross-view evidence.
Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads using quantized history.
Across five benchmarks and two backbones, it achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings and can outperform unquantized inference.
The optimized backend reaches 5.05× physical KV compression, 23.1% lower latency, and up to 5.4× larger batch size under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.

bullets: Speculative decoding faces uncertainty from both target-model predictions and sampling randomness.

DICE synchronizes verification draws with drafting and guides draft-tree node selection and asynchronous prefetching.
It requires no additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution.
The method reports throughput gains of up to 24.6 percentage points over strong baselines across diverse settings.

papers.abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.
authors: Sarah Parisot, Melanie Fernandez Pradier, David Bignell, Sergio Valcarcel Macua, Katja Hofmann
bullets: The study separates prediction type—categorical versus continuous—from generation strategy using controlled 2D and 3D environments.
Categorical models achieve higher rollout validity in 2D and stronger long-horizon performance in 3D, particularly for stochastic entities.
Greedy decoding gives categorical models the highest rollout validity, while sampling provides the best-calibrated stochastic predictions.
Continuous models exhibit dynamics failures such as disappearing characters; categorical models remain competitive even with lossy visual tokenization.
Results support categorical prediction as a compute-efficient approach to learning world dynamics, beyond matching next-frame appearance.

papers.abstract: Nautical charts encode safety-critical maritime information through standardized symbols, attributes, text, and heterogeneous geometries. Interpreting these charts and assessing the navigational significance of successive chart updates requires recognizing nautical features, determining their spatial relationships, and applying navigational knowledge. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising approach to nautical-chart interpretation, yet systematic evaluation of their fine-grained nautical feature recognition, chart-based spatial reasoning, and application of navigational knowledge to assessing chart changes remains limited. We introduce ENC-QA, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 77,312 questions derived from 6,612 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs). The benchmark evaluates four complementary capabilities: ENC Perception, Spatial Reasoning, Joint Perception and Spatial Reasoning, and Application. Of these, 8,227 questions form a progressive subset that decomposes selected chart-change cases into linked questions progressing from change detection to criticality assessment, enabling case-level analysis of how models use perceptual and spatial evidence to determine the navigational significance of chart changes. Evaluations of 10 open-weight VLMs reveal substantial limitations in fine-grained nautical feature recognition and feature-grounded spatial reasoning. Controlled evidence interventions show that relevant perceptual and spatial information improves change-criticality accuracy. Our findings establish ENC-QA as a diagnostic resource for nautical-chart understanding and safety-critical navigational decisions. We will release the benchmark and evaluation code upon publication.
authors: Jiyoon Pyo, Jacob Arndt, Yao-Yi Chiang, Dalton Lunga
bullets: Introduces 77,312 questions from 6,612 NOAA Electronic Navigational Charts.
Evaluates ENC perception, spatial reasoning, combined perception and reasoning, and navigational application.
Includes 8,227 progressive questions linking chart-change detection to criticality assessment.
Evaluations of 10 open-weight VLMs reveal substantial weaknesses in nautical feature recognition and feature-grounded spatial reasoning.
Evidence interventions indicate that relevant perceptual and spatial information improves change-criticality accuracy.

papers.abstract: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.

bullets: Soft anchor-routing pathways can produce highly redundant summaries, whereas exclusive patch partitions prevent collapse by construction.
The proposed focus anchors concentrate anchors near learned importance peaks while preserving exclusive Voronoi regions.
On CIFAR-100, exclusive routing is 2.4–3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention; focus anchors add 1.5 points on a cluttered canvas.
For full-HD traffic-sign recognition, both anchor variants match dense local-window attention at about one-fifth the FLOPs; fixed partitions train 1.5× faster per step.
Hard exclusive assignment was the most stable and accurate tested option, but anchors use more memory and do not outperform the trained ResNet-18 in this regime.

papers.abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

The most consistent models were not necessarily the most factual.
GRPO fine-tuning a 7B ALM improved claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61 while preserving per-dimension answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.
authors: Jakub \v{S}m{\'i}d, Pavel Kr{\'a}l
bullets: Evaluates seven instruction-tuned open-weight LLMs across 12 languages, three domains, and four prompting paradigms.
Direct monolithic prompting outperforms chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential-refinement pipelines.
Dense models consistently outperform sparse mixture-of-experts models.
Aspect-term recall is the main bottleneck; multi-step decomposition often reduces extraction quality.
Multi-step prompting increases token use by up to 2.38× without improving F1, while refinement can over-correct smaller models.

papers.abstract: A comic-book character, a photorealistic cityscape, an oil-painted coffee cup -- such stylistically diverse references provide visual guidance across shots and frames, yet generating a coherent multi-shot video that unifies their visual styles while preserving subject identities and scene content remains challenging. Existing methods maintain cross-shot continuity through additional attention control or memory processing. However, they struggle to resolve disparate per-shot styles or handle reference-target duration mismatches within a single framework. We introduce Refrain, a unified model that learns cross-shot consistency through a self-supervised reconstruction task. Reference clips from the same original video are deliberately perturbed with distinct visual edits, and the model recovers the unedited source footage under a shared style prompt. The resulting pipeline yields DurMix-300K, which pairs independently edited references of varying durations with their original videos. Operating on the A$^2$O principle (Any Reference, Any Duration, One Timeline), Refrain maps image and video references onto a shared temporal canvas without auxiliary conditioning modules. For evaluation, experiments show that standard CLIP or DINO metrics frequently overlook stylistic clashes or misinterpret intended narrative cuts as inconsistency. We propose Shot-Debiased Consistency (SDC), which uses an extensive real-video bank to establish a baseline for style variation associated with content changes within shots. By discounting this baseline divergence, SDC evaluates cross-shot style shifts against real-world distributions, where smaller residual differences indicate higher stylistic continuity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Refrain achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-shot consistency, while excelling at shot timing, reference adherence, and text alignment.
authors: Hongru Yan, Yue Wu, Jian-Wei Zhang, Liangbin Xie, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses stylistic clashes and reference–target duration mismatches in multi-shot video generation.
Uses self-supervised reconstruction: perturbed reference clips are restored to their original footage under a shared style prompt.
Introduces DurMix-300K, pairing independently edited references of varying durations with original videos.
Implements the A²O principle—Any Reference, Any Duration, One Timeline—without auxiliary conditioning modules.

Proposes Shot-Debiased Consistency (SDC) to evaluate cross-shot style continuity against real-video variation; experiments report state-of-the-art consistency and strong timing, adherence, and text alignment.

papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to ground instructions in changing observations, coordinate heterogeneous tools, and recover from failures that can propagate through downstream operations. Although existing LLM-based agents retain experience and refine reusable skills, successful local repairs do not by themselves establish complete-task gains over the current shared procedure library. We present EvoTER, an experience-driven framework that enables embodied agents to self-evolve tool-use skills without updating model parameters. EvoTER operates through a three-role evolution loop: Explorer records tool-use trajectories; Diagnoser distills successful and failed executions into skills for tool selection, parameter computation, postcondition checks, and recovery; and Validator retains candidate revisions only when they improve complete-task success in fresh sessions. In simulation, EvoTER improves overall task success from a pre-evolution baseline of 53.60% to 80.40%. In real-world experiments, simulation initialization reduces the attempts required to acquire short-horizon skills, while continued real-world evolution improves long-horizon success from 20% to 80%-100% across tasks and enables the evolving skill library to incorporate new tool functionality introduced after simulation development. Project page: https://evoter-project.github.io/
authors: Yingting Zhou, Yuyin Zhou, Yongliang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao

Uses an Explorer–Diagnoser–Validator loop to record trajectories, distill skills, and retain revisions only when complete-task success improves in fresh sessions.
Learns skills for tool selection, parameter computation, postcondition checking, and failure recovery.
Raises simulated task success from 53.60% to 80.40%.
Real-world evolution improves long-horizon success from 20% to 80%–100% across tasks and adapts to newly introduced tool functionality.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained recognition benefits from high resolution, but not every image region needs it. We study a foveated Vision Transformer (FoVT) that uses last-block class attention from a 224-pixel glance to select regions for refinement. Fine patches from the 448-pixel image replace the selected coarse cells, and the same backbone classifies the mixed-resolution input. We evaluate FoVT on five benchmarks with two seeds and 26 configurations per dataset. Attention beats random selection on all five benchmarks, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points on the smallest objects. At equal transformer cost, Holm-corrected tests detect no FoVT deficit relative to a port of the official CF-ViT, but no dataset shows a corrected FoVT advantage in both seeds. FoVT requires no feature reuse, distillation loss, or selection schedule. Reusing coarse features shows no significant benefit and costs 1 to 3 points when the reuse module is trained at the head learning rate. Skipping refinement for the most confident 19 to 24 percent of images leaves accuracy unchanged to two decimal places. At the transformer cost of uniform 336-pixel inference, gated FoVT improves accuracy on four benchmarks, with the largest gains on NABirds and FGVC-Aircraft and no significant gain on Stanford Dogs. Foveation primarily saves computation: relative to a uniform 448-pixel model trained with the same auxiliary glance loss, ungated FoVT uses 44 percent fewer transformer operations, with no significant accuracy difference on four benchmarks and a 0.53-point deficit on FGVC-Aircraft. Wall-clock savings are smaller than the reduction in transformer operations.
authors: Boris Kriuk, Mohamed Sobhy
bullets: A 224-pixel glance uses last-block class attention to select regions for 448-pixel refinement within the same backbone.

At equal transformer cost, FoVT shows no corrected accuracy deficit versus ported CF-ViT, but also no consistent corrected advantage.
Gating refinement for the most confident 19–24% of images preserves accuracy; at uniform 336-pixel cost, gated FoVT improves four of five benchmarks.
Ungated FoVT reduces transformer operations by 44% versus uniform 448-pixel inference, but wall-clock savings are smaller and FGVC-Aircraft shows a 0.53-point deficit.

Stage 2 re-embeds the top-K cells from the full-resolution image as 4K fine tokens (orange), which replace the corresponding coarse input embeddings. The same backbone processes the mixed sequence ZK and produces ℓf . Selection indices are detached. papers.abstract: Linear manufacturing typically operates in highly structured settings with standardized objects, allowing robots to execute pre-programmed motions based on precise models. In contrast, circular manufacturing involves dynamic and less controlled environments, where product components can vary due to appearance and physical changes across different product generations. In this context, uncertainty arises from both the unknown or partially observed states of components (e.g., damaged surfaces, altered shapes) and the unstructured disassembly environment, often characterized by heavy clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing viewpoints. This demands a flexible and adaptable robotic grasping system that can cope with unexpected object changes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an autonomous grasp learning framework designed for highly uncertain and variable conditions. The framework explicitly distinguishes between uncertainty due to noisy or incomplete sensory observations (aleatoric uncertainty) and uncertainty due to limited knowledge and distribution shift (epistemic uncertainty). Moreover, the framework employs an active perception strategy to reduce visual ambiguity: semantic and spatial scene understanding is achieved using vision language models (VLMs), while view planning enables the robot to adjust its viewpoint to improve observability. In addition, the approach leverages large-scale human demonstration data to learn interaction patterns, which are then transferred to robotic end-effectors, enabling robust manipulation in these variable settings. Quantitative validation, including the utility of active vision on disassembled components in practice, is expected to form an important part of future work.
authors: Yitian Shi, Rosa Wolf, Rania Rayyes
bullets: Targets uncertain disassembly environments with changing object appearances, damaged surfaces, clutter, occlusions, and limited viewpoints.
Separates aleatoric uncertainty from noisy or incomplete observations and epistemic uncertainty from limited knowledge or distribution shifts.
Uses active perception, including view planning, to reduce visual ambiguity and improve component observability.
Applies vision language models for semantic and spatial scene understanding.
Transfers interaction patterns learned from large-scale human demonstrations to robotic end-effectors; quantitative validation is identified as future work.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed CIRCA-Grasp framework. In the digital asset pipeline, existing CAD models are used to generate analytic antipodal grasps and simulation-based training environments, which support pretraining of the probabilistic grasp learner vMF-Contact [4]. In the physical asset pipeline, large-scale human demonstrations are transferred through HOGraspFlow [10] to provide hand-object interaction priors, while real-world robot executions continuously generate grasp experiences for deployment and adaptation. During inference, VISO-Grasp [5] integrates the uncertainty-aware grasp model with active view planning to search for and grasp partially visible or occluded objects in clutter. All simulated and real interactions are stored in a grasp learning database, enabling continual improvement of the grasp policy across perception, planning, and execution.

Fig. 3. The connection between CIRCA-Grasp and the knowledge-based Intralogistics system from [14]. From the knowledge representation’s perspective, CIRCA-Grasp is the instantiation of the :GraspLearningSystem within the knowledge graph. (*Note: we use the same color scheme as [14], Fig. 7., to make them comparable)

Fig. 1. While linear production involves uniform objects with known geometries that are easily localized via pose matching (i.e., objects are typically “in distribution” (ID)), circular factories introduce significant distribution shifts. The high variance and unknown states of recycled materials require advanced, uncertainty-aware manipulation strategies to reliably grasp “out-of-distribution” (OOD) objects in cluttered environments.

papers.title: An Autonomous Adaptive Learning System for Robotic Grasping in the Circular Factory
papers.tldr: An autonomous grasp-learning framework combines uncertainty modeling, active perception, VLM-based scene understanding, and human demonstrations to help robots handle variable, cluttered components in circular manufacturing.

papers.abstract: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. One is based on a decomposition of mutual information (MI) into a set of Conditional MIs (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens. A second, higher-order attention, introduces correlations between contiguous key and query tokens. A third introduces correlations between a set of key and query tokens and uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to obtain an attention expression spanning a sequence of tokens. All these methods may enhance the information content of the autoregressive probabilities that are used in inference/generation. Applications to contrastive decoding and a systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities are presented.
authors: R. I. Cukier
bullets: Motivated by limitations in standard autoregressive attention used by decoder LLMs.
Introduces attention based on mutual-information decomposition into conditional MIs linking key tokens with query-token pairs.
Develops higher-order variants modeling contiguous key/query tokens and larger token sets.
Uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to derive sequence-spanning attention expressions.
Discusses applications to contrastive decoding and systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes new higher-order attention mechanisms for decoder LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Enhancing Attention with Higher-Order Attention
papers.tldr: The paper proposes higher-order attention mechanisms to enrich autoregressive information by modeling dependencies among multiple key and query tokens.

papers.abstract: Many high-accuracy referring expression comprehension (REC) methods produce image-dependent multimodal representations. These representations must be recomputed for every video frame, even when the referring expression remains unchanged. Fast open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World instead pre-encode text once and reuse it throughout the stream. However, encoding each referring expression as a single embedding prevents explicit token-level correspondence. We propose Ref-YOLO-World, which separates text-side computation that depends only on the referring expression from image processing and reuses its outputs across frames. Two lightweight modules inject cached per-token text features into YOLO-World's detection path. Ref-YOLO-World achieves 81.29% Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg val, the highest among REC models with a decoupled text branch, and consistently outperforms a fine-tuned YOLO-World. Precomputation reduces per-image inference time by 18.5%, yielding 47.0 FPS. A Core ML version runs at 15.73 FPS on an iPhone 15 Pro, demonstrating efficient on-device REC. Code is available at https://github.com/sakusaku3939/Ref-YOLO-World.

papers.abstract: Layer skipping can reduce large language model inference costs, but a request budget does not specify how to allocate layer execution across generated tokens. We introduce \method{}, which allows tokens to execute different numbers of layers while matching each request's mean executed depth to a continuous budget. At each routed layer, a router reads the current token state and its request's budget and decides whether to execute the Transformer block. Tokens that skip the block pass through a lightweight residual adapter and write no key/value (K/V) entry at that layer. A single checkpoint serves requests with different budgets in the same batch. Across three LLaMA backbones, six quality metrics, and 13 budgets, AVERT is best or tied for best in 206 of 234 comparisons. Across single- and mixed-budget batches, the mean absolute per-request budget error is at most 1.15 percentage points. When grouping requests by budget leaves batches underfilled, mixing budgets reduces decode time per output token (TPOT) by 4.3--21.2%.
authors: Pengjie Zheng, Mengwei Xie, Huan Yang, Si Wu, Pengfei Hu, Feng Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of allocating a request-level layer-execution budget across generated tokens.
A router uses each token’s state and request budget to decide whether to run each Transformer block.
Skipped tokens use a lightweight residual adapter and do not write K/V entries at that layer.
One checkpoint supports different budgets within the same batch.
Across three LLaMA backbones, six metrics, and 13 budgets, it was best or tied in 206/234 comparisons; mixed-budget batching reduced TPOT by 4.3–21.2%.

papers.abstract: We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape. We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.

Learns from 3D scans of 31 dogs performing natural movements.
Combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space.
Supports downstream tasks including surface reconstruction and image-based pose/shape regression.
Shows that a limited set of anatomically valid degrees of freedom can accurately estimate canine pose and shape.

papers.abstract: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.
authors: Mohab Kishawy, Chengzhou Tang, Shahram Shirani, Jun Chen
bullets: Addresses nonuniform illumination and camera tone compression that global per-view correction cannot capture.
Represents each Gaussian with albedo and shading latents, separating surface color from illumination.
Models each view’s degradation as a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve.
Predicts gain bases from observations and solves view-specific coefficients during training, without paired normal-light supervision or stored per-view parameters.
Achieves the best reported NIQE and CLIP-IQA scores and highest blind-study ratings on Gaussian-DK; results are competitive on LOM.

papers.abstract: Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.
authors: Xinyu Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Yuxin Gao, Anxiang Ma, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Frames visual invocation as predicting whether source text leaves translation-relevant uncertainty unresolved.
Introduces a three-label visual-dependency dataset: no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed.
Proposes PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic router that selects text-only or multimodal translation before visual encoding.
English-to-Chinese experiments show a favorable COMET–compute trade-off, with substantially fewer visual calls and comparable quality to always-on multimodal inference.
Analysis indicates the router separates genuine visual dependence from ambiguity resolved by sentence context.

papers.abstract: Offline chain-of-thought (CoT) compression creates shorter supervision for efficient reasoning, but per-example compressors repeatedly process similar expressions across traces, wasting compressor budget. Methods that reuse identical text across examples miss longer shared expressions when names, numbers, or formulas change from one question to another. We introduce CRAFT, which abstracts problem-specific details into slots to uncover partially lexicalized expression templates (PLETs) and clusters wording variants into families. Compressing each family representative once yields shared deletion or rewriting edits, which are applied with each occurrence's own details to construct compact, ordinary-text training targets. Compared with per-example rewriting, CRAFT Rewrite reduces weighted compressor budgets by a median 90.7% with a median accuracy loss of 1.21 percentage points, while generating shorter reasoning. Against cross-sample encoding, it shortens reasoning across all eight model-dataset settings by 25.3% on average and improves accuracy in five.
authors: Shibo Wang, Yuzhe He, Yifeng Zhao, Yunjiao Zhou, Zepeng Ning, Hanzhang Zhou, Kezhi Mao, Junlang Qian
bullets: Per-example CoT compressors waste budget by repeatedly processing similar expressions.
CRAFT abstracts names, numbers, and formulas into slots to discover partially lexicalized expression templates and wording families.
It compresses one family representative, then transfers its deletion or rewriting edits to each occurrence’s specific details.
CRAFT Rewrite cuts weighted compressor budgets by a median 90.7% with a median accuracy loss of 1.21 percentage points.
Compared with cross-sample encoding, it shortens reasoning by 25.3% on average across eight model-dataset settings and improves accuracy in five.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
authors: Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang
bullets: Addresses weak memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience in VLM-based manipulation agents.
Uses an Actor–Reflector framework: the Actor executes tasks, while the Reflector turns interaction evidence into reusable operational guidance.
Combines hierarchical short- and long-term memory with evidence-based failure reflection and recursive harness self-improvement.
Achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench, plus 96.7% average success across three real-world tasks.
Evaluates generalization, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation under environmental variation.
