papers.abstract: Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Specifically, we track per-sample loss dynamics using exponential moving averages (EMA) to obtain three complementary signals that capture current learning difficulty, ongoing learning improvements, and potential degradation. To accommodate evolving training dynamics, we introduce Adaptive Metric Fusion, a contextual bandit-based mechanism that dynamically adjusts the relative importance of these signals based on training feedback. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.
authors: Hai Gan, Suorong Yang, Guang Li, Baile Xu, Furao Shen
bullets: Addresses the limitations of hardness-only data selection, which can overlook how samples evolve during training.
Tracks per-sample loss with exponential moving averages to estimate difficulty, improvement, and degradation.
Uses contextual-bandit Adaptive Metric Fusion to adjust signal importance based on training feedback.
Adds bounded staleness compensation to prioritize samples that have been selected less recently.
Across vision and language tasks, LeDAS matches or surpasses full-dataset training at a 50% selection ratio and remains robust to noisy or corrupted data.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed LeDAS framework. At each training epoch, LeDAS characterizes sample-level learning dynamics using three metrics: hardness, progress, and deterioration. It then adaptively fuses these signals via a contextual bandit guided by target model features. Staleness Compensation further adjusts sample selection priorities based on historical selection patterns. The selected subset is finally used to update the target model, thereby establishing a closed-loop data selection framework.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). DLMs generate text through iterative denoising, exposing partially masked states whose internal representations change throughout the generation process. This raises a DLM-specific question: can selective forgetting improve by identifying forget-data-associated features and adapting their suppression across denoising stages? We conduct a controlled investigation of this question in LLaDA-8B-Instruct. To evaluate the unlearning of knowledge plausibly encoded during pre-training, we use WMDP as our forget-domain benchmark. Using top-k sparse autoencoders and denoising-state replay, we compare static and stage-adaptive feature suppression. We find substantial shifts in forget-data-associated features across denoising stages, but tracking these dynamics alone does not reliably improve the forget-retain trade-off at the evaluated operating points. Together, our study provides an initial empirical foundation for developing and evaluating machine unlearning as a post-training privacy mechanism in DLMs.
authors: Yunha Seo, Changhoon Kim
bullets: Machine unlearning in diffusion language models is underexplored because their internal representations evolve across iterative denoising.
The study evaluates LLaDA-8B-Instruct using WMDP as a forget-domain benchmark.
Top-k sparse autoencoders identify forget-associated features, while denoising-state replay enables comparison of static and stage-adaptive suppression.
Forget-associated features shift substantially across denoising stages.
Tracking these shifts alone does not reliably improve unlearning performance at the evaluated operating points.

papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.
authors: Xuzhe Dang, Stefan Edelkamp
bullets: Very large imagined gradients are poorly validated: simulator-confirmed return changes fall from 94% at low norms to 1% above 30× the batch median.
The method caps each rollout’s action-gradient norm at 10× the batch median, samples starts by predicted gradient norm, and resets episodes with the lowest predicted returns.
On unseen Unitree G1 motions, normalized return improves from 0.953 to 0.967, while the lowest 1% of clips improve from 0.65 to 0.76.
Persistent-fall clips decrease from 15–18 to 7–10, and baseline final performance is reached in 40% of its iterations and half the training time.
On LAFAN1, the method achieves 0.935 versus 0.906 for prior work.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA.
authors: Jianghan Chao, Wenhui Tan, Hang Su, Qiuyu Tian, Tanxiao Li, Bingzi Zhang, Zequn Liu, Ruihua Song, Yingce Xia

Improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2–27.1 points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1–20.1 points across three frozen planner stacks.
Cross-model transfer is only partial, indicating harnesses remain strongly model-conditioned.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.
authors: Nan Tang, Han-Tao Zhang, Jing-Cheng Pang, Hao-Nan Wang, Hao-Xiang Ren, Yi-Fei Sheng, Jun-Yin Ye, Tian Xu, Fan-Ming Luo, Hao-Xin Lin, Yang Yu

Introduces Latent Subchunk Rollouts to connect latent imagination with frozen VLA action-chunk execution.
Applies a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum for learning from short imagined rollouts.
Reports strong task performance and training efficiency across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot.

papers.abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.
authors: Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, Christian Chwala
bullets: Targets the gap between snapshot-based skill evaluation and temporal coherence needed for sub-daily climate-impact applications.

Trains a diffusion U-Net with a noised previous high-resolution state, enabling continuous interpolation between autoregressive and per-timestep-independent sampling through one inference-time noise parameter.
On hourly European precipitation and 2-meter temperature downscaling, autoregressive rollouts remain stable for up to six months, with only slight early ensemble-spread contraction.
Autoregressive precipitation better preserves daily maxima, while independent generation underestimates them by up to 2×; temperature differences are negligible.
Noise-free conditioning diverges, indicating that the noise-conditioned scheme is important for stable long rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed temporal-noise-conditioned diffusion framework. (a) Training: The conditional diffusion model learns to emulate high-resolution RCM fields from coarse GCM input. The previous-hour RCM state is additionally provided as temporal condition input, corrupted with randomly sampled noise. (b) Inference: The conditioning noise level is controlled by the parameter τ . At its maximum value (τ = 999), the temporal condition consists of pure noise, resulting in per-timestep independent (PTI) samples (dashed lines). This regime also serves to initialize the autoregressive rollout. At a lower noise level (e.g. τ = 50), the previous timestep’s prediction is perturbed with noise and used as the temporal conditioning input. This provides informative temporal context, resulting in temporally consistent autoregressive (AR) sampling (solid lines).

Figure 2: Hourly precipitation (mm/h) for a rain event evolving over 12–13 August 2021 (00:00– 03:00 on 12 August and 00:00 on 13 August shown), with the corresponding 24-hour aggregation (mm/day, rightmost column), for the GCM (conditioning input, top row), the RCM (reference, 2nd row), the AR Emulator (3rd row) and the PTI Emulator (bottom row).

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based temporal sequence generation with controllable consistency; relevant to video and world-model generation.
papers.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
papers.tldr: A noise-conditioned diffusion downscaling model provides a tunable trade-off between temporally coherent autoregressive rollouts and independent per-timestep generation without progressive degradation.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
authors: Anqi Li, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high cost of rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences for each decision.
Probes a few candidates at multiple token budgets and selects the smallest budget that maintains their ranking.
Requires no training or task labels; the first observation-processing step remains exact and context frames are cached.
Across seven navigation and manipulation tasks, matches dense planning success at 2.3× speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×.
Evaluated in a closed-loop study spanning more than 80,000 episodes with frozen checkpoints.

(b) Every candidate rollout computes the first step in full, reads the context frame from a key–value cache instead of recomputing it, and computes the newest frame of later steps at b⋆ positions.

Every later step recomputes a two-frame window, but only the newest frame’s output is kept; the context frame is recomputed solely to provide keys and values, and its output is discarded. papers.selection_reason: Latent world model planning acceleration via rollout compression; fits world models and token-level efficiency.
papers.title: SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
papers.tldr: SOAR accelerates latent-world-model planning by adaptively compressing rollouts while preserving candidate-action rankings.

papers.abstract: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.
authors: Gautam Kumar Jain, Atharva Mahindrakar, Shubham Phoolari, Ignacio Alvarez, Carsten Markgraf, Constanze Hungar, Christoph Lauer, Julian Staehler
bullets: Learned scene facts did not measurably improve two tested planner components, despite better fact accuracy after fine-tuning.
A rule-based checker rejects or shortens paths that contradict stated facts, directly linking interventions to those facts.
On navhard, the checker gained 2.4 EPDMS points over the frozen planner; its advantage over a same-frame control was statistically uncertain.
Using exact map and annotation facts produced a statistically supported 3.6-point margin over its control.
A fact-independent path scorer and plan memory improved navhard from 41.2 to 51.8; fact-based distance bounding added 0.3 there but reduced navtest by 2.0.

papers.abstract: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are safe in every world of the belief, whatever the others do within their public types. Agents learn inside their types, which are built and checked one agent at a time and run without communication. We prove type soundness and team safety, give a synthesis that is sound and complete, build types from guards when worlds are infinite, and show that shields are a special case. All proofs are mechanised in Rocq. On nine benchmarks, no typed learner causes a safety violation, and task performance does not differ significantly from that of two recent multi-agent shielding methods. Where a contract-based method fails at five and ten agents, types for ten agents are built in under a second. In the two continuous benchmarks, Lagrangian learners cause thousands of violations in every training run.
authors: Lorenzo Bacchiani, Mario Bravetti, Giovanni Pau, Roberto Girau
bullets: Agents’ types track observation-based beliefs and allow only actions safe in every possible world and under all teammates’ permitted behaviors.
Types are constructed and checked one agent at a time, letting agents learn within safety-preserving protocols without communication.
The work proves type soundness and team safety, provides sound-and-complete synthesis, supports infinite worlds via guards, and subsumes shields as a special case.
All proofs are mechanised in Rocq; across nine benchmarks, typed learners caused no safety violations and matched two shielding methods in task performance.
Types scaled to ten agents in under a second where a contract-based method failed; Lagrangian learners produced thousands of violations in each continuous-benchmark training run.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning, directly relevant to learned control and safety in embodied agents.
papers.title: Learning Inside Types: Epistemic Typestates for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Epistemic typestates provide a formally verified, communication-free way to ensure safety in multi-agent reinforcement learning while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: Whole-body segmentation tools such as TotalSegmentator and MOOSE split more than 100 classes across five or six networks. The reason is memory. Standard 3D inference, as implemented in nnU-Net and MONAI, holds a logit for every class and voxel, on the working grid and again on the scanner's grid. For a median whole-body CT at 125 classes, that is 76 GB. We show that this memory wall lies in what inference materializes, not in the task, and remove it without approximation. Every step after the network is local along one axis, so its outputs can be streamed through a ring one patch thick. The classification head commutes with blending and resampling, so the ring carries the network's features instead of the class logits. Memory thus no longer grows with classes times volume, and the label map on the scanner's grid stays exact. This holds for any model with a pointwise affine head, without retraining. Many-class models, previously impractical, become deployable. One model trained on all classes matches or slightly exceeds the toolkits' five or six specialists in segmentation quality and runs 5.8-15x faster end to end, with 3.2-7.6x less RAM and under 8 GB of VRAM. We provide the method as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator and MOOSE. The code is part of nnU-Net (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet), and unified models for both toolkits will be released.
authors: Fabian Isensee, Jakob Wasserthal, Lalith Kumar Shiyam Sundar, Maximilian Rokuss, Moritz Langenberg, Constantin Ulrich Harsy, Stefan Michael Happold, Klaus H. Maier-Hein
bullets: Standard inference materializes per-class logits on multiple grids, causing extreme memory use for whole-body CT segmentation.
The method streams intermediate features through a one-patch ring instead of storing class logits, while preserving exact outputs.
It applies to models with a pointwise affine classification head and requires no retraining.
A single all-class model matches or slightly exceeds specialist-toolkit quality, runs 5.8–15× faster, and uses 3.2–7.6× less RAM with under 8 GB VRAM.
The approach is provided as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, and MOOSE.

Bottom row: ours blends F features in a ring (here r = 193), applies H per completed slice, and uses two slices of logits for R, then argmax, fused. Dashed arrow: B commutes with H (Proposition 1). papers.selection_reason: Streaming inference method that removes the memory wall for many-class 3D segmentation, directly relevant to memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Segment Everything, Materialize Nothing: Exact Streaming Inference for Many-Class 3D Segmentation
papers.tldr: An exact streaming inference method removes the class-dependent memory bottleneck in many-class 3D segmentation, enabling one unified model to run substantially faster with much lower memory.

papers.abstract: Public benchmarks guide model selection, post-training rewards and claims of progress in artificial intelligence, yet leaderboards report aggregate scores without verifying whether each task's prompt, environment and grader agree on what counts as success. How often that agreement fails in contemporary evaluations, and in which direction confirmed defects move scores, has remained unmeasured across grading designs. Here we synthesize task-level quality reviews of 749 tasks across eight frontier benchmarks and 767 public model evaluations spanning closed-form question answering, document rubrics and agentic execution to assess whether prompts, environments and graders align. Task validity stratifies sharply by grading architecture. Closed-form benchmarks revised after public error reporting reach 92.5% verified validity, compared with 29.3% across six multi-step suites that nevertheless already supply 161 verified complex tasks. Rubric suites fail through mismatches between prompts and reference checklists, whereas execution harnesses add incomplete state assertions, shared-channel leaks and grading-time collisions. Across confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions while 28.3% permit shortcut passes, indicating that raw leaderboard ceilings understate frontier capability on many practical tasks. Grading committed patches inside a fresh container cuts confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% in shared containers to 2.7% (a 5.5x drop, and 0% in read-only or static suites), showing how targeted maintenance restores existing benchmarks at low cost. As the initial milestone of the long-term Benchmarks' Last Exam initiative, this synthesis launches sustained expansion across wider benchmark coverage and deeper evaluation-quality dimensions so that pursuing leaderboard gains directly advances genuine model capability.
authors: James Zhu, Zekki Cat
bullets: Task validity varies sharply by grading design: revised closed-form benchmarks reached 92.5% verified validity, versus 29.3% across six multi-step suites.
Rubric evaluations commonly mismatch prompts with reference checklists; agentic harnesses add incomplete state checks, shared-channel leaks, and grading-time collisions.
Among confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions, while 28.3% enable shortcut passes.
Using fresh containers for grading cut confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% to 2.7%; read-only or static suites recorded none.
The initiative provides an initial synthesis and plans broader coverage and deeper evaluation-quality analysis.

papers.abstract: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

papers.abstract: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

papers.abstract: We introduce Tasklets, a benchmark of small synthetic tasks for evaluating the computational capabilities of language model sequence-mixing layers. These tasks probe foundational capabilities such as recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking. Such tasks are widely used in architecture research, but differences in task selection, formulation, and evaluation make comparisons across studies difficult. Tasklets brings these tasks together, organizing them by the capabilities they test and providing a shared setup for evaluating how different architectural layer types learn fundamental computations. We compare a broad range of layer types through controlled experiments with small models. Our task implementations and evaluation code support reproducible, low-cost testing of new architectural proposals: https://github.com/zaydzuhri/flame/tree/tasklets.

papers.abstract: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $\delta$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.

papers.abstract: When interacting with objects of unknown physical properties, humans sometimes probe, over-exert, stagger, and adjust through iterative adaptation instead of succeeding immediately. We argue that this process is an expressive but largely overlooked aspect of human-object interaction in motion synthesis. Both kinematic data-driven methods and physics-based controllers tend to produce flawlessly executed motions: the former lack sufficient data for learning fine-grained adaptation, while the latter use reinforcement learning (RL) and privileged object dynamics to learn robust, deterministic behaviors. We propose ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), a test-time latent adaptation framework built on an RL-trained physics-based control policy. During policy training, we encode diverse object dynamics contexts into a structured latent space. At test time, Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) iteratively optimizes the latent code for an object with unknown physical properties. Temporary mismatches between this code and the true object dynamics produce an expressive progression from tentative, error-prone trials to proficient interaction. Adaptation behaviors inevitably come with occasional failures, so a high-level planner is introduced to handle failed cases to maintain full, consistent animations. We demonstrate our framework's effectiveness on a large-object transportation task, where such adaptation is especially pronounced. To train our framework, we introduce a mass-diverse object dataset with rich physical-property annotations. Across carrying and push-pull, our method pairs over 90% success with markedly higher posture diversity, and is rated the most lifelike in our user study on animation liveliness.

papers.abstract: Online batch selection lowers the cost of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by replacing each candidate batch with a smaller informative subset. Existing selectors typically depend on a held-out validation or proxy set, or else rely on Euclidean facility-location objectives over unpreconditioned gradients whose diameter-shifted similarities are distorted by heavy-tailed gradient norms and cross-layer anisotropy. We introduce PRISM (Preconditioned Ray-Isotropic Submodular Matching), a validation-free online batch selector that aligns candidate gradients in a factored second-moment metric and casts subset construction as conic facility location over positive ray projections. Computing the required pairwise geometry through factored preconditioned ghost inner products avoids materializing per-example parameter gradients, while the conic objective remains normalized, nonnegative, and monotone submodular---guaranteeing a $(1-1/e)$ greedy approximation whose additive error scales with total batch gradient energy rather than the worst-case outlier diameter. Assigning each candidate to its best-aligned selected ray induces closed-form radial projection weights that automatically shrink orthogonal or noisy examples toward zero. We derive a nonconvex convergence bound showing that optimization error is governed directly by the conic representation cost. Across four LLM fine-tuning configurations spanning 1.5B to 8B parameters, PRISM outperforms full-batch training, Euclidean facility location, and zeroth-order selectors, and rivals or surpasses validation-guided baselines without held-out data.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn language model agents often receive only a single binary reward at the end of a long interaction trajectory, making it difficult to separate decisive decisions from routine steps or estimate accurate intermediate values. Prefix-tree methods improve sample efficiency by merging trajectories that share action histories, yet two structural flaws remain: naive pooling mixes stale off-policy outcomes into critic targets with fixed weights, and uniform or entropy-driven branching wastes continuations on dead-end states whose outcome is already settled. We introduce WEIR (Watershed Exploration and Intrinsic-Drift Shrinkage), an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework grounded in a Doob turn-variance conservation identity. WEIR maintains a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with exponentially discounted visit counts and trains a prefix-conditioned critic toward a minimax drift-aware shrinkage target that adapts from single-trajectory returns at rare nodes to pooled empirical means at dense nodes. Using the same pre-update critic, WEIR allocates rollout budgets across tasks via Neyman stratification $B_q \propto \sqrt{\hat{p}_q(1-\hat{p}_q)}$ and directs within-task branches to watershed forks where high survival-headroom uncertainty coincides with steep value cliffs. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, ALFWorld, and WebShop on Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, WEIR achieves $32.18\%$ and $37.85\%$ average QA exact match and $84.83\%$ and $87.81\%$ ALFWorld success rates, outperforming CAPO by $1.50$--$3.74$ points while generating $28$--$29\%$ fewer rollout tokens than chain sampling.
authors: Pixel Nomand, Elena Voss, Marcus Hale, Sofia Reyes
bullets: Addresses sparse end-of-trajectory rewards and inefficient exploration in long agent interactions.
Builds a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with discounted visits and a prefix-conditioned critic.
Uses adaptive shrinkage targets that interpolate between individual returns at rare prefixes and pooled means at dense prefixes.
Allocates budgets by task uncertainty and explores watershed forks with high survival uncertainty and sharp value changes.
Across QA, ALFWorld, and WebShop, reports improved performance over CAPO while using 28–29% fewer rollout tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WEIR. (I) Completed trajectories are canonicalized by ordered actions into a persistent prefix tree Tq with exponentially discounted counts Ñ (k) u , producing minimax drift-shrinkage targets yτ,t. (II) The pre-update critic V̄k scores trunk prefixes to assign task budgets via Neyman stratification Bq ∝ √ p̂q(1− p̂q) and selects branch points at watershed forks combining survival uncertainty and value cliffs. (III) The prefix critic Vϕ fits yτ,t while the actor πθ optimizes a turn-aligned, task-balanced clipped surrogate using turn-level GAE.

papers.title: WEIR: Watershed Exploration and Drift-Aware Prefix Shrinkage for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: WEIR improves multi-turn agent reinforcement learning by combining drift-aware prefix-value estimation with uncertainty-guided rollout allocation, achieving stronger task performance with fewer rollout tokens.

papers.abstract: Serving engines treat the ways of running a greedy language model as interchangeable: cached or not, padded or not, alone or batched, one token or several verified at once (speculative decoding). In finite precision they round differently. We measure how often the greedy text of Qwen3-0.6B (bfloat16, 128 new tokens, GSM8K and ARC prompts) differs from a reference that decodes one token per pass. Verifying 4 guessed tokens per pass changes 60% of 150 prompts and padding changes 68%; every first divergence has a top-1 minus top-2 logit gap of 0.375 or less. A split of the noise shows that cache entries written by multi-token passes are about as noisy as the multi-token pass itself. A margin gate (fall back to one token when the gap is below a bound calibrated on separate GSM8K prompts) whose fallback reads that cache does not help: 58 of 100 prompts differ, against 61 of 100 for plain verification. Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes leaves 0 of 100 different but costs 7.2 model passes per token, against 1.0 for the reference. Fixed-width decoding makes drafted and plain decoding identical (0 of 100 prompts differ) at 0.75 passes per token. On shifted MMLU and HellaSwag prompts the rebuild gate leaves 0 of 60 different, plain verification 48 of 60. On 138 further and shifted prompts the bound was exceeded at 0.6% of positions and missed 0 of 309 flips. One GPU, one drafter, small models.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Navin Kumar R
bullets: Multi-token verification changed outputs on 60% of prompts, while padding changed 68%; divergences occurred only when the top-1/top-2 logit margin was at most 0.375.
Cache entries written during multi-token passes were a comparable source of noise to the passes themselves.
A margin-based fallback that reused the noisy cache barely helped: 58/100 prompts differed versus 61/100 with plain verification.
Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes eliminated observed differences, but increased cost to 7.2 model passes per token versus 1.0 for the reference.
Fixed-width decoding matched plain decoding on all tested prompts at 0.75 passes per token; scope was limited to one GPU, one drafter, and small models.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes rounding noise and cache effects in speculative decoding for LLM inference, directly contributing to efficient inference and cache management.
papers.title: Vega-Fafnir: Is Greedy Decoding the Same Decoding? Where Rounding Noise in Speculative Verification Comes From and What Removing It Costs
papers.tldr: Finite-precision rounding makes supposedly equivalent greedy and speculative decoding produce different text, but fixed-width decoding removes the mismatch more efficiently than rebuilding the cache.

papers.abstract: General-purpose whole-body trackers can execute diverse humanoid motions, but they require dense reference trajectories. However, tasks usually specify only where, in which posture, and when the robot should arrive, leaving the motion in between to a separate planner. Inspired by human motor coordination, our key idea is that a low-level controller can organize the intervening motion and its pace by itself from sparse goals with arrival times. In this paper, we propose S-BFM, a novel behavioral foundation model superior in its autonomy: it generates whole-body transitions from target postures, poses, and arrival times alone. Specifically, we first introduce Spatial Grounding, which adds world-frame position and heading to a forward-backward behavior representation through spatial reconstruction. Then, Time-Conditioned Distillation is designed to learn transitions and pace from real motion through closed-loop imitation of a dense-reference teacher. Lastly, Generative Fine-Tuning is introduced to broaden the covered distances and arrival times with a distilled motion generator. In simulation, S-BFM lowers global joint-position error by over 32% relative to the best baseline under fixed and mixed horizons, and raises fixed-goal reach from 43.5% to 74.6% while cutting terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m. We further deploy S-BFM on the full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid. Sparse spatiotemporal goals thus suffice for natural, well-timed whole-body motion.
authors: Kun Yang, Xuanyu Chen, Jing Tan, Yanjing Liu, Yubo Zhao, Renjing Xu, Addison Lin Wang
bullets: Addresses the need for autonomous motion generation when tasks provide only sparse spatial and temporal goals.
Uses Spatial Grounding to incorporate world-frame position and heading into behavior representations.
Applies Time-Conditioned Distillation to learn transitions and motion pacing from a dense-reference teacher.
Uses Generative Fine-Tuning to extend the range of achievable distances and arrival times.

In simulation, reduces global joint-position error by over 32%, improves fixed-goal reach from 43.5% to 74.6%, and lowers terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m; it is also deployed on the full-size AGIBOT A3.

papers.abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question in one pass: each option has a name and a written description. A new skill costs a training run, so we test whether published recipes for merging fine-tuned models (weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE) work for it, and whether the theories behind them hold. All 156 models start from one released checkpoint: four plain fine-tunes, five specialists (each adds one kind of training row), joint fine-tunes on all rows, and prediction ensembles. Items are held-out, synthetic and LLM-labelled. In-family, each skill is scored on new items of its own kind, and "kept" is the share of a specialist's gain over the plain fine-tune. Averaging four specialists keeps 52% [38, 64] with +1.7 points of general accuracy; adding the full vectors keeps 42% [3, 63] with -9.0; TIES, which trims and resolves sign conflicts, keeps 64% [50, 76] with +1.5; joint fine-tunes, which see all the rows, keep 120% [104, 162] and 116% [104, 149]. DARE does not repair the full sum (-0.4 points), and ensembles of the models' predictions keep 26% to 54% depending on how they are combined. Swapping the seed of one specialist moves the average by up to 8 points (23 for the full sum). Of 10 predictions fixed in advance, 1 held, 1 held partly, 7 failed and 1 could not be tested. Out-of-family (benchmark questions, code-mixed tickets), the four-way average, joint models and ensemble stay within 2.6 points of the plain fine-tune, but full-vector sums lose up to 7.7. Labels are LLM-made, data synthetic, one base model.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Navin Kumar R, Akhil P
bullets: The study tests weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE, joint training, and prediction ensembling across 156 models sharing one base checkpoint.
Averaging four specialists retains 52% of their gains and improves general accuracy by 1.7 points; TIES retains 64% with a 1.5-point gain.
Full task-vector addition performs poorly, losing 9.0 accuracy points; DARE does not repair it, and prediction ensembles retain 26–54% of specialist gains.
Joint fine-tuning on all training rows retains 116–120% of specialist gains, outperforming merging methods.
Results are sensitive to random seeds, and external validity is limited by synthetic, LLM-generated data and a single base model.

papers.abstract: Gameplay videos are a rich source of experience for learning virtual-world dynamics, yet their frames contain heads-up displays (HUDs) that follow interface rules rather than scene dynamics. Removing HUDs would make this footage directly usable for learning world dynamics. However, training a removal model requires paired clips with and without HUDs, whereas real recordings contain only HUD-overlaid footage. Existing work synthesizes pairs by compositing HUD graphics onto HUD-free footage, requiring a separately curated clean corpus and producing HUDs that only approximate real ones. Models trained on such pairs leave 40 to 50% of real HUD elements untouched. We instead recover pseudo-clean targets directly from real recordings by inpainting HUD regions with a pretrained video diffusion model. Preventing HUD traces from leaking into recovered targets is challenging because latent video autoencoders mix information across mask boundaries. Our training-free recovery pipeline, GameScrub-Data, pre-fills HUD regions with flow-guided background estimates before encoding, excludes HUDs from scene conditioning, and confines restoration to masked regions through pixel-space compositing. The resulting pairs train GameScrub, a video diffusion removal model that handles diverse HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images. On the in-the-wild Game2World benchmark, GameScrub achieves an artifact-adjusted removal score of 71.95, compared with 57.86 for the strongest reference-free GameCleaner configuration, and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%. These results demonstrate that real recordings with recovered targets can support effective HUD removal, advancing HUD-free gameplay data for world models and controllable video generation.
authors: Mohammad Areeb Qazi, Yiyan Hu, Yanan Wang, Xuezhi Liang, Xin Li, Fan Yang, Xin Gao, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Real gameplay is valuable for world-model learning, but HUD overlays obscure scene dynamics and lack clean paired training data.
GameScrub-Data recovers HUD-free targets using flow-guided pre-filling, HUD-excluded conditioning, and masked pixel-space compositing.
The resulting video diffusion model removes HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images.
On the Game2World benchmark, it scores 71.95 artifact-adjusted removal versus 57.86 for GameCleaner and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%.
The approach is scoped to improving HUD-free gameplay data for world modeling and controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.
authors: Xu Yuan, Liangbo Ning, Yujuan Ding, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan
bullets: Targets the loss of local multimodal evidence and high overhead in text-centric and earlier Vision-RAG systems.
Builds semantically complete regions with Content-Adaptive Regionalization.
Represents each page with local region vectors plus a global vector, trained using multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning.
Uses late-interaction matching to estimate region relevance, then rearranges selected regions into a compact visual context.
Across five benchmarks, it improves retrieval and generation over corresponding baselines while reducing visual tokens and computation.

papers.abstract: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.
authors: Jan Miko{\l}ajczyk, Igor Rostkowski, Bartosz Og\'orkiewicz, Szymon Skierski, Sylwia Opat, Wojciech Rybak, Miko{\l}aj Sczogiel, Rados{\l}aw Pa{\l}ys, Jan Gogulski, Bartosz Ko\'scio{\l}ek, Andrzej Pijanowski, Szymon Kowalski, Marcin Misiewicz
bullets: TDMA communication delay grows with swarm size and causes collisions through stale neighbor estimates at the safety filter.
Without delay, up to 100-agent swarms remain collision-free; delays beyond roughly 125–175 ms, or 75–100 ms with held measurement noise at 100 agents, can break safety.
At the mean-field layer, delay mainly increases density noise and reduces throughput by at most about one tenth, without biasing local density.
Lightweight neighbor-position predictors restore safety and extend tolerated communication periods by about 1.4–2.3×, depending on predictor and noise conditions.
Prediction should be enabled only beyond the uncompensated safety limit, because its estimation errors can otherwise introduce collisions; widening safety margins performs worse in bottlenecks.

papers.title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter

papers.abstract: Reliable comparisons of continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) require evaluating both model fit and the distribution of generated text. Two common practices leave this goal only partially addressed. Likelihood-based evaluation often reports a variational upper bound on discrete negative log-likelihood, whose slack can confound comparisons. Generated-sample-based evaluation commonly combines generative perplexity with within-sequence unigram entropy; both scores can remain favorable even when a sampler produces the same text on every draw. We introduce \textbf{Open CDLM}, a benchmark for evaluating CDLMs and their samplers, and describe the design of an accompanying open-source library to support reproducible comparisons. For likelihood-based evaluation, we clarify which comparisons of model fit are supported by reported perplexity bounds and how those conclusions depend on the evaluation procedure. For sample-based evaluation, we use \textit{Kernel Text Discrepancy} (\textbf{KTD}) to compare collections of generated and real texts, alongside diagnostics for diversity, validity, and coverage. In controlled OpenWebText experiments, replacing a collection of texts with copies of a single selected passage improves both conventional generation scores. MAUVE detects the resulting collapse, and its response to other perturbations depends on the text representation and the type of perturbation. This work marks the beginning of Open CDLM as an open-source project for CDLM research. We will maintain and extend the library over time and welcome contributions from the community.
authors: Hao Jiang, Ruixi Chen, Jiayi Han, Yulei Sun, Yujian Chen, Gen Li, Brian. K Chen, Guang Cheng, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Highlights that variational perplexity bounds may obscure reliable model-fit comparisons.
Shows that generative perplexity and within-sequence unigram entropy can reward collapsed samplers producing the same text repeatedly.
Uses Kernel Text Discrepancy (KTD) with diversity, validity, and coverage diagnostics to compare generated and real text collections.

In controlled OpenWebText experiments, conventional generation scores improved under single-passage copying, while MAUVE detected the resulting collapse; its sensitivity varied by representation and perturbation.
Positions Open CDLM as an extensible project for reproducible CDLM and sampler comparisons.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.

Achieves mean AUROC 0.890 for classification and mean quadratic weighted kappa 0.530 for severity grading across 10 unseen external datasets.
Supports detection, severity grading, measurement estimation and cardiac-structure segmentation across 62 clinical findings.

papers.abstract: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.
authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Liuxuan Sun, Zheyuan Lai, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of quality-labeled alternative trajectories in single-trajectory human driving logs.
Generates alternatives by smoothly deforming logged trajectories and scoring their simulated execution against traffic.
Uses scored alternatives to supervise proposal generation, residual-flow refinement, and trajectory-quality scoring.
A shared JEPA-based video encoder provides temporal context for refinement and scoring without costly online vision-language-model conditioning.

Ranks first among compared NAVSIM-only planners; DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art compared results on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, with 73% lower mean forward-pass latency than ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

papers.abstract: We present Ego4Gen (Egocentric 4D Future Generation), a world model for 4D future generation in robotic manipu lation. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly generates temporally aligned RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow, explicitly pre dicting the evolution of scene appearance, spatial struc ture, and motion. Built on Cosmos3-Nano, Ego4Gen ex tends the pretrained generative backbone through modality routed LoRA and asymmetric attention, using geometric pseudo-labels from MotionCrafter to learn to predict future geometry and motion latents. These latents can either be decoded into explicit 3D structure and motion or mapped to robot actions. To this end, we also introduce FlowIn verse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network trained in two stages to translate predicted 4D latents into robot ac tions. Experiments show that these geometry and motion latents outperform the evaluated latent-action and video latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings. Closed loop policy evaluations further demonstrate their utility for translating predicted 4D futures into robot control. To gether, these results support geometry-grounded motion to kens as a world-action interface, connecting 4D future gen eration with robotic manipulation and suggesting a path to ward reduced reliance on action-labeled data.
authors: Yang Liu, Chao Ye, Jiahao Zhang, Zeyuan Hou, Ruijie Fang, Xiyin Ni, Xinyang Ren, Weiyang Lin
bullets: Targets 4D future generation for robotic manipulation while modeling scene appearance, structure, and motion jointly.
Extends Cosmos3-Nano with modality-routed LoRA, asymmetric attention, and MotionCrafter-derived geometric pseudo-labels.
Introduces FlowInverse, a lightweight two-stage inverse-dynamics network that maps predicted 4D latents to robot actions.
Geometry and motion latents outperform evaluated latent-action and video-latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings.
Closed-loop policy evaluations demonstrate that the predicted futures can support robot control and reduce reliance on action-labeled data.

papers.abstract: Byte-level BPE vocabularies retain 256 single-byte fallback tokens. When converting such a model into a pure byte-level model, these tokens provide the starting embeddings. How much training have they received? We estimate byte-token exposure in Qwen3.8 using two independent routes. First, we tokenize 540 MB of public corpora covering 40 domains and 33 languages, then combine per-domain token shares with assumed pretraining mixtures. Single-byte tokens account for 13 to 36% of tokens, mostly ASCII; genuine UTF-8 fallback bytes (0x80-0xFF) account for 0.15 to 0.27% under mainstream mixtures, or about 2 billion occurrences per trillion pretraining tokens. Fallback rates vary by four orders of magnitude across languages, reflecting how well each script is covered by the vocabulary. Second, we analyze embedding and output-matrix row norms for four open models, using untrained padding rows as a zero-exposure baseline and ordinary tokens with known frequencies for calibration. In all four models, the 13 bytes that cannot occur in valid UTF-8 remain at initialization, while every legal high byte lies in a high-frequency band. For Qwen3.8, the norm-based estimate agrees with the corpus estimate within a factor of four. The norm-frequency relation eventually folds, so inversion is useful only as a model-specific, order-of-magnitude estimate. No private data were used.
authors: Liwei Zhang, ZhiMing Tong, Mochen Guan, Linzhe Li
bullets: Analyzes Qwen3.8 using 540 MB of public text spanning 40 domains and 33 languages.
Single-byte tokens comprise 13–36% of tokens, while genuine high-byte UTF-8 fallbacks comprise 0.15–0.27% under mainstream mixtures.
Fallback frequency varies by four orders of magnitude across languages, depending on vocabulary coverage of each script.
Embedding and output-matrix norms provide estimates consistent with corpus-based estimates within a factor of four for Qwen3.8.
Norm-based inversion is model-specific and only reliable at order-of-magnitude precision because the norm–frequency relation eventually folds.

papers.selection_reason: Estimates byte-token exposure in BPE pretraining; relevant to LLM tokenization and pretraining analysis.
papers.title: How Many Bytes Has a BPE Model Seen? Estimating Byte-Token Exposure in Pretraining from Corpus Statistics and Embedding Norms
papers.tldr: The study estimates how often byte fallback tokens are encountered during BPE pretraining, finding that legal UTF-8 fallback bytes are rare but measurable and can be approximated from corpus statistics or embedding norms.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.
authors: Guangzhao Dai, Guoxin Lian, Shuo Wang, Shengbin Yue, Qianru Sun, Xiangbo Shu, Bin Zhu
bullets: Addresses the dependence of VLN performance on manually designed tools, memory, and agent roles.
Collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, then uses a designer agent to revise and retain effective harnesses across iterations.
Uses privileged simulator diagnostics only for harness design, while the navigating LLM operates with a single RGB camera and primitive actions.
Reports consistent gains across LLMs from four vendors, including an 85.64% success rate on R2R-CE val-unseen with GPT-6-Astra.
Shows generalization to RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot.

papers.title: NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. Moreover, an initial preference for refusal does not necessarily translate into sustained refusal behavior throughout generation. Together, these findings reveal a critical gap between recognizing harmful requests and consistently refusing to fulfill them. To address this gap, we introduce SAFEHOLD, a novel provider-enforced defense framework that preserves safety alignment during harmful fine-tuning by treating refusal as a sustained generation process rather than a single response decision. Specifically, SAFEHOLD preserves the aligned model's full-vocabulary response distribution at the initial generation position through decision-boundary anchoring, while supervising the complete refusal sequence through refusal-path reinforcement. We conduct extensive experiments evaluating safety, utility, and internal mechanisms. SAFEHOLD reduces average ASR by 72.03 percentage points relative to undefended fine-tuning, outperforming five SOTA defenses by 24.32 to 70.87 percentage points. Meanwhile, it improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 percentage points over undefended fine-tuning, while maintaining an average XSTest over-refusal rate of only 2.73 percent. Overall, these results demonstrate that SAFEHOLD effectively mitigates safety degradation during harmful fine-tuning while preserving benign-task utility.
authors: Miaoqing Tian, Ruohan Li, Qian Lu, Haipeng Qu
bullets: Fine-tuning on untrusted data can make safety-aligned code models comply with harmful requests, even when harmfulness remains detectable internally.
Refusal is not reliably sustained throughout generation; recognizing harm and consistently refusing are distinct capabilities.
SAFEHOLD uses decision-boundary anchoring to preserve the aligned model’s initial response distribution and refusal-path reinforcement to supervise complete refusals.
It reduces average attack success rate by 72.03 percentage points versus undefended fine-tuning and outperforms five compared defenses.
The method also improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 points, with a 2.73% average XSTest over-refusal rate.

papers.abstract: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.
authors: Jonathan von Rad, Pontus Stenetorp, Yao Lu
bullets: Studies how tokenizer vocabulary allocation shapes multilingual representations during pretraining.
Pretrains 39 mono- and bilingual decoder-only models across English, German, French, Arabic, and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer.
Improved allocation raises alignment in early-to-mid layers and increases cross-lingual knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons.

Cross-script transfer remains lower even with fair vocabulary allocation, suggesting the script barrier is not solely a tokenizer artifact.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive inference in large transformer models is limited by token-level sequential execution, resulting in high latency and low GPU utilization. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this bottleneck by introducing a draft-and-verifier model. However, the drafting stage remains sequential, leaving the verifier idle and underutilizing compute. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play drafting adaptive drafting method that parallelizes inference across transformer layers during draft generation. Starting from a shared hidden state, our approach evaluates multiple layers in parallel and verifies consistency by measuring divergence in hidden-state space. Layer-wise draft states are accepted when deviations are small; otherwise, a correction step is applied. By exploiting redundancy across transformer layers, our method accelerates draft generation and improves hardware utilization without modifying architectures or requiring retraining. Experimental results on NLP tasks show that our method speeds up the drafting stage by up to $1.65\times$ with minimal degradation in accuracy, while maintaining the same performance as SD.
authors: Divya Jyoti Bajpai, Arun Verma, Manjesh Kumar Hanawal
bullets: Addresses sequential draft generation, which leaves the verifier idle and underutilizes GPUs.
Evaluates multiple transformer layers in parallel from a shared hidden state.
Accepts layer-wise drafts based on hidden-state divergence and corrects inconsistent states.
Requires no architecture changes or retraining and maintains the performance of speculative decoding.
Evaluated on NLP tasks, with up to 1.65× faster drafting and minimal accuracy degradation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Vanilla versus Adaptive Layer-parallel Drafting (ALD). Vanilla drafting executes layers sequentially, leaving parallel compute underutilized. ALD evaluates future layer transformations concurrently using proxy hidden states and adaptively controls their advancement through a similarity check, reducing drafting latency while preserving draft quality.

Figure 3: Effect of the similarity threshold τ on drafting speedup and draft-model quality, measured using BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L. Lower τ permits more aggressive layer-parallel proxy execution and increases speedup, while higher τ produces more conservative execution and better preserves draft quality. The default setting τ = 0.95 provides a favorable operating point between these objectives.
