papers.abstract: PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.
authors: Awais Naeem, Zhongling Xu, George Huang, Amy Coffey, Nkechi Okonkwo, Mario Saab-Chalhoub, John Lee Sang, Dina Kokh, Muhammad Zulfiqar, Ankita Shukla, Hairong Wang, Chandra Krishnan, Ying Ding
bullets: Includes 157 cases, 229 original images, and 6,870 augmented images spanning organ, pathology, anatomy, and magnification metadata.
Provides open-ended, five-option multiple-choice, and yes/no questions, with paired correct and incorrect answers for many open-ended items.
Uses ratings from five additional pathologists and two vision-language-model judges to assess item quality.
Offers balanced metadata-based manifests for subgroup evaluation and paired answers for constructing preference examples.
Six models were evaluated zero-shot across all three question formats, without reported comparative performance in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PathOPEN construction and evaluation. Two clinical pathologists collected 157 cases and authored open-ended, multiple-choice (MCQ) and yes/no questions. The example shows one original image, its MCQ with the correct answer and one of four distractors, and four augmentations of the same image. The listed transformations are examples from the augmentation pool. Applying 30 augmentations per available original image yielded 6,870 derived images from 229 originals. Derived images inherit their source questions, answers and metadata. The PathOPEN dataset includes these records and four balanced manifests that select existing augmentations separately for each metadata field. Selections can overlap. Original records and comparator datasets enter the relevant evaluations. Benchmark 4 uses a separate evaluation set of 174 augmented images (Section 2.6.3). Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model (VLM) judges score items using rubrics. Six answering models respond zero-shot across the three question formats. Table 1 gives the dataset and rater scope for each rubric benchmark.

Figure 2: Composition of the PathOPEN metadata. a, b, Case counts by organ system and categorization. c, Counts of the 229 available original images by magnification. d, The fourteen most frequent regional anatomy classes shown in the plot, with 110 cases across the remaining 97 classes. e, Question–answer composition by item type. f, Magnification co-occurrence within cases: diagonal cells count cases with only that magnification, and off-diagonal cells count cases with both magnifications. g, Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients for all four metadata fields, including every class; the diagonal represents equal class proportions. h, Case counts for the 13 most frequent organ systems and 8 most frequent categories. The displayed cells contain 134 of 157 cases, and 41 of the 104 combinations are observed. Grey marks combinations with zero cases. Panel g uses case-level weighting for magnification (Supplementary Note 2). Axis labels use abbreviated display forms where needed; Supplementary Table S7 maps them to the full stored values.

Figure 7: Zero-shot answering across datasets, formats and metadata strata. a–c, Per-model MCQ accuracy, close-ended accuracy and open-ended BERTScore F1. Dashed lines mark dataset-specific MCQ chance levels (2–16 options) and the 50% close-ended chance level. BERTScore F1 is rescaled so that zero denotes similarity no greater than unrelated text; filtered PathVQA falls below zero for two of six models. d, Model ranks within each format (1 = best). Table 8 gives the Spearman rank correlations. e, Kruskal–Wallis H for performance by magnification, for each model and format; 2 of 18 tests reach uncorrected P < 0.05. f–k, Performance by magnification (left) and organ system (right) for MCQ (f, g), close-ended (h, i) and open-ended questions (j, k). Item counts are printed per bin, with counts below n = 30 in red. The comparator records used here lack this metadata. a and b show bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; c shows point estimates. Open-ended results in d, e, j and k use token F1 (Section 2.7.2). Section 4.4 gives the rank and magnification tests and their interpretation. Table 7 reports pooled comparisons.

Figure 5: Wrong-answer difficulty tiers, judge agreement and distractor attraction. a, Pathologist-assigned tiers for native open-ended answers and multiple-choice question (MCQ) distractors. Both Benchmark 2 criteria are pooled. The denominators are 668 native and 1,773 MCQ score pairs with a tier from both the pathologist and Qwen. b, Confusion matrices for Error Proximity and Deductive Plausibility alone, with 1,248 InternVL and 1,221 Qwen score pairs across both answer types. Rows give the pathologist tier and columns the judge tier. Below the diagonal, the judge assigned a harder tier. c, Distractor attraction, measured as the percentage of offered distractors selected within each tier. Five of six models select near-miss distractors more often than far-miss distractors. Item-level accuracy, annotated in the panel, follows the expected direction for only 2 of 6 models. Benchmark 2 scores of 2, 1 and 0 define near-miss, moderate-miss and far-miss tiers; −1 has no tier. Section 4.2 and Table 6 give counts, agreement coefficients, full-pool results and the limits of the three-bin significance test.

Figure 3: Selection and text characteristics of the PathVQA comparator. a, Filtering stages. Images with more than 10 detected nuclei were retained as a proxy for H&E content. We then require at least five words for both the question and answer in open-ended pairs and for the question alone in close-ended pairs. The final subset has 612 open-ended and 3,005 close-ended pairs after applying the length filter. The length filter excludes 86% of open-ended pairs that passed image selection. b, Openended question and answer length distributions for raw PathVQA (dotted lines) and the image-filtered set (solid lines). c, Percentages of open-ended questions, open-ended answers and close-ended questions in three word-count bands (< 5, 5–9 and ≥ 10 words). H&E denotes the image-filtered set. Panels b and c compare the first two stages in a, before the length filter. Section 2.4 gives the filtering procedure and counts.

Figure 4: Ratings of pathology question–answer pairs. a, Word-count distributions for questions, correct answers and wrong answers; violins show the distributions and lines mark medians. Four asterisks denote P < 10−4 in two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests. Filtered PathVQA provides no matched openended wrong answers. b, Percentage of pathologist ratings scored −1 (unable to evaluate) per criterion. The PathOPEN denominators are 231 for each Benchmark 1 criterion and 230 for Benchmark 3. c, d, Rank-biserial effects against filtered PathVQA for Benchmarks 1 and 3, respectively. In c, the first native PathOPEN open-ended slot contributes 231 human ratings per criterion, against 624 reasoning and 622 grounding ratings for PathVQA. Each judge scored 229 versus 612 items. The historical PathVQA totals come from the Benchmark 1 score columns. These include 12 reasoning and 10 grounding scores recorded on close-ended rows (Section 2.6.2). In d, the human comparison uses 230 versus 50 items and each judge comparison uses 229 versus 50. e, Exact agreement, quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ and Gwet’s AC1 between the Qwen judge and the pathologist who rated each item. f, Effects against Quilt-VQA, with 229 versus 724 open-ended items and 229 versus 257 yes/no items per judge. g, Mean scores across disjoint pathologist pools: dots mark means, bars their ranges and adjacent values the spreads; n.s. denotes Kruskal–Wallis P ≥ 0.05. Effects have bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (2,000 resamples), with negative values indicating higher PathOPEN scores; the dashed line marks zero. Encoded −1 values remain in these summaries. Section 4.1 gives the denominators for pathologists and each judge.

Figure 6: Judge assessment of MCQ options and full-context answering. a, b, Mean Benchmark 5 scores by criterion and dataset for correct options (5a) and distractors (5b). Circles denote InternVL and diamonds Qwen; connectors show their score differences, colours identify datasets and whiskers show bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. The judges reverse their dataset ordering on both distractor criteria, so their results are shown separately. c, Standalone Completeness score distributions for InternVL. d, Zero-shot multiple-choice question (MCQ) accuracy with the image and all options present; dashed lines indicate dataset-specific chance levels for option counts from 2 to 16. e, f, Judge–judge quadratic-weighted κ for 5a and 5b, with separate scales. Benchmark 5 has no pathologist baseline: these coefficients measure agreement between the two judges. Short criterion labels in the panels refer to the full rubrics in Supplementary Tables S5 and S6. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 report the option assessments and full-context answering results, respectively.

Figure 8: Ratings of augmented images and class balance after selecting subsets. a, Benchmark 4 ratings from five pathologists and two judges. Dots show the percentage receiving the maximum score; grey bars show the remaining percentage, broken down by score at right. b, Visual Grounding ratings on augmented images (Benchmark 4) and originals (Benchmark 1), using unpaired pools and differently worded criteria. c, Largest-to-smallest class ratios before and after field-specific retention, on a logarithmic scale. d, Ranked class counts before retention (dashed) and after retention (solid), including the flat tail of retained rare classes. e, f, Gini coefficients and normalised Shannon entropy. Uniform 30× augmentation has the same class proportions as the originals and is omitted from these panels. g, h, Gini coefficients and selected image counts across the retention-cap sweep (Section 2.3.2). Colours identify metadata fields. The four manifests each select existing augmentation files for one field and may overlap. Section 4.5 gives the balance results; Table 9 reports augmented-image ratings and agreement.

Table 1: Evaluation design. Each row identifies the object receiving a rubric score. MCQ-derived correct and wrong answers are rated under Benchmarks 1 and 2 as open-ended records; Benchmark 5 separately assesses the options in their MCQ role. The full rubrics are in Supplementary Tables S1–S6.

Table 2: PathOPEN record counts for collected slots and available files. Each question applies to every image in its case. The collected counts include the image slots for cases 9 and 79, which retain their text and metadata. The available counts include only records linked to files. Augmented counts are 30 times the available original-image counts. MCQ denotes multiple-choice question. Pooled correct and wrong counts combine native open-ended answers with individual MCQ options. Section 3 describes the units and relationships.

Table 7: Pooled zero-shot performance across datasets. Means pool six answering models, treating each (model, item) pair as one observation in the Items column. Percentile bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) use 2,000 resamples of those observations. Multiple-choice question (MCQ) and close-ended accuracies are percentages; above-chance accuracy is a percentage-point difference from each dataset’s chance level. Open-ended scores are token F1 multiplied by 100, using the full reference set. Rank-biserial correlations are positive when the first named dataset tends to rank higher. For above-chance MCQ scores the tests compare the ranks of individual model–item scores after subtracting each item’s guessing baseline. The order of these ranks can differ from the order of the dataset means. Mann–Whitney U tests are Holm-corrected within format. The bootstrap treats repeated items and within-case observations as independent, so intervals may understate uncertainty from those dependencies (Sections 2.7.3 and 4.4).

Table 6: Judge and pathologist assignments of wrong-answer difficulty tiers. The upper and middle blocks use Error Proximity and Deductive Plausibility, with 1,248 InternVL and 1,221 Qwen score pairs. Both near-miss ratios use the pathologists’ frequency in the InternVL-matched pool as their denominator. The middle block gives each judge’s distribution conditional on the pathologist tier. The lower block summarises quadratic-weighted κ across both criteria and six answer slots per judge. By authoring route, OE-native denotes native open-ended wrong answers, and MCQ-derived denotes multiple-choice question distractors. Near, Moderate and Far abbreviate near-miss, moderate-miss and far-miss. Scores of −1 carry no tier. Section 4.2 describes the evaluation pools and agreement.

Table 9: Pathologist ratings and judge–pathologist agreement on augmented images. The upper block gives each pathologist’s mean score, maximum-score percentage and unscorable percentage under Benchmark 4; P1–P5 identify the five pathologists. Spread is the range of their means, and P is the Kruskal–Wallis test across their disjoint pools. These summaries retain encoded −1 values. The lower block gives exact agreement, quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and Gwet’s AC1 on shared judge–pathologist items. The three statistics describe agreement under the concentrated score distributions (Section 4.5).

Table 4: Unscorable-item rates across pathologist pools. Entries give the percentage of items scored −1 (unable to evaluate) by each pathologist (P1–P5). Range is the largest minus the smallest percentage, in percentage points; n−1 is the pooled count of unscorable ratings. B1 and B3 denote Benchmarks 1 and 3; their full criterion names are given in Supplementary Tables S1 and S3. The disjoint item pools combine rater and item-composition differences; −1 does not identify a single cause (Section 4.1).

Table 3: Answer ratings and unscorable items in PathOPEN and filtered PathVQA. Scores use {−1, 0, 1, 2}; −1 denotes inability to evaluate. Means, effects and per-pathologist summaries include −1 alongside scores for items that could be rated. Means and effects pool the five pathologists; maximumscore and unscorable percentages average their percentages. Effects are rank-biserial correlations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with negative values indicating higher PathOPEN scores. Rater spread is the range of pathologist means across disjoint pools. B1 and B3 denote Benchmarks 1 and 3. The shortened criterion labels refer to Knowledge Interpretation and Deduction and Visual Grounding (B1), and Visual Grounding/Reasoning (B3), as defined in Supplementary Tables S1 and S3. Historical PathVQA Benchmark 1 counts include entries recorded on close-ended rows (Section 2.6.2). Section 4.1 gives denominators and tests.

Table 5: Mean scores across pathologist pools. P1–P5 identify the five pathologists, each rating a disjoint item pool; n is the pooled rating count per criterion. Means and Kruskal–Wallis tests retain encoded −1 values (Section 2.7.3). Spread is the range of the five means; the test compares their score distributions, with n.s. denoting P ≥ 0.05. B1 and B3 denote Benchmarks 1 and 3, whose full criterion names appear in Supplementary Tables S1 and S3. These separate pools do not support per-item inter-rater coefficients (Section 4.1).

Table 8: Model rank correlations across question formats. Spearman correlations compare the six models’ mean performance on PathOPEN for each pair of formats. MCQ denotes multiple-choice question. None of the three observed correlations reaches P < 0.05; six-model estimates leave uncertainty about the relationship between rankings. Section 4.4 also reports the MCQ–open-ended correlation after averaging across datasets.

papers.selection_reason: Pathologist-curated VQA dataset with paired answer preferences; relevant to multimodal LLM training and evaluation.
papers.title: PathOPEN: A pathologist-curated histopathology dataset for visual question answering
papers.tldr: PathOPEN is a pathologist-curated histopathology visual question-answering dataset designed for clinically grounded evaluation and preference learning.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.
authors: Caoyuan Ma, Wendi Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Muyao Niu, Yujie Lu, Zengxi Zhang, Ji Zhao, Shuai Dong, Wenpu Liu, Ziyue Wang, Wenzheng Chang, Taiqiang Wu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Haiyuan Wan, Xuehui Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Wenqi Shao, Yinqiang Zheng
bullets: Links a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop with shared goals and evaluators.
Agents observe only workstation camera views and use either a single-arm probe or dual-arm dexterous hands.
Across five models and 40 tasks, desktop performance exceeded physical performance; hands generally outperformed the probe.
Trajectory analysis shows strategic adaptation toward keyboard input, but execution fails from missed presses, wrong targets, and unintended contacts.
The benchmark quantifies the gap between digital task competence and physical execution.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of ROSWORLD. The live OSWorld desktop is rendered on the simulated monitor. The model observes camera views and controls the robot to interact with the keyboard and mouse. Contact-generated input events are delivered to the VM, closing the physical–digital loop. Task success is scored by OSWorld’s official application-state evaluators.

Figure 8 Failure modes at the operation level. Rows are model and embodiment; an attempt is an executed step that intends an input. (a) Outcome of each attempt: the intended input arrives, nothing is pressed (miss), a neighbouring or wrong target is pressed, a body part other than the effector presses something, or other input arrives. (b) Input faults per attempt. (c) Share of key presses made by a robot part other than the effector, attributed from the simulator’s per-link contact forces; for the probe, presses with the tip more than 3 cm away or out of contact are assigned to the arm or probe shaft.

Figure 7 Operation-level failures in the robot’s own camera views. Dashed green marks the key the model planned; solid red marks what was pressed. (a) The probe rests on F1 but the key travels 1.4 mm, short of the 2 mm actuation point. (b) The probe lands between F10 and F9 and presses F9. (c) GLM-5.3-Flash moves its probe tip while the forearm lies on the keyboard and presses keys 35 times; its reply in the same step reports a “breakthrough” in arm tracking. (d) For Ctrl+U the left hand holds Ctrl, but the right hand strikes Y instead of U.
Figure 4 Successful model–task pairs by application domain.

Figure 3 Physical success against the share of input attempts that deliver the intended input (as in Figure 8a). Arrows go from the probe (open) to the hands (filled); the shaded band spans the GPT models.

Figure 6 Input mix on the desktop and through the robot. OSWorld bars count PyAutoGUI calls (terminal scripts folded into keys/typing); probe and hands bars count input events delivered by the physical devices. Chord : a modifier held together with another key; key collision: any other key overlap, e.g. neighbouring keys struck together. n: calls or events.

Figure 5 Does the OSWorld route survive physical execution? Each model’s OSWorld trajectory is aligned with its physical trajectory on the same 40 tasks. Keeps route: the operation is reproduced with the same input modality; switches modality : the same operation through another input; changes route: the physical run gets past the operation by other means; never reaches: the run ends before it.
Figure 9 GPT-6 Astra: successful tasks out of 40 by decision budget in OSWorld and with each embodiment. Curves are computed from recorded runs.

Figure 2 Robot-camera observations connect reading the display with locating the physical controls. The cameras show the screen and controls from oblique and top-down viewpoints, with occasional robot occlusion.

Table 1 ROSWorld against related benchmarks. We couple the digital computer-use tasks with embodiment evaluation. RealVM : tasks run inside a real VM with live desktop or web applications; Physical contact : a simulated or real robot physically interacts with the environment; Camera view : the screen is observed only through cameras; Embodiments: more than one robot embodiment. ✓: yes; ◦: partly; –: no.

Table 3 Successful tasks out of 40 (% in parentheses) in OSWorld and with the single-arm probe and dual-arm hands. Retained: tasks completed successfully in both OSWorld and the physical condition (probe / hands).

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for physical execution of computer tasks by robots, directly relevant to embodied AI.
papers.title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
papers.tldr: ROSWorld measures how much computer-use capability is lost when agents must physically operate a keyboard and mouse through a robot.

papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.
authors: Chuhan Jiao, John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Guy Rosman, Andreas Bulling
bullets: Addresses visual perspective taking beyond state estimation, reconstruction, and discrete question answering.
Uses backbone-agnostic geometric modules with scene coordinate maps, 3D ray-space token alignment, and visual-memory-based view completion.
Handles extreme viewpoint changes, dynamic occlusions, and sparse overlap between collaborators’ views.
Across three video diffusion backbones on CoMind, improves visual quality, scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion over prior cross-view generation methods.
Enables applications in human–robot collaboration and synchronized multi-perspective video generation for robot learning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Ego2Ego. Given the ego person’s egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and both camera trajectories, Ego2Ego generates the collaborator’s egocentric video with a pretrained video diffusion transformer equipped with three geometry-grounded modules. All conditions are encoded by the frozen VAE and form a single token sequence with the noisy collaborator latent. (1) Since the same surface appears entirely different from the two viewpoints and hands occlude the scene, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into every view, colouring each pixel by its 3D coordinate in a shared frame, so that the same scene point carries the same colour across views and provides a shared spatial reference. (2) To relate tokens across substantially different viewpoints, relative geometric attention aligns the geometric components of keys and values to each query token’s ray-aligned frame. (3) To recover regions the ego person does not currently observe, the ego person’s visual memory supplies past ego-person frames together with their renderings.
Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Two test examples, each at two time steps. For each baseline, we show the version with the higher PSNR in Tab. 1.

Figure 6. Counterfactual trajectories. Top: the collaborator stays outside the ego person’s view; rows show frames from the start, middle, and end of the clip. Bottom: the ego person observes the collaborator in the first row; the collaborator’s path is solid while the collaborator is observed and dashed afterwards, and the purple frustum shows the counterfactual orientation, rotated by 45◦ about the vertical axis from the real one (blue). In both examples, the ground-truth frames follow the real trajectory and are shown for comparison only; in the bottom example, the ground truth matches the counterfactual pose in the first row.
Figure 8. Qualitative results without visual memory. Four frames sampled across two test clips at the start of a recording session.
Figure 5. Additional qualitative comparison. Six test clips, each at two time steps (top and bottom rows). For each baseline, we show the version with the higher PSNR in Table 1 of the main paper.

Figure 4. Geometric conditions. Ego person and collaborator views of two test clips at the same time step. The collaborator’s RGB frame (GT) is shown only for reference. Black pixels are not covered by the point cloud. Scene coordinate colours are contrast-stretched for display with one linear map per clip.

Figure 7. Qualitative comparison with and without DGR at inference. (a) Both participants work side by side at the counter (overlapping views). (b) The ego person works at the cutting board while the collaborator washes at the sink (non-overlapping views).
Figure 9. Failure cases.

Table 1. Comparison to cross-view video generation methods on CoMind. CV: initialised from the cross-view pretraining released by the authors. Layout and Hand: Layout mIoU and Hand-mIoU. Bold: best; underlined: second best. †Released model, not fine-tuned. ‡Trained only without cross-view pretraining (Sec. 4.1).

Table 3. Ablations on the proposed modules. Starting from the base model, we add DGR, RGA, and the ego person’s visual memory one at a time. The last two rows replace the scene coordinate maps of the full model with sparse points or depth maps. Bold: best per backbone.

Table 5. Performance stratified by collaborator visibility in the ego person’s video. Test clips are grouped by the number of frames in which the collaborator’s head centre projects into the ego person’s view: never visible (0 frames, 46%), partly visible (1–24 frames, 34%), and mostly visible (≥ 25 of 49 frames, 20%). Bold: best; underlined: second best.
Table 2. Results by collaborator visibility in the ego person’s view (never: 0, partly: 1–24, mostly: ≥ 25 of 49 frames; see the supplementary material for all baselines and LPIPS).

Table 6. Inference with and without DGR. Comparison of the Plücker-conditioned base model, the full model evaluated with all scene coordinate maps zeroed at inference (Full model w/o DGR), and the full model with DGR across all three backbones. Bold: best per backbone.
Table 4. Plücker ray maps and motion term on Wan2.2-5B. Bold: better per block.

papers.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
papers.tldr: Ego2Ego generates a collaborator’s continuous egocentric video from another person’s video, shared scene geometry, and the collaborator’s camera trajectory.

papers.abstract: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.
authors: Zian Deng, Tianyi Zhang, Zilong Zheng, Ziyu Liu, Tao Zhang, Yao Lyu, Shengbo Eben Li
bullets: Motivation: Future visual prediction is often retained during training even though it is unnecessary at inference, adding cost and complexity.
Method: Fine-tunes an image-generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action-regression adapter while reusing the native generative objective for perception co-training.
Architecture: A shared image-editing interface supports current-scene perception, future prediction, and combinations without task-specific perception heads.
Results: Achieves 99.10% success on LIBERO, 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus, and strong robustness on real-world manipulation tasks.
Efficiency: Uses one backbone forward pass and reaches 20.9 ms per action chunk on an H100, with reported 1.7–3.4× speedups over VLA and WAM baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation and overview of GenPA. (a) Given a scene image, a manipulation instruction, and an editing request, GPT Image 2 visualizes a goal state or sketches end-effector paths in image space, illustrating the potential of image generation models for spatial understanding and visual planning (generation details in Appendix F). (b) GenPA jointly trains action prediction and perception with shared backbone weights and uses only the action path at deployment. The action regression adapter has 19M parameters in the LIBERO configuration.

Figure 2: Architecture of GenPA. (a) The action path extracts instruction-conditioned observation features from the image generation backbone. A lightweight regression adapter reads these features and predicts an action chunk conditioned on proprioception. (b) The perception path reuses the generator’s native image-editing interface to learn image-form perceptual targets with a rectifiedflow objective. The two paths use separate forward passes with shared backbone weights. Only the action path is used at inference.

Figure 4: Aligned LIBERO observations and supervision targets in agent and wrist views. D, N, P, S, and G denote current depth, normals, pointmaps, segmentation, and grounding. F and FD use RGB and depth from the same future frame. All panels show training data, not model predictions.
Figure 3: H100 action-chunk latency. Totals are timed separately; Vision and Backbone are jointly profiled for compiled π0.5.

Figure 6: Real-world setup and USB manipulation. (a) The robot platform and camera locations. (b) Example execution sequences under standard conditions, background perturbation, and lighting perturbation (top to bottom), progressing from left to right. The task is to unplug a USB connector from the left hub and insert it into the right hub.

Figure 7: Original scene and generated goal-state and motion-sketch images used in Figure 1(a).

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been associated with localized parameter regions, enabling targeted model editing and intervention. However, it remains unclear whether a region identified before model optimization remains an effective intervention target afterward. We evaluate the functional persistence and parameter overlap of coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA-based adaptation. Although re-extracted regions exhibit substantial parameter reorganization, ablating the original region after optimization eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions, while magnitude-matched controls preserve performance. Partition analysis further shows that the shared subset of the original and re-extracted regions accounts for most of the observed ablation effect in the majority of conditions. These results demonstrate that parameter overlap and functional persistence are distinct: capability regions can remain causally effective intervention targets even when their parameter realization changes substantially.
authors: Jiwoo Kum, Chanwoo Kim, Doyun Kim, Seonghyeon Cho, Sihyeon Lee, Chanjun Park
bullets: Studies coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA adaptation.
Re-extracted regions show substantial overlap changes with the original regions after optimization.
Ablating the original regions eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions.
Magnitude-matched controls generally preserve performance, supporting a region-specific effect.
Shared parameters between original and re-extracted regions explain most ablation effects in most conditions.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.
authors: Sihyeon Lee, Jiwoo Kum, Jihun Song, Chanwoo Kim, Chanjun Park
bullets: Studies prompts assigning two opposing personas with no priority rule across eight conflict types and five LLMs.
Models acknowledged incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but surfaced it in only 22% of task responses.
One persona dominated 45% of dual-persona responses; 35% of compromise-labeled responses still showed directional bias.
Prompt framing substantially changed arbitration’s visible form, more than ordinary paraphrasing.
The results motivate evaluations of conflict disclosure, resolution strategy, and favored persona.

papers.abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.
authors: GiHyun Kim, JinMo Yang, Hyung-Sin Kim
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between light collection and motion blur in robot-camera depth sensing.
Uses a frozen depth model and a learned predictor of reference-relative disagreement to score candidate camera settings without ground truth at deployment.
A contextual Gaussian-process controller selects subsequent exposure and gain using recent scores plus motion, camera, and illumination context.
Evaluated across nine scene-illumination conditions, it reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned Abs_rel by 14.6% versus built-in auto-exposure and 10.0% versus the best evaluated prior controller.
Demonstrates online control on a mobile robot with the affine-invariant Depth Anything v2 variant.

papers.abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (ORBIT), an algorithmic intervention that mitigates this collapse at inference time. ORBIT estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations, targeting the cross-lingual degradation induced by low-resource evidence. Experiments across 81 configurations reveal that ORBIT substantially recovers both accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings, exposes calibration offset norms as a diagnostic proxy, and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines.
authors: Huy Trieu, Duy-Minh Nguyen-Tran, Thanh-Dat Nguyen, Huy Tien Nguyen, Tung Le
bullets: Addresses the disproportionate cross-lingual accuracy collapse of small vision-language models on low-resource evidence.
Estimates offset vectors from parallel claim–evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations.
Evaluated across 81 configurations, ORBIT substantially improves low-resource accuracy and F1-score.
Calibration offset norms provide a diagnostic proxy for cross-lingual degradation.
Outperforms translation-based and other activation-steering baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.
authors: Kangyi Wu, Pengna Li, Yucheng Wang, Yance Fang, Xihan Ma, Zhizhong Su, Yang Wu, Ye Deng, Jinjun Wang, Jianyi Liu
bullets: VLN agents must plan beyond their current visual observation while following language instructions.
The paper argues that future representation should include goal-directed spatial states and route structure, inspired by predictive-map views of navigation.
FS-Nav predicts short-horizon waypoints and mid-horizon corridors from spatial memory and language instructions.
These future states are communicated to a vision-language navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces.
Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no further experimental details.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FS-Nav. The Future State World Model encodes the accumulated spatial memory and navigation instruction, fuses their geometry and language features, and predicts a short-horizon waypoint together with a mid-horizon corridor. The Future State Renderer deterministically renders the same prediction as either a top-down canvas or a first-person overlay. Conditioned on the instruction, observation history, and rendered guidance, the Future-State-Guided Navigator generates an action chunk and interacts with the environment in a closed loop. Flame symbols indicate trainable modules.

Figure 1: Motivation and key properties of future-state world model. (a) FS-Nav represents the upcoming route with a short-horizon waypoint and a mid-horizon corridor. (b) On a single RTX 4090, future-state prediction takes 66.7 ms, over 500× faster than generating a five-frame future observation with Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. (c) The waypoint and corridor each improve navigation performance, with their combination achieving the highest SR on R2R-CE validation unseen.

papers.abstract: We propose the three-dimensional Skyrme model as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods and construct fully three-dimensional Skyrmions with baryon number $B=1,\ldots,4$ without imposing a symmetry ansatz, with high precision. For $B=2,3,4$, the relaxation of these Skyrmions starts from $B$ unit-charge lumps with random positions and orientations, which carry no symmetry information. The known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic Skyrmions nevertheless emerge spontaneously. The resulting variational energies for $B=1,\ldots,4$ lie slightly below the published reference values. The neural method highlights the high accuracy for retaining the topological charge, differing from $B$ by at most $10^{-6}$ in the highest-precision solutions. Our numerical method goes through physical constraint tests such as the Derrick virial relation and the Faddeev--Bogomolny bound, together with evaluation / verification through independent quadratures and resolution sweeps. We then compare Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in more than a thousand training runs, both with and without a rational-map ansatz. With default settings, KANs appear markedly superior, but most of the gap disappears once the MLP activation function and learning rate are tuned. KANs remain more parameter-efficient and more robust at fixed epoch budget, while MLPs with the tuned activation function perform at least as well at fixed wall-clock time. We also argue that continuous gradient descent cannot smoothly change the topological sector of our neural field, clarifying the origin of topological freezing observed in our neural variational solvers. Our results on the neural methods applied to Skyrmions pave a research ground for AI-agentic benchmarks for classical topological solitons, toward AI-assisted soliton physics.
authors: Koji Hashimoto, Masaki Murata, Gakuto Ogiwara
bullets: Skyrmions with baryon numbers B=1–4 are obtained without imposing symmetry, with toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic structures emerging spontaneously.
The computed energies lie slightly below published reference values and satisfy virial, topological-bound, quadrature, and resolution checks.
Topological-charge errors are at most 10⁻⁶ in the highest-precision solutions, indicating strong charge preservation.
KANs outperform default MLPs and remain more parameter-efficient and robust under fixed epoch budgets; tuned MLPs match or exceed them at fixed wall-clock time.
The study attributes topological freezing to the inability of continuous gradient descent to smoothly change the neural field’s topological sector.

Boxes across the full width are for both tracks. Each box starts with its name in bold and gives the section that describes the step.

The blue dashed line and the yellow dotted line are 5000-epoch runs that start from random initial data and hold the far field at the vacuum through the far-field penalty. The blue dashed run measures B on r ≤ 60, and the yellow dotted run measures B on r ≤ 12. The horizontal axis counts the epochs of the energy minimisation, so the imprinting of the green run is not shown, and it ends at epoch 5000, where the two random-start runs end; in the rest of the green run B stays within 0.001 of 2. The vertical axis is cut at 2.25: the yellow dotted line leaves the frame at epoch 3983, where B reaches 17.2. The text explains the three runs.

All panels of a row use the same isosurface level: 50% of the maximum baryon density in the last panel (epoch 20 000) of that row. At epoch 0 the dots mark the centres of the imprinted lumps (section 3.4); at B = 3 and at B = 4, two of the lumps form one surface. The surfaces at epoch 0 are drawn translucent so that the dots are visible.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$\Delta$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.
authors: Bokai Ji, Jiapeng Chen, Yi Zhang, Zeyuan Ding, Yong Dai, Xiaozhu Ju, Jian Tang, Lemao Liu, Dejing Dou, Yong Li
bullets: Non-following models encode target information, but it is less linearly decodable than in instruction-following models.
The proposed LDS auxiliary objective promotes linear decodability of the instructed target during training.
On LIBERO-CF, LDS improves InternW0-$\Delta$ to 74.6% success and 89.2% grounding, gains of 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
A prior-instruction competition mechanism explains failures as prior signals dominating instruction signals.
Training-free interventions and broader evaluations support the mechanism and show LDS transfers across manipulation tasks and visual domains.

papers.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking
authors: Davide Gardenal, Mingxuan Liu, Flavio Vella, Quentin Guimard, Elisa Ricci
bullets: Introduces TTU, which requires continuous tracking through object transformations and maintenance of semantic state graphs.
Proposes TIPO, a training-free generate–evaluate–judge framework for detecting and labeling split and merge events.
Uses mask components, overlap-based proposal scoring, and MLLM verification for transformation understanding.
Introduces VISTA, a benchmark with 50 sequences, 124 assembly events, 132 disassembly events, and over 26,000 frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA and runs 6×–15× faster than prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TIPO. At each frame It, the tracker provides the set of per-object masks. The pipeline operates in four stages (1–4): (1) extraction of the disjoint components and mask sampling, (2) generation of all possible assembly and disassembly states, (3) evaluation of the state proposals based on mask overlap metrics, (4) validation of the highest-scoring proposal by the MLLM Judge and semantic labeling. Lastly, the state graph and the tracker are updated with the validated state.

Figure 9. Overview of the VISTA Annotation Tool. Our custom interface couples automated object tracking with expert human verification to construct high-fidelity state graphs. (Top) The landing page features an interactive video player, central tracker controls, and lateral panels for object and graph management. (1) Add Object: The annotator registers a new distinct entity ID in the system. (2) Segment and Track: By clicking on the object within the video frame, the annotator prompts the segmentation model to extract the spatial mask and initiates temporal tracking. (3) Log Transformation: At the exact frame of a physical state change, the expert opens a dialog box to explicitly link the pre- and post-transformation object tracks and assign a semantic action label (e.g., “Unscrew”). (4) Transformation Logged: The validated event is immediately committed to the state graph and displayed in the right-hand panel for continuous review.

Figure 3. Qualitative results on VISTA. Visualizing the TIPO pipeline on cascaded transformations. The state graphs map part-whole interactions and semantic actions, while the masks show robust spatial continuity across multi-step assembly and disassembly sequences.

Figure 16. Additional qualitative results of TIPO on the VISTA benchmark. We present two assembly sequences with their corresponding state-graph predictions. Five chronological video frames for each sequence are displayed above their respective state graph, illustrating how composite objects evolve over time. The top row details the multi-step construction of a drawer assembly from flat boards, while the bottom row shows a digital camera that receives its memory card and battery before being inserted into its pouch. These examples demonstrate the capability of the framework to model multi-step assemblies and part-whole interactions.

Figure 17. Failure cases of TIPO on the VISTA benchmark. We present two disassembly sequences from the Assembly101 [27] subset with their corresponding state-graph predictions. The top row shows the disassembly of a toy dump truck, while the bottom row features the complex disassembly of a toy garbage truck. Dashed red circles and boxes denote false negatives, i.e., objects and transformations present in the ground truth but undetected, such as the missed screws and wheels. A red action in a dashed red box denotes a false positive, i.e., a transformation incorrectly predicted by the pipeline, such as the hallucinated separation of the top cap.

papers.abstract: Parametric body models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying humanoid policies to particular input formats. AnyBodyCodec learns a shared representation through native conversion, then reuses it for new body models and control with its core frozen. Encoders map MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA to aligned slots; native decoders recover target controls. The 1.090M-parameter converter covers nine routes and reaches 16.801 mm input-reference MPJPE across six cross routes: the 2.887M Transformer bank reaches 16.390 mm and its parameter-matched version 18.866 mm. Three measured routes take 7.43-7.67 ms on an RTX 4090. Adding ANNY shows that comparable conversion accuracy can accompany different action consistency under one frozen controller. Under a matched PPO budget, aligned slots support 60.78% full-action success across three formats. Separate 160-hour training reaches 66.10% source-weighted validation success, and the controller is deployed qualitatively on a physical G1 through three visual front ends. Together, these results establish reuse through both native geometric fidelity and downstream policy compatibility.
authors: Qianxing Li
bullets: Addresses incompatible pose and shape interfaces that tie humanoid policies to specific body models.
Encodes MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA into aligned slots and uses native decoders for target-control recovery.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.
authors: Changin Choi, Jungwon Park, Jungmin Ko, Jimyeong Kim, Wonjong Rhee
bullets: Targets the challenge of finding and connecting evidence across distant intervals in videos lasting hours or days.
Builds three memories: searchable segment captions, entity-event records, and entity-aware episode context.
Induces a compact library of memory skills from successful agent trajectories for iterative retrieval, reasoning, and verification.
Achieves the best results on three week-long egocentric benchmarks, with up to 9.4% improvement over the strongest baseline on Ego-R1 Bench.
Ablations show that all memory components and memory skills contribute, including better temporal evidence localization.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.
authors: Jiakang Huang, Xueyan Zhang, Renyi Cai, Jingcheng Niu, Jiaru Li, Yining Wang, Josh Zhang, Jiahe Jiang, Jinman Zhao, Gerald Penn, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
bullets: Existing merging rules lose accuracy unevenly across tasks, with recoverable information remaining in each task’s residual.
HR-Merge weights residuals by each task’s validation headroom, re-merges them with the base operator, and adds the result back at a validation-selected strength.
It is a wrapper around any model-merging method and falls back to the base merge when refinement does not help.
On six LLaMA-3 8B NLI adapters, it improved TIES normalized accuracy from 93.29 to 94.29, mainly helping the weakest task.
Across CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improved or preserved accuracy and achieved the best model in every reported setting.

papers.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.
authors: Zhen Zhang, Changyi Yang, Xuehai He, Chengzhi Liu, Yutong Yin, Ziyue Liu, Zhuoran Yin, Yangmin Li, Zhihan Liu, Jisen Li, Mingyu Jin, Chuhan Li, Zhaotian Weng, Ruoyu He, Wenyao Gao, Jiaxin Deng, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Wenhao Chai, Chenyang Zhao, Zhuofan Ying, Kieran Liu, Andrew Chen, Pony Ma, Zhaoran Wang, Alkesh Patel, Zhe Gan, Xin Eric Wang

Distills each expert into a single soft prompt and composes experts by concatenating prompts, requiring no joint training.
Recovers at least 90% of teacher gains in 22 of 23 math, coding, and agent settings; independently trained prompts compose effectively.
With multiple experts, performance improves as experts are added and matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79).
Generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks with minimal serving overhead: throughput remains within 1.5% of the backbone and reaches 2.40× rank-4 LoRA throughput.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have recently attracted increasing attention in motion planning due to their ability to model high-dimensional and multi-modal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion-based planners still struggle to reliably satisfy geometric feasibility in unseen cluttered environments with complex obstacle layouts. To address this challenge, we propose GeoSDF-Diff, a geometry-aware diffusion planner that incorporates multi-scale SDF conditioning into trajectory denoising. The key idea is to provide the denoiser with both route-level geometric context and fine local clearance evidence, enabling generated trajectories to better adapt to unseen complex obstacle layouts. Specifically, a Geometric Encoder extracts multi-scale SDF features and injects them into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention. We further introduce a trajectory-level training objective that combines SDF clearance, violation emphasis, smoothness, and path-length regularization, so that local infeasibilities are penalized during training rather than corrected only at inference time. Experiments on held-out cluttered environments show that, without post-hoc trajectory repair or sampling-time guidance, GeoSDF-Diff achieves a 65.2% average success rate across diverse test scenarios, outperforming strong diffusion baselines by 25.4% to 28.5%.
authors: Yueming Li, Zhanjiang Yang, Yang Shen, Meng Li, Lijun Sun
bullets: Addresses unreliable collision-free planning in complex, unseen obstacle layouts.
Encodes route-level and local geometric information using multi-scale signed distance fields (SDFs).
Injects SDF features into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention.
Uses a trajectory-level objective combining clearance, violation, smoothness, and path-length terms.
Achieves a 65.2% average success rate without post-hoc repair or sampling-time guidance, outperforming diffusion baselines by 25.4–28.5%.

papers.title: GeoSDF-Diff: Geometry-Aware Diffusion Planning for Collision-Free Trajectories
papers.tldr: GeoSDF-Diff improves diffusion-based motion planning in unseen cluttered environments by conditioning denoising on multi-scale geometry and explicitly penalizing trajectory infeasibility during training.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.

Uses training-free action-intent-guided prefix skipping and inner-chunk prediction reuse.
Evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action conflicts to determine when cached computation is safe.
Reports 1.41×–5.44× GPU inference speedups with minimal task-success degradation across several WAMs and benchmarks.
Achieves 1.46× end-to-end speedup on a Franka Research 3 robot while maintaining success rate.

papers.title: ReActWAM: Action-Consistent Caching for Efficient World-Action Models

papers.abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.
authors: Hwee Young Kang, Irwin De Tao Chin, Wen-Haw Chong, Hai Leong Chieu
bullets: Addresses capability degradation caused by domain specialization and interference in conventional parameter-space model merging.
Uses covariance-driven, ranked generalized eigendirections to construct a low-rank projection gate for specialist updates.
Optimizes specialist activation capture under a regularized budget limiting perturbation to the base model’s outputs.
Produces a single static merged checkpoint and achieves competitive Pareto trade-offs across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA settings on Qwen3 models.
Evaluated retention trade-offs include up to 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention in the reported settings.

papers.title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance

papers.abstract: Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.
authors: Zhiqiang Yuan, Qiwei Yan, Liwei Yang, Jinzhe Liu, Yang Liu, Zhongyan Hou, Liyan Xu, Peixiang Luo, Jiapei Zhang, Ying Deng, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Targets on-device deployment, where separate specialized models duplicate capacity under tight memory and compute budgets.
Introduces MGVB to allocate a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained visual information.
Uses ULKD for soft teacher guidance and SEMO for loss/exposure regulation and memory-constrained optimization.
Improves joint representation-generation performance, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74 across five evaluation groups.
Achieves slightly higher balanced performance than the strongest separate-model stack with 61.9% less resident weight memory and 2.64× higher HCD.
papers.selection_reason: Unified on-device multimodal LLM with visual token budgeting and multitask optimization; directly fits multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs
papers.tldr: WePM unifies vision-language representation, generation, and decision capabilities in one memory-efficient pocket model by reconciling visual-scale and multitask training conflicts.

papers.abstract: Bayesian state estimators, such as Kalman filters, estimate states from noisy observations based on dynamical models. However, obtaining accurate models can be challenging when the system involves effects that are difficult to model faithfully, such as friction, impacts, and deformation in contact-rich manipulation. Uncertainty in system parameters, inputs, and disturbances, together with simplified noise models, can further introduce simulation-to-reality mismatch and degrade estimation accuracy. These limitations motivate learning a distribution over state trajectories conditioned on observations and controls without explicitly specifying the underlying physical models. We introduce NormFlowSDE, an amortized Bayesian state estimator that learns a distribution over state trajectories by combining neural stochastic differential equations with conditional normalizing flows. Its key design choice is to utilize the capability of normalizing flows to learn stochastic behavior of variables, while leveraging the continuous-time dynamics of SDEs to model the evolution of states over time. Once trained, the model draws state paths for new measurement sequences without per-sequence optimization. In addition, we connect NormFlowSDE to stochastic continuous-time dynamics by proving weak convergence of a mean-centered, drift-corrected inference scheme to an It\^o diffusion under stated assumptions. Finally, we benchmark NormFlowSDE against direct estimators and learned particle filters based on normalizing flows on partially observed dynamical systems, including simulated systems and real-world robot datasets. The results show that NormFlowSDE attains the lowest estimation error with calibrated uncertainty intervals on both robot datasets and filters four times faster than the fastest particle filter on every dataset.
authors: Yi Zhang, Lars Mikelsons
bullets: Addresses state-estimation errors caused by difficult-to-model dynamics, parameter uncertainty, disturbances, and simplified noise assumptions.
Combines neural stochastic differential equations with conditional normalizing flows to represent continuous-time stochastic state evolution.
Amortizes inference: after training, it samples state paths for new measurement sequences without per-sequence optimization.
Provides a theoretical weak-convergence result linking its drift-corrected inference scheme to an Itô diffusion under stated assumptions.
Achieves the lowest estimation error with calibrated uncertainty on robot datasets and filters four times faster than the fastest learned particle filter across evaluated datasets.

papers.abstract: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each new base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.
authors: Yajun Liu, Jinxi Wu, Juan Pablo Mill\'an Raya, Xuesong Zhou
bullets: Addresses manual or unreliable open-map extraction of lane and junction data for transportation models.
Uses a Perceive–Anchor–Verify–Edit workflow: VLMs make limited judgments while code measures, links observations to IDs, and checks consistency.
At signalised intersections, exact lane-layout accuracy improves from 49–64% with a single request to 86–91% for two VLMs.
For planning-driven network edits, 16 of 18 edits pass all network checks; model-written code produces none that pass every check.
Scope: evaluated on 44 approaches and 18 edits, with remaining errors involving design or coding mistakes.
