papers.abstract: Long-form generation is increasingly important for agentic LLM systems, yet current reinforcement learning methods typically optimize an entire document with a single outcome-level reward. This delayed and coarse-grained supervision makes it difficult to localize errors and assign credit across semantically distinct parts of the output. To address this, we propose a short-horizon framework that reformulates long-form generation through semantic decomposition into segment-level decisions. Each segment is generated with prefix-conditioned context, allowing cross-segment coherence to be preserved while keeping supervision local. The generated segments are then scored with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, enabling explicit local supervision at the segment level. These local rewards are used to compute step-wise advantages, yielding localized policy updates. To isolate the effect of supervision granularity, we instantiate both outcome-level supervision and our short-horizon process reward method (SH-PRM) under the same GRPO framework. Across multiple LLMs and two long-form generation benchmarks, SH-PRM consistently outperforms outcome-level supervision and strong inference-time baselines under the same optimizer and comparable budgets. Further analyses suggest that these gains primarily arise from improved credit assignment. Overall, our results suggest that aligning supervision granularity with the semantic structure of long-form generation is an effective design principle for long-form LLM training.
authors: Heyang Xu, HanWen Hao, Qianren Mao, Zhuo Liu, Qili Zhang, Sheng Yang, Jianxin Li
bullets: Long-form reinforcement learning struggles to assign credit when a whole document receives only one coarse outcome reward.
The method decomposes outputs into semantically meaningful segments generated with prefix context to preserve coherence.
Rubric-based rewards assess each segment for adherence, coherence, and relevance, producing step-wise advantages and localized policy updates.
Implemented within the same GRPO framework, SH-PRM outperforms outcome-level supervision and inference-time baselines across multiple models and two benchmarks.
Analyses attribute the gains mainly to improved credit assignment.

figures.caption: Figure 5: The unified system prompt used for report generation across all models (Base, ORM, and SH-PRM) to ensure evaluation fairness.

Figure 1: Document-level versus segment-level supervision for longform generation. Under ORM (left), the full document receives a single document-level reward, and the resulting advantage is shared across segments, coupling their updates and potentially obscuring local errors. Under our SHPRM (right), generation is decomposed into segments with prefix-conditioned context, each of which receives a local rubric-based reward and a localized update. This change in supervision granularity enables more precise credit assignment by penalizing problematic paragraphs while preserving credit for strong ones.

Figure 2: Training dynamics and stability analysis. (a) & (b): Our SHPRM method (Red) maintains a steady upward trajectory and superior sample efficiency, whereas ORM baselines either collapse or prematurely plateau. Note: The y-axis represents a unified outcome quality score evaluated on a held-out validation set. (c): The microscopic cause of this difference. The Collapsed ORM (Blue) exhibits gradient explosion, and the Stabilized ORM (Green) shows a large gradient spike (> 3.0). In contrast, our SH-PRM (Red) maintains a stable gradient norm (∼1.0), indicating that segment-level rewards provide a much cleaner and more stable optimization signal.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.
authors: Yongkang He, Xiaofen Xing, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Existing models can preserve global appearance while missing local interaction details, causing implausible contact effects and robot-object behavior.
MoReWorld uses a shared motion region to guide local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning.
The motion region is inferred at test time from visual history and robot actions, without future observations or ground-truth motion labels.
On WorldSimProbe, it achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with strongest results in local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. An overview of MoReWorld. (b) During training, WAFT optical flow yields moving/static labels m, s, and URDF rendering yields the environment mask E = 1− ρ that excludes the robot region; their product gives the motion-map labels. (c) The gated future motion Ck and the robot appearance r are injected into the Wan input. (d) A shared Wan denoising transformer jointly processes RGB and VGGT latents and predicts the RGB velocity, clean future VGGT features, and an auxiliary flow velocity, supervised with the motion-region weighted loss.

papers.abstract: In-context segmentation uses annotated references to specify the target and its extent in a query image. Accurately transferring this reference-specified foreground requires recovering target regions while suppressing irrelevant predictions. We propose ReSA, a reference-guided framework that unifies query adaptation and mask selection through a shared reference kernel. ReSA leverages foreground and background reference prototypes to constrain prediction changes during adaptation and guide foreground selection through reference-weighted reconstruction. This shared guidance promotes consistent use of reference information across prediction refinement and mask formation. ReSA further selects among adapted predictions and aligns boundary refinement with the selected foreground threshold. We establish a theoretical bound connecting reference-response changes during adaptation and soft reconstruction. With a frozen visual encoder and lightweight test-time adaptation, ReSA requires no offline task training. Ablation studies demonstrate improved foreground retention and effective suppression of false-positive regions, while qualitative results show more complete masks with fewer isolated artifacts. Across ten object, part, and cross-domain segmentation benchmarks, ReSA achieves the highest average mIoU among the evaluated methods, reaching 62.6% in 1-shot and 71.8% in 5-shot.
authors: Dezhao Su, Bingxu Hou, Jingdi Lei, Lin Qian, Likai Wang, Yunyun Wan
bullets: Uses foreground and background reference prototypes to constrain query adaptation and suppress irrelevant regions.
Applies reference-weighted reconstruction to select masks, with boundary refinement aligned to the chosen foreground threshold.
Works with a frozen visual encoder and lightweight test-time adaptation, requiring no offline task training.
Ablations show better foreground retention and fewer false-positive artifacts; results span ten benchmarks, reaching 62.6% mIoU in 1-shot and 71.8% in 5-shot.
Provides a theoretical bound linking reference-response changes during adaptation with soft reconstruction.

papers.abstract: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.
authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Jiajun Zha, Hanqing Wang, Zhenhao Zhang, Huihao Jing, Shing-Chi Cheung, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang
bullets: Auditing five public benchmarks reveals image-only label predictability; same-image prompt probes achieve 0.9645 AUROC without seeing images.
A controlled evaluation crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, preventing any single-modality rule from exceeding 0.500 group-ranking accuracy.
Linear probes on intermediate states reach 0.958 for Qwen3-VL-8B and 0.930 for SmolVLM2-2.2B, indicating scene-intent conjunctions are decodable.
Concatenated image and text representations recover most of the signal, so decodability alone does not prove a fusion mechanism.
Probe-based screening is cheap but generalizes poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Image-first causal masking makes the final prompt token the earliest state that sees both modalities, and controlled modality ablations expose which modality each evaluation suite rewards. Panel a plots measured Qwen3-VL-8B attention weights over token blocks [v1, . . . ,v4,r1, . . . ,r3,e]: visualto-text attention v → r,e is identically 0.0, while the final prompt token e attends across visual and textual keys. Panel b confirms bit-exact visual invariance max |∆hI|= 0.0 under matched-length prompt swaps in image-first prefill versus 155.7 in a prompt-first control. Panels c and d show fixed-probe prompt interventions shifting scores by 0.26–1.86 SD and flipping 6.3%–32.2% of predictions on public benchmarks alongside 65.7%–93.4% on same-image intent pairs. Panel e contrasts retrained modality ablations: on same-image pairs the blind text probe matches the joint probe, whereas on symmetric four-way scene-action groups the joint probe far exceeds the 50.0% unimodal ceiling.

Figure 1. Safety benchmarks can be solved from one modality, and a symmetric control is needed to test joint scene-intent information. Panel a, top: on identical MOSSBench photographs paired with benign and harmful prompts, a probe that sees a blind gray canvas reaches 0.9645 to 0.9846 AUROC, so the text alone decides the label. Panel a, bottom: our four-way MSSBench control crosses a safe and a hazardous scene with an observation and an action request, so that risk requires both modalities; an intermediate joint probe ranks the unsafe case first in 0.958 of groups, against a 50.0% bound for any single-modality rule. Panel b, a secondary result: on Qwen3-VL-8B a cached probe costs 0.234 ms per request at batch size 1, against 95.82 ms for an independent safety pass, and in a separate end-to-end run it adds 0.36% to the 68.0 ms prefill.

Figure 3. Cross-benchmark transfer fails through ranking collapse, which threshold recalibration cannot repair. In panels a and b, applying a source-calibrated 5%-FPR threshold across VSCBench and MSSBench over L1–L4 inflates hollow-circle FPR up to 79.5% on MSSBench→VSCBench. Recalibrating at the 95th percentile of labeled benign target scores with fixed probe weights places all 16 solid-circle points at 4.2%–5.1% FPR, shown with 95% Wilson intervals; because the same benign rows set and evaluate the threshold, this FPR is in-sample by construction. In panel c, transferred AUROC drops to 0.48–0.67, well below the 0.80–0.98 target ceiling. In panel d, percentile-calibrated recall at 5% FPR reaches 6.4%–14.4% TPR, and oracle-threshold recall shown as diamonds reaches 6.9%–14.8% TPR, far below the 34.4%–88.9% target ceiling bars.

Figure 4. Image-disjoint splits remove shared-image leakage, and cached probing anchors the lowlatency deployment frontier. Realized test TPR in panel a and realized test FPR in panel b show 95% Wilson intervals under a 5% calibration FPR target on image-disjoint splits: cached probes lead on both SmolVLM2 suites, within-benchmark safety passes lead on both Qwen3-VL suites, and the hollow circle marks the inflated 88.0% recall produced by request-grouped leakage on Qwen3-VL with MSSBench. Panel c plots the four Qwen3-VL-8B screening routes from Table 4 against batch-1 marginal latency, spanning 0.234 ms for cached probing to 95.82 ms for an independent safety pass.

Singleton images give zero entropy and an exact lookup by construction. †Equal to 0.5000 by construction, since each image carries both labels. Columns report ranges across depths L1–L4, corresponding to layers {4,11,23,35} on Qwen3-VL-8B and {3,7,15,23} on SmolVLM2-2.2B. Detection columns compare cached pooled visual-token probes against within-benchmark safety passes at a 5% calibration FPR target; requestgrouped MSSBench reflects 58.5% shared-image overlap. Diagnostic control rows report image (I,∅), blind text (∅,U), and joint (I,U) probes at L2: test AUROC on paired intent, and four-way group-ranking accuracy against the 0.50 unimodal ceiling. ∆ is AUROC(I,U)−AUROC(I,∅) in benchmark and paired rows, and the joint pooled AUROC minus the best single-modality pooled AUROC in four-way rows.

papers.selection_reason: Audits vision-language safety representations and exposes unimodal shortcuts in multimodal understanding.
papers.title: Unimodal Shortcuts and Joint Scene-Intent Dependence in Vision-Language Safety Representations
papers.tldr: Situational safety benchmarks can be solved through unimodal shortcuts, so high accuracy does not establish that vision-language models jointly represent scene and user intent.

papers.abstract: Given a pretrained general latent-conditioned whole-body humanoid controller, say a behavioral foundation model (BFM), how can we elicit complex and contact-rich out-of-distribution behaviors? Raw joint-action exploration enables direct, task-specific adjustments but can disrupt coordination learned by the pretrained controller, whereas latent exploration retains that coordination but is difficult to steer toward desired physical effects. To combine the complementary strengths of these exploration spaces, we propose Latent Jacobian Steer (LJS), which couples sampling in direct joint-action space with the semantics of the learned frozen controller's input latent space. For a task specified through desired physical effects, we sample task-relevant joint-action perturbations and map them through a damped local inverse of the policy Jacobian to obtain candidate latent ($z$) commands. These commands are executed through the frozen pretrained policy, while exploration is directed toward the physical outcomes required by the new task. Candidate outcomes are evaluated in simulation and composed into latent-command sequences that accomplish the task. Ablations show that neither action-space nor latent-space exploration alone provides the same capability as their coupling. Across diverse out-of-distribution tasks, simulation-based searching using this method produces contact-rich behaviors, including hurdling, manipulating articulated objects, and opening doors through non-prehensile contact. Over ten seeds, LJS completes more of each humanoid task than when searching in either space alone. Beyond humanoids, it also steers a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy through four assembly tasks better than searching in goal space directly.
authors: S K Swaminathan, Shivam Sood, Shreyansh Kansal, Chengyang He, Guillaume Adrien Sartoretti
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of steering latent-conditioned humanoid controllers toward physical effects without disrupting learned coordination.
Maps task-relevant joint-action perturbations through a damped local inverse policy Jacobian to generate latent commands.
Executes candidates with the frozen pretrained policy, evaluates outcomes in simulation, and composes successful latent-command sequences.
Produces behaviors such as hurdling, articulated-object manipulation, and non-prehensile door opening across diverse out-of-distribution tasks.
Also improves steering of a goal-conditioned dexterous hand policy on four assembly tasks compared with direct goal-space search.

papers.title: Latent Jacobian Steer: Eliciting Contact-Rich Out-of-Distribution Behaviors from Pretrained Humanoid Controllers

papers.abstract: We present Zing-1.0, a Playable World System built on Controllable Rendering. An executable engine resolves player actions under the world's rules and produces proxy video from the updated state. A streaming video model synthesizes the player's view from this proxy, and the runtime delivers it to inform subsequent actions. (1) Principle and system. We formulate Controllable Rendering and define the interfaces among world construction, world execution, observation synthesis, and the interaction runtime. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation-independent specification of a Playable World System. (2) AI-native engine. WorldKit provides structured authoring tools and reusable character, camera, and control components for coding agents to construct executable proxy worlds. It supports extensible interactions and precise geometric motion control while separating executable behavior from final visual appearance. (3) Streaming renderer. We adapt MiniMax-H3 for block-causal autoregressive generation and incremental decoding. Proxy video constrains structure and motion, while text and separate scene and subject references specify appearance. We train the generator on diverse tasks and distill it to generate each block in a few denoising steps. The renderer leads the compared streaming editors on OpenVE (3.90) and LongV2VBench (3.44). On StreamEval, Zing-1.0 scores 57.86 on instruction editing and 54.06 on reference editing, exceeding the published baselines on both tracks. (4) Interaction infrastructure. We build an Interaction Runtime that routes player actions to WorldKit while supporting in-play prompt and reference updates. Cross-block joint execution and sparse attention with compressed K/V reduce inference overhead. With the DiT on a single H200 and encoding and decoding on one H100 each, the serving system achieves a steady-state throughput of 23.82 FPS at $832\times480$.

A block-causal streaming renderer uses proxy video for structure and motion, with text and references controlling appearance.
Reports strong benchmark results, including 3.90 on OpenVE, 3.44 on LongV2VBench, and higher-than-published-baseline scores on both StreamEval tracks.
The runtime supports in-play prompt/reference updates and reaches 23.82 FPS at 832×480 using specified H200/H100 hardware.

Dashed arrows indicate initialization from H3’s video AdaLN branch. (c) The streaming decoder uses cached K/V to decode one latent at a time. papers.abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. Yet many end-to-end driving planners evaluate every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. On three planners with different scene representations (learned registers, a perception-supervised bird's-eye-view grid, and a coarse image-token grid), adding this gaze improves planning scores. In ablations, path-aligned patches outperform both a matched number of randomly selected patches and attention over all patches. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.
authors: Jiawei Sun, Maosen Li, Jiamin Shi, Xiaoxu Zheng, Jiun Tian Hoe, Yechao Bai, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of scoring all trajectories from the same compressed scene representation.
Generates trajectory hypotheses from shared features, then uses trajectory-aligned camera corridors to select native-resolution patch features.
Refines and ranks each proposal using visual evidence specific to its path, requiring only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration.
Across three planner representations, path-aligned gaze improves planning scores and outperforms random or all-patch attention.
Ranking with gaze provides larger gains than refinement alone; the method operates without perception labels and reports results on WOD-E2E, NAVSIM, and Bench2Drive.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of GGDriver. Every decoder layer performs a global glance over shared scene tokens, predicts a trajectory, projects its corridor into the cameras, and gazes at the full-resolution patches of the covered blocks. The scorer ranks each proposal after the same gaze along that proposal’s path. The projection needs only the trajectory and the camera calibration. Sizes are per camera, height × width × channels.

Figure 1. Glance at what is shared, gaze at what differs. A glance at a coarse view of the scene, shared by all planning queries, yields the trajectory hypotheses (left), here a right turn, a straight continuation and a left turn. Each hypothesis then gazes at the full-resolution patches of the image blocks its own path passes through (middle). This evidence refines each hypothesis and conditions the scorer that ranks them (right): the hypothesis decides which evidence is acquired.

Figure 3. The gaze reads the evidence against the glance (GGDriver, NAVSIM-v1 navtest). (a) Trajectory of the selected proposal generated in the glance stage, its corridor and the gaze blocks it selects; (b) gaze attention over these blocks; (c) bird’s-eye view. The glance drives into the vehicle ahead (i, ii), misses a right turn (iii), drifts across the centre line (iv) or cuts across the kerb (v, vi); the gaze reads the evidence against it, and the final trajectory follows the human one.

papers.abstract: Real-time human-robot social interaction requires continuous coordination between speech and physical behavior. Existing systems often separate interaction agents from motion generation, complicating coordination as conversational states change. We propose \textbf{Embodied Interaction Policy (EIP)}, a unified streaming framework that couples an Audio-Interaction expert with a motion expert through layer-wise joint attention. This allows motion generation to directly access the evolving interaction context. A chunk-wise causal mask prevents access to future context, while a vocal token encodes speaking state and the semantic emotion of the response. We construct \textbf{Embodied Interaction Dataset (EI-Data)} from co-speech and dyadic interaction data and train our model in two stages to learn state-adaptive and emotion-conditioned behavior. Combined with the frozen interaction expert, EIP supports continuous robot motion during proactive responses and interruption-aware turn-taking. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate improved motion quality over representative gesture-generation baselines. Compared with a representative cascaded system, EIP achieves higher interaction success and reduces warm-start latency by 64\%. Physical deployment and user studies further demonstrate improved motion naturalness and interaction comfort.
authors: Youqiang Gui, Yunfei Liu, Lijian Lin, Ye Zhu, Jianan Wang, Cheng Peng, Yu Li
bullets: Addresses coordination challenges caused by separating conversational agents from motion generators.
Couples an Audio-Interaction expert with a motion expert using layer-wise joint attention and causal chunk-wise masking.
Uses vocal tokens to represent speaking state and response emotion, trained on the EI-Data dataset in two stages.
Supports continuous motion during proactive responses and interruption-aware turn-taking.
Evaluations report better motion quality, higher interaction success, 64% lower warm-start latency, and improved naturalness and comfort in deployment studies.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Suryabhan Singh Hada, Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao, Qun Gu, Libin N. George, Wenhuan Sun, Neha Monga, Richard Williamson, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of lengthy chain-of-thought without sacrificing transparency through lossy token dropping or latent representations.
Learns semantic-span tokens with BPE in the Private Use Area and fine-tunes expanded-vocabulary LLMs using strict 1:1 supervision.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four benchmarks.
Cuts total generated tokens by 14.7% on average and reasoning-trace length by up to 27.1%, with a 1.6-point average accuracy cost.
The lossless approach can be combined with existing irreversible compression methods.

papers.abstract: Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.
authors: Hyunseok Oh, Youngki Lee
bullets: The work addresses energy-efficient, lifelong prediction over continuous data streams.
It proves that a discrete SNN can continuously track the instantaneous output of its corresponding firing-rate ANN.
LIF-Stream converts ANNs into SNNs that reuse prior activation states and compute only frame-to-frame updates.
The method reduces the average number of time steps per frame while maintaining high-accuracy predictions.
Across three large-scale streaming benchmarks and distinct modalities, it achieves the best reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off among high-accuracy SNN methods.

papers.abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipelines and vision-language models exhibit high accuracy on standard OCR and document-understanding benchmarks, yet they systematically underperform on document patterns that are operationally critical in financial workflows. These patterns include vertical or rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine-print regulatory clauses, degraded scans, and complex multi-column layouts. While underrepresented in public datasets, they constitute a substantial portion of real-world failure cases. We introduce SAVIOR, a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets such high-impact failure scenarios to adapt vision-language models for robust financial OCR. We further propose PaIRS, a structure-aware evaluation metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves a word recall of 0.93. When the resulting layout-aware OCR output is used as context for document question answering, it attains an F1 score of 0.89, outperforming both open- and closed-source models such as GPT-4o, Mistral-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, and DeepSeek-OCR.
authors: Akshata A Bhat, Sharath Naganna, Saiful Haq, Prashant Khatri, Krishna Chaitanya Reddy Tamataam, Neha Arun, Niyati Chhaya, Pushpak Bhattacharyya
bullets: Targets failure cases often missed in benchmarks, including rotated text, logo-embedded names, fine print, degraded scans, and complex layouts.
Introduces SAVIOR, a data-curation methodology for adapting vision-language models to robust financial OCR.
Proposes PaIRS, a metric that evaluates layout fidelity using pairwise spatial relationships between tokens.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves 0.93 word recall and 0.89 F1 for downstream document question answering.
The reported results outperform the compared open- and closed-source OCR and vision-language systems.

papers.abstract: While chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from language models, it is unclear which words in the context actually steer the CoT. We identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): language models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant context words, even as the same models deny those words' relevance when asked. To localize PCI, we introduce Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis, which removes one context word at a time from the otherwise intact context to isolate its marginal effect on the next-token distribution; words whose removal flips the prediction (pivot words) are passed to the same LLM to self-judge whether it recognizes this predictive dependence. Across four models and three benchmarks, language models largely do not know which words steer their reasoning, a mismatch we call the Generation-Judgment Contradiction. Inspired by this phenomenon, we propose Online KV Suppression: it scores every prompt word's influence over the whole chain of thought in a single pass, then zeroes the KV-cache entries of the highest-influence word the model itself judges inert and redecodes. This single-word intervention improves CoT accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, by up to 8.9 percentage points on math reasoning benchmark.

bullets: Identifies Phantom Context Influence: semantically irrelevant words can disproportionately alter chain-of-thought reasoning.
Introduces Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis to measure each word’s marginal effect on next-token predictions.
Finds a Generation-Judgment Contradiction across four models and three benchmarks: models often fail to identify words steering their reasoning.
Proposes Online KV Suppression, which removes the model-judged inert word with the greatest measured influence during decoding.
Improves chain-of-thought accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, with gains of up to 8.9 percentage points on a math benchmark.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Words Steer Their Reasoning?
papers.tldr: Language models can be steered by irrelevant words without recognizing their influence, but suppressing such words during generation improves reasoning accuracy.

papers.abstract: Growers and traders rely on root morphology to assess wild ginseng, yet breakage can obscure important structural traits. We study point cloud completion to provide geometric references for morphological analysis. Does providing more observed points always improve 3D completion? We test whether selected subsets improve recovery of the original missing region while keeping the pretrained completer fixed. We introduce BioCL-POS, an external selector that predicts how the completer responds to candidate inputs. For each candidate, we predict the displacement and distance from shared spatial locations to the nearest points in its completion. We use these spatial responses to estimate recovery quality and supervise them with measurements from actual completions. At inference, we select an input from the observed geometry and run the completer once. We evaluate four frozen completers on controlled gaps in ginseng and tree data at 5%,10%, and 20% omission, and examine 30% omission on ginseng. At 5--20% omission, we outperform full-input completion and all five alternative selectors on both datasets with all four completers. We achieve lower mean reconstruction error and higher mean F-score and coverage. We thus show that selecting observations can improve geometric recovery without retraining the completer, providing more accurate geometric references for subsequent morphological analysis.
authors: Yulu Wang, Tingting Yao, Taolue Liu
bullets: Addresses whether using all observed points is always best when reconstructing missing root geometry.
Uses an external selector to predict a completer’s spatial response to candidate observation subsets.
Selects one input based on predicted recovery quality, then runs the pretrained completer once.
Outperforms full-input completion and five alternative selectors across four frozen completers on ginseng and tree data with 5–20% omissions.
Improves reconstruction error, F-score, and coverage; performance is also examined at 30% omission on ginseng.

papers.abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $\gamma$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.
authors: Xiaotao Zhang, Lin Qian, Hao Zhang, Xuanrui Cui, Yuehao Huang, Yunzi Wu, Yucheng Deng, Jiankun Dong, Hujun Yin, Xinhai Li, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Supports complete mobile-manipulation tasks in a persistent physical world, where agents compose motion tools and learned skills.
BenchForge links structured objectives to physical task instances, reference programs, instructions, and goal evaluators while allowing multiple valid solutions.
Collects contact-rich demonstrations and aligned observation–action records through autonomous, assisted, and human-guided execution.
Enables program refinement and policy learning from tool traces, with shared task-goal criteria for evaluation.
Benchmarks representative agents and demonstrates contact-data collection and trace-informed program revision; the abstract does not report quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Completing a manipulation task does not establish that a robot follows the requested goal rather than a familiar routine. ManipScope is an evaluation-only diagnostic benchmark for robotic instruction following under changed task requirements. Built on RoboTwin 2.0's simulation resources, it specifies 48 held-out scenes across six task families with explicit source-task links; policies are trained on unmodified RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrations, and no demonstrations of the scenes are provided, so success requires reusing skills under a changed request rather than fitting supplied examples. Beyond task success, ManipScope provides a chain of diagnostics in which each step tests one explanation of a failure. For twelve policy checkpoints, 84.6% of failures in 13,200 episodes on eleven selection scenes displace a distractor, and gripper records show that failed episodes usually grasp a non-target. When the target is reassigned among the candidates on identical initial states, ten checkpoints follow every instruction on 3.9% of 1,000 states, below the 16% of an instruction-blind chooser, while a GPT-6 agent run as positive control reaches 88%. The failure recurs on unmodified training tasks and is not explained by missing manipulation skills, so success in these scenes largely reflects instruction-independent preferences; two checkpoints trained on the same data nevertheless follow color instructions. In a feasibility test, letting an agent select the target and the policy execute partly restores instruction following. Case studies with future-video and internal-intervention probes further show that forecasts and execution can agree on the wrong target and that action changes need not transfer the goal. Success, consistency, and sensitivity must each be checked against the requested goal.
authors: Jiacheng Li, Yaping Li, Congsheng Xu, Qingchen Liu, Haonan Wang, Zhijie Deng, Jiahu Qin
bullets: Evaluation-only benchmark with 48 held-out scenes across six task families, using changed requirements and no demonstrations of test scenes.
A diagnostic chain separates task failure explanations, including distractor displacement, target selection, execution, and internal decision processes.
Across 13,200 episodes, 84.6% of failures displaced a distractor; target reassignment showed only 3.9% instruction-following across 1,000 states for the tested checkpoints.
The issue persists on unmodified training tasks and is not simply missing manipulation skill; some checkpoints trained on the same data do follow color instructions.
Results indicate that success, consistency, and sensitivity should each be evaluated against the specified goal; target selection before policy execution partly improves following.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

papers.abstract: Manual assembly remains difficult to monitor because operator actions, components, and task progress must be interpreted together. This paper presents a modular framework based on a single overhead red-green-blue (RGB) camera, combining object detection, hand-motion tracking, region-aware interaction detection, finite-state verification, task-specific pose classification, and configurable visual guidance. The system was evaluated during pneumatic-piston assembly and disassembly with eight participants under three assistance conditions: full, mid, and no guidance. Mixed-effects analysis identified an association between assistance condition and a composite measure of motion quality, with lower estimated scores under mid and no guidance relative to full guidance. However, the condition-by-trial interaction was not statistically significant, and the estimated differences in learning trajectories remain descriptive. No condition differences were detected in completion time or failed-stage counts. The study demonstrates the integration of visual perception, procedural verification, and configurable operator feedback in a single-camera workflow. Selecting assistance according to operator expertise remains a design objective for future investigation.

papers.abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.
authors: Ziyi Ding, Yiwei Wang, Zhongxing Wei, Xianxin Lai, Yechi Liu, Xiaodi Huang, Jinghua Hou, Xiaoquan Sun, Haijier Chen, Zhe Liu, Yinan Chen, Junqiao Zhao, Xiao-Ping Zhang, Jiayu Chen
bullets: Problem: Egocentric frame changes mix hand manipulation with camera motion, making action targets ambiguous.
Method: Supervises latent action codes with measured wrist translation and rotation while providing camera motion separately to the forward model.
Design: Pools object representations around each hand and decodes wrist motion in a shared reference frame; inference uses only two RGB frames.
Evaluation: Tests hand-motion retention and robustness to synthetic viewpoint and lighting changes, alongside LARYBench tasks.
Results: Achieves the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight models and 79.38% mean LIBERO success, outperforming behavior cloning and other latent-action models on average.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.

CCR applies the frozen reference model’s conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL.
Across multiple rewards and backbones, CCR maintains competitive reward while more consistently preserving quality than standard RL and generic regularization.

papers.abstract: Agents for Image Restoration (IR) aim to leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously perceive image degradation and invoke IR tools. However, existing IR agents typically rely on fine-tuning MLLM parameters to adapt to new IR tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting of IR knowledge. To address this limitation, we propose a skill-augmented IR agent, dubbed SIR-Agent, that maintains IR knowledge in a scalable skill library and uses Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to facilitate efficient skill-library evolution. Specifically, we design a Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR) to evolve the skill library. The CFSR analyzes restoration chains to identify and revise weak operations in existing skills. The compatibility of a revised skill with known tasks decides if it replaces the original skill or is appended independently. Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.

papers.abstract: While existing methods for reconstructing deformable object manipulation have made impressive progress, they typically represent a thin object with a single particle set that must serve two purposes at once: modeling bending, and resolving contact with the robot. To bridge this gap, we present HermiteTwin, a framework that reconstructs a physical digital twin of a thin deformable object from multiview video of a robot manipulating it. Our key idea is to represent deformation and contact separately, each at its own resolution. The object is simulated as a bicubic Hermite shell, a coarse grid of $C^1$ elements whose nodal positions and derivatives define a smooth surface with Kirchhoff--Love bending, while the gripper acts through dense samples in material space that are captured, clamped, and released, and whose attachment forces reach the shell through the Hermite basis. This decoupling keeps the physical state compact while contact stays fine-grained. We identify effective material and contact parameters with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based refinement, and drive a reconstructed Gaussian appearance model with the simulated shell. In experiments on real cloth and foam manipulation, HermiteTwin outperforms the state-of-the-art spring--mass twin across reconstruction, resimulation, and future prediction.
authors: Kangrui Zhang, Mu Huang, Xing Shen, Tiantian Liu, Bo Ren
bullets: Addresses the conflict between representing bending and resolving robot contact with a single particle set.

Represents gripper interaction through dense material-space samples whose forces are transferred to the shell via Hermite basis functions.
Estimates material and contact parameters with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based refinement, and drives a Gaussian appearance model from the simulated shell.
Outperforms a spring–mass digital twin in reconstruction, resimulation, and future prediction on real cloth and foam manipulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HermiteTwin. From multiview video of a robot manipulating cloth, we fit a rest surface S0 to the first-frame object points and reconstruct a Gaussian appearance model G. The gripper captures dense samples in material space (red); each attached sample ri lies in one element, and its attachment residual reaches the 16 nodal vectors of that element through the Hermite weights J⊤ i (inset). The effective parameters θ are identified by minimizing a full-rollout observation loss with CMA-ES followed by adjoint-based Adam. The identified twin resimulates the recorded motion, predicts held-out frames, and drives the Gaussian appearance in synthesized scenes.

papers.abstract: Point cloud denoising and upsampling require samples that accurately recover the underlying surface from noisy or sparse observations. A central challenge in both tasks is preserving surface coverage while refining point locations. We introduce GAAFormer (Geometry-Anchored Attention Transformer), a unified generative octree transformer that performs both tasks with a shared network. Its decoder anchors attention neighborhoods to geometry, providing spatial context for occupancy prediction and point generation. Fixed voxel windows and alternating shifts preserve the grouping of surviving nodes as the output tree changes. The design retains the encoder, positional encoding, prediction heads, and parameter count of a serialized-attention backbone. We establish a deletion-consistency property of the neighborhood rule and evaluate both tasks using the same model. On PUNet, GAAFormer achieves a mean Chamfer distance (CD) of $6.0643\times10^{-5}$, reducing CD and Hausdorff distance by 3.35% and 19.34%, respectively, relative to the serialized backbone. For upsampling, it achieves CD values of $0.8475$, $1.7057$, and $1.0147$ ($\times10^{-5}$) on PU-GAN, PU1K, and Sketchfab, respectively, with improvements in CD, Hausdorff distance, and point-to-surface distance over the same backbone on PU-GAN and Sketchfab. These results establish a single architecture for point cloud denoising and upsampling. Within the shared encoder-decoder, the same geometry-anchored attention module improves both noise removal and dense point generation without task-specific redesign or additional parameters.
authors: Haoxi Tian (School of Civil Engineering,Geomatics, Southwest Petroleum University)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering accurate surface geometry while preserving coverage in noisy or sparse point clouds.
Uses a generative octree Transformer whose decoder anchors attention neighborhoods to geometry for occupancy prediction and point generation.
Fixed voxel windows, alternating shifts, and a deletion-consistent neighborhood rule preserve grouping as the output tree changes.
Retains the serialized-attention backbone’s encoder, positional encoding, prediction heads, and parameter count.
Improves denoising and upsampling metrics over the serialized backbone, with gains reported in Chamfer, Hausdorff, and point-to-surface distances on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Initial public offering (IPO) filings describe what a company does and what it intends to become. Yet whether individual forward-looking claims are subsequently realized is difficult to assess. We introduce Vision Follow-Through (VFT), a benchmark and agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment. \vftclaims{} contains 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 IPO filings, while \vftverify{} adds verifiability tiers, follow-through outcomes, and cited later evidence for 1,000 claims. Across language models, classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings. Extraction coverage also varies sharply by category, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered far less often than Market Opportunity claims. Follow-through assessment poses a separate challenge: model judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than exhibiting a single consistent bias. These results show that reliable assessment of corporate follow-through requires both finding the relevant claims and grounding subsequent judgments in later evidence.
authors: Vidhyakshaya Kannan, Shiv Banafar, Michael Galarnyk, Sagnik Nandi, Soumeya Kannan, Shauray Arora, Abanoub Abdelmalak, Sudheer Chava

papers.abstract: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.
authors: Oliver Lundqvist, Fabricio Oliveira
bullets: Addresses optimal control under parametric uncertainty, where surrogate errors can mislead gradient-based optimization.
Uses a physics-informed DeepONet to predict trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation and reuse the operator across targets and horizons.
Applies one parallel Newton correction to the dynamics, yielding second-order state-error control based on the residual alone.
On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, matches batched Adam and Ipopt accuracy at equal sample size while running 8× faster than Adam on GPU and 15× faster than Ipopt on CPU.

papers.abstract: A streamed video generator releases each chunk the moment that it is produced, so a safety decision that waits for the finished clip arrives after the harm has been seen. We measure a guardrail by exposure, the harmful frames a viewer is shown, and ask where a fixed moderation budget should be spent. The accurate detector reads decoded frames with a video language model and is too expensive for every chunk, so our guard reads hidden states the generator has computed already and spends a cheap score on deciding when to call it. On 599 streams from a distilled causal generator the undefended model shows 46.25 harmful frames of 81. The video model on every chunk leaves 0.91 frames at 80.1 scored per benign stream, and the same model triggered by our guard leaves 2.35 at 5.3. Spending that budget at random leaves 37.20 frames, so the gain is in the ordering, and a frame detector in the same role gives up almost six, so the judging stage must read the chunk as a clip. The ordering is worth more as the stream lengthens, and the guard carries to a second system. An independent guardrail model agrees with our oracle at $\kappa=0.74$, and a blinded audit by 50 participants puts its precision at 96.1% and recall at 82.8%. Warning. This paper contains examples of generated content that some readers may find disturbing or offensive in nature.
authors: Yuxin Cao, Ziqi Ding, Jiayu Zhang, Xianglin Yang, Wei Song, Jin Song Dong
bullets: Streaming generators can expose harmful frames before a completed-clip safety check finishes.
The guard uses generator hidden states to decide when to invoke an expensive video-language-model detector on decoded chunks.
On 599 streams, guard-triggered checking reduced exposure to 2.35 harmful frames using 5.3 scored chunks per benign stream, versus 37.20 with random allocation and 0.91 with checking every chunk.
Clip-level judging was substantially more effective than using a frame detector, and the ordering benefit increased with stream length and transferred to a second system.
An independent guard agreed moderately with the oracle (κ=0.74); a 50-person blinded audit measured 96.1% precision and 82.8% recall.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.
authors: Junyi He, Xu Peng, Chengming Xu, Sixiao Zheng, Donghao Luo, Chao Wen, Peng Tang, Xijie Huang, Chengjie Wang, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses weakened classifier-free guidance and negative prompting after diffusion distillation.
Separates positive and negative text conditions and combines their attention responses with opposite signs in one visual backbone.
Uses a Scale-Time Polarity Mixer to adapt prompt influence based on guidance scale and denoising timestep.
Achieves 81.46 VBench in four-step video generation and higher target-removal rates than corresponding teachers on NegElement-1K.
Evaluated across Wan2.1 and Qwen-Image using DMD and LCM distillation, supporting broad applicability.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGLE employs a fine-grained dataset to screen visually-grounded attention heads, followed by entity-aware grounding to extract target-specific regions. It then integrates hierarchical evidence construction and question-guided routing to select optimal view combinations, feeding them into the frozen MLLM to enhance fine-grained visual understanding. Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B demonstrate that EAGLE consistently improves performance across both backbones and achieves SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K compared with existing methods using the same backbone.
authors: Zhongjian Zou, Quan Qian
bullets: Addresses unreliable attention-head grounding and weak connections between local details and global scene context.
Screens visually grounded attention heads using a fine-grained dataset, then extracts entity-specific regions.
Builds hierarchical evidence and uses question-guided routing to select complementary image views.
Improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B across evaluations, achieving reported SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K with matched backbones.

Question-guided routing selects the final views for the frozen MLLM.

(b) HiDe’s token-wise crops lead to “silver”, whereas EAGLE combines “soda” and “can”, refines the region, and answers “green”.

papers.selection_reason: Improves frozen MLLMs for fine-grained high-resolution visual grounding and understanding.
papers.title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
papers.tldr: EAGLE improves fine-grained high-resolution image understanding by grounding target entities and routing hierarchical visual evidence into frozen MLLMs.

papers.abstract: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.
authors: Zihao Zheng, Hangyu Cao, Yulong Han, Xichang Wu, Zhihao Mao, Maoliang Li, Jiayu Chen, Hailong Zou, Donggang Cao, Xuanzhe Liu, Hong Mei, Xiang Chen
bullets: Addresses latent mismatch and navigation errors caused by asynchronous inference and communication delays on resource-constrained robots.
Identifies a compact Critical Subspace where action-relevant mismatch is concentrated and tracks it via fast-system feature drift.
Uses Critical Feature Drift Entropy for adaptive latent-refresh scheduling and Critical Drift Continuity for edge-side compensation during latency spikes.
Combines subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh, and continuity-guided compensation.
Reports 1.7–2.4 percentage-point success-rate gains, 2.7–10.0% lower amortized computation time, and 18.4–22.3% fewer FLOPs than the strongest baselines.

papers.abstract: Inference-time methods that lift a small open video generator toward a proprietary one are compared through preference scores, which never say how much of the gap to a target video they close. We introduce the oracle control ladder, which hands a fixed student progressively richer information from a target clip and reads the closure of each fidelity metric at each rung as an empirical headroom reference for the methods that must synthesize that information. On 954 clips of the principal student, a dense caption reproduces little of the appearance and almost none of the motion of a target, a first frame closes half of the appearance gap and a tenth of the motion gap, a depth video closes three quarters of the motion gap and leaves color untouched, and the two together close 64 to 94% of every fidelity gap across four teachers, while a second student agrees on the rungs that it accepts. An item response model forecasts which rung closes which clip with held-out AUC of 0.76 to 0.95 on the fidelity criteria and serves as the prior of a budgeted selection policy. When controls are free, a fixed dense-control rung is hard to improve upon, and once controls are priced the policy lies above the fixed-rung frontier at matched cost and survives critics that ruin critic-driven search.
authors: Ziqi Ding, Yuxin Cao, Kai Ye, Yaobo Yang, Wei Song
bullets: Preference scores do not quantify how much of a teacher–student fidelity gap inference-time methods close.
An oracle ladder measures empirical headroom by progressively giving the student captions, frames, and depth videos from the target clip.
Dense captions add little appearance or motion fidelity; first frames mainly help appearance, while depth strongly helps motion.
Combining first-frame and depth controls closes 64–94% of fidelity gaps across four teachers, with similar rung behavior for a second student.
An item-response model predicts useful control rungs (held-out AUC 0.76–0.95), supporting a budgeted policy that beats fixed-rung choices at matched cost.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.
authors: Hao Zhang, Bin Xiao, Kefeng Zhang
bullets: Problem: Sparse attention can reduce computation, but searching the entire visible history makes key retrieval a bottleneck for very long contexts.

Method: Partition history into independently indexed time buckets, organize keys into balanced directional groups, and use group centers for coarse page selection before refining candidates to select Top-K positions.
Implementation: Reordered pages, fused index-construction stages, shared fixed-candidate storage, and asynchronous index maintenance improve retrieval and inference efficiency.
Result: At 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection 4.70× over DSA and combined selection plus attention 35.60× over full attention.
Scope: The reported gains target long-context inference with incrementally arriving keys and prefix reuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of LRSA. (a) Each completed bucket is independently partitioned into capacity-balanced directional groups, which are packed into member pages. With the default capacities, the expanded page contains eight groups of eight keys, with one center per group. (b) Queries score group centers and select the Top-Kpage pages using the maximum group score within each page. Retrieved members are combined with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates, deduplicated, and scored to select the final Top-K positions for attention. papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically assigns a uniform advantage to every token. Token-reweighting heuristics like the 80/20 mask favor high-entropy tokens, but fail to measure a token's actual impact on the outcome. We formalize this impact as the forking value: the variance of the success probability over the policy's next-token choices. The expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance. Token credit is thus, in expectation over a prompt's responses, a fixed budget spent at the forks. This motivates weights that redistribute credit within a response. The forking value factorizes into a fork consequence, which requires costly continuations to estimate, and a fork probability, which the softmax provides. On Qwen3-8B-Base, this fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank at class-specific rates, revealing that most tokens carry negligible forking value. CreditFilter weights each token by an exponential window over the same rank. The window is calibrated to this fork-probability envelope, under an approximately flat fork consequence. CreditFilter needs no extra forward passes and is stabilized by difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback. Averaged over three seeds, it outperforms DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500 and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on AIME24 and AIME25. Its dynamically adaptive variant matches it. The ablations show that both parts matter: ranking tokens within each response rather than across the batch, and matching the window's decay rate to the envelope. Code is available at https://github.com/yoctta/CreditFilter.
authors: Hanqing Zhao, Liuyue Xie, Rong-Cheng Tu, Xu Zhang, Davide Modolo, Dacheng Tao
bullets: RLVR’s uniform token advantages overlook that only a small subset of tokens substantially affects outcome success.
The method defines token impact through forking value and uses softmax-derived fork probability as a cheap proxy.
It applies an exponential weighting window over each response’s within-response entropy rank, calibrated to the observed decay envelope.
Difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback stabilize training without requiring additional model evaluations.
Across three seeds on Qwen3-8B-Base, CreditFilter improves over DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500, 10.5 on AIME24, and 9.1 on AIME25; both within-response ranking and decay matching are important.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CreditFilter, a method for calibrating token weights in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) based on the 'forking value' of tokens, improving performance on mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.title: CreditFilter: Calibrated Token Weights over the Within-Response Entropy Rank for RLVR
papers.tldr: CreditFilter reallocates RLVR token credit toward within-response high-impact forks using calibrated entropy-rank weights, improving mathematical reasoning performance without extra forward passes.

papers.abstract: Driving world-action models generate planned trajectories through iterative action denoising, with each update depending on the preceding state. This sequential dependency incurs substantial inference latency, limiting timely planning. Speculative inference offers an opportunity to reduce this latency by predicting future denoising states for parallel target evaluation, but requires efficient proposal generation and suitable verification for continuous actions. We present Trailblazer-F, a speculative action-flow inference framework in which a lightweight drafter acts as a trailblazer, charting a candidate denoising path through the compact, structured waypoint space so that the target model can verify multiple steps in parallel and advance with fewer sequential updates. Our method maintains planning quality while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.Across all 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, Trailblazer-F maintains near-baseline planning performance, with PDMS changes of +0.04 and -0.08 points for SimWAM and DriveWAM, respectively. Paired inference measurements on an NVIDIA L20 GPU yield 2.31x and 1.55x speedups. Real-vehicle experiments on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin further demonstrate 1.96x and 1.37x speedups, together with close qualitative trajectory agreement with native sampling. our code is here https://github.com/DanileHaibo/Trailblazer-F
authors: Haibo Hu, Lianming Huang, Qiao Li, Nan Guan, Chun Jason Xue
bullets: Addresses latency from sequential action-denoising updates in driving world-action models.
Uses a lightweight drafter to predict candidate paths in compact waypoint space while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.
Enables the target model to verify multiple denoising steps in parallel.
Across 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, PDMS changed by only +0.04 for SimWAM and −0.08 for DriveWAM.
Achieves 2.31×/1.55× speedups on an NVIDIA L20 and 1.96×/1.37× on Jetson AGX Orin, with close qualitative trajectory agreement.

papers.abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same spherical range image encoding, yielding a fixed-size policy observation for end-to-end training and direct deployment without teacher--student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation. Experiments show that our range-image policies achieve stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, while ablations confirm the importance of the proposed sensing components. More visualizations and real-world videos are available at the \href{https://lidar-img.github.io/}
authors: Nian Liu, Xinyi Tong, Ming Ren, Long Ye, Zhaofeng He
bullets: Addresses depth-sensor sim-to-real gaps and drift-prone elevation maps.
Recovers real LiDAR angular sampling and reproduces it in simulation via GPU ray casting.
Encodes simulated and real returns identically as fixed-size spherical range images.
Enables end-to-end policy training and direct deployment without distillation, mapping, or adaptation.
Experiments report stronger transfer than depth- and elevation-map baselines; ablations support the sensing design.
