papers.tldr: Spherical range images with LiDAR-specific simulation enable robust, direct sim-to-real transfer for legged-robot locomotion.

papers.abstract: A visual agent acts on what it sees: it taps and types on a screen, or points on a camera image to show a robot where to act. One wrong step can fail its task, yet the right action is often among its own samples, passed over by its greedy decode. Choosing it is a visual judgment, since an action is best judged where it acts, not by its text or coordinates alone: as text, a tap is two numbers; drawn on the screen, it is the Post button of an empty draft. We find that this is decisive: given the screenshot and a tap's coordinates, a decision model chooses among GUI-R1-3B's samples significantly worse on average than when the tap is drawn where it lands. Bel turns this finding into a method that trains nothing and needs only a frozen policy's samples and an image on which each action can be drawn. It marks each candidate on its own copy of the image it acts on, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is the right decision, so that every kind of action shares one scale, and acts on another candidate only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails it by a margin. On recorded GUI steps, for each of three policies, Bel significantly beats greedy decoding on mobile, web and desktop screens alike and, on the same candidates, gives each a significantly higher mean step success than voting, CATTS, the trained GUI-Critic-R1 and two prompted Qwen3-VL judges shown the same marks; it also significantly improves the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B on every step-level test set. With GUI-R1-3B's thresholds unchanged, Bel significantly raises live AndroidWorld and MiniWoB++ task success for two other policies and robot-pointing success for three policies on each of two groups of benchmarks. Judging each action where it acts thus gives step-level policy improvement of visual agents without training, with significant gains for GUI agents and robot pointing.
authors: Jiajun Fan, Ziwen Wang, Zhaoyu Zhu, Changyi Yang, Neil He, Chaoran Cheng, Ge Liu
bullets: A single wrong action can fail a task, while the best action may be present among a policy’s sampled candidates but missed by greedy decoding.
Actions are evaluated visually by drawing each candidate at its execution location, rather than judging text or coordinates alone.
A frozen decision model assigns each candidate a shared probability of being correct and replaces greedy actions only when they fall below a threshold and margin.
Across recorded GUI steps, Bel outperforms greedy decoding, voting, CATTS, GUI-Critic-R1, and prompted visual judges.
It also improves live GUI task success and robot-pointing success across multiple policies and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.
authors: Xiaoyu Luo, Chengxing Lin, Jiaxin Huang, Jiale Liu, Jingyu Guo, Sirui Chen, Aolin Li, Shaoli Huang, Cheng-zhong Xu, Hui Kong
bullets: Addresses transformer context limits and redundancy in streaming visual observations.
Uses navigation context to prioritize informative evidence and combines language with spatial information.
Stores spatially grounded history in episode-local nonlinear fast weights as Adaptive Parametric Memory.
Maintains independent memories across decoder depths to support multiple abstraction levels and limit cross-layer error propagation.
Reports strong performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by letting a target model verify several draft tokens in one forward pass. Earlier neural drafters such as EAGLE extend each candidate sequence one token at a time. Recent work has turned to parallel drafters such as DFlash, which predict a whole block at once. Another approach uses n-gram retrieval to find an earlier occurrence of the current context suffix and copy the tokens that followed it directly into the draft. We introduce CoPyro, which feeds these copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of masks. The drafter learns from context which tokens to keep and which to revise as it predicts the block in its usual forward pass. Across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B, CoPyro improves overall acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with gains of 2.19-5.08% when trained on 100K samples. With DFlash trained on 710K samples, overall gains range from 1.08% to 2.00% across the tested model sizes and temperatures. Code generation benefits most in both settings. On Qwen3-8B, processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round in Transformers.
authors: Hong-Kai Zheng, Piji Li
bullets: Addresses the limited draft quality of parallel drafters by leveraging tokens copied from earlier matching context suffixes.
Feeds copied proposals into the drafter instead of masks, allowing it to retain or revise them during its normal block prediction.
Improves overall acceptance length for all four tested parallel drafters across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B.
Reported gains are 2.19–5.08% with 100K training samples and 1.08–2.00% with DFlash trained on 710K samples; code generation benefits most.
Proposal processing adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round on Qwen3-8B in Transformers.

papers.abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.
authors: Chong Tian, Yu Wang, Steve Liu, Qirong Ho, Xiuying Chen
bullets: On-device agents may violate policies after making only correct decisions earlier in the same session.
A correct release of one item can bias the agent to release a later item that remains restricted; repeated requests across sessions compound the risk.
The failure, termed correct-precedent generalization, appears in 13 open-weight models from nine developers.
History interventions suggest agents transfer the prior release decision instead of rechecking the new item's status.
Paired Decision Distillation (PDD) uses a weakly affected teacher and a LoRA adapter to restore safe rates to nearly 100% without extra prompts or model calls.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies a failure mode in on-device LLM agents (correct-precedent generalization) and proposes Paired Decision Distillation (PDD) to restore safe behavior, offering a technical solution for agent safety and adaptation.
papers.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Correct decisions can create harmful precedent in on-device LLM agents, while Paired Decision Distillation nearly eliminates the resulting policy violations.

papers.abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.

Ahmed, Franck Dernoncourt, Ryan A. Rossi
bullets: Defines StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects across seven categories, including concrete habits and patterns to avoid.
SP-Refine extracts a style profile with quoted evidence, drafts from user samples, and revises the draft twice using the profile and self-evaluated style scores.
Across three LongLaMP tasks and three LLMs, it beats the retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE/METEOR comparisons, with 10.2% average and up to 35.8% gains.
Ablations show profiles work best as revision guidance alongside user samples; profile-only generation performs worse, while a cheaper single implicit-inference call is competitive.
Oracle results indicate that larger refinement gains depend on reference information unavailable during inference.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces StylePrism and SP-Refine for personalized long-form text generation, making style extraction an explicit step in the inference process to improve personalization quality.
papers.title: Explicit Style Extraction for Personalized Long-Form Text Generation
papers.tldr: StylePrism and SP-Refine improve personalized long-form generation by explicitly extracting a user’s writing style and using it to guide iterative drafting and revision.

papers.abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. Starting from a 4-bit Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint, we apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to the vision, language, attention, and MLP modules and train with instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 examples. We compare this model with an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline, a zero-shot Qwen3-VL configuration, and additional internally evaluated alternatives. On the 1,198 valid CROHME test examples, the CROHME-only model obtains 524 exact matches (43.74%) and a corpus BLEU-4 score of 77.67, compared with 4.92% and 43.26 for the task-specific ViT baseline. An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment issue rather than an automatic benefit from more data. The principal contribution is therefore an evidence-backed, resource-efficient formulation of HMER as multimodal structural generation, together with a controlled data-composition ablation and an analysis of the remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct structure.

bullets: HMER must recover both symbol identities and two-dimensional mathematical structure, not just locally plausible tokens.
The approach fine-tunes Qwen3-VL-4B with rank-16 LoRA across vision, language, attention, and MLP modules using instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 data.
On 1,198 valid test examples, the model achieves 43.74% exact match and 77.67 corpus BLEU-4, versus 4.92% and 43.26 for an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline.
Adding 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples reduces exact match to 42.32%, indicating a domain-alignment problem rather than an automatic benefit from more data.
The study highlights a remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct mathematical structure.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA) of a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) for handwritten mathematical expression recognition, addressing resource constraints and multimodal structural generation.
papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Qwen3-VL for Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition
papers.tldr: A 4-bit Qwen3-VL adapted with rank-16 LoRA can recognize handwritten mathematical expressions as structured Symbol Label Graphs under limited compute, achieving 43.74% exact match on CROHME 2019.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.
authors: Pan Wang, Jie Peng, Zhimin Li, Jingxian Chen, Hui Ji, Huanrui Yang, Pengfei Zhou, Tianlong Chen, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between modality encoder cost and the predictive value of deeper processing.
Uses combinatorial anytime training to supervise fusion across all cross-modal depth combinations in one full-depth pass.
A training-free, validation-calibrated allocator selects the lowest-error depth configuration within each sample’s FLOPs budget.
On CMU-MOSEI, it stays within one percentage point of full-depth accuracy while reducing measured FLOPs by 45%, or 82% with skip-enabled training.
When vision dominates computation, it reduces visual depth for 56% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy; scope is demonstrated on CMU-MOSEI.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DepthMSA, a budget-aware framework for multimodal sentiment analysis that allocates different encoding depths to different modalities to reduce FLOPs while maintaining accuracy. papers.title: DepthMSA: Combinatorial Training and Budget-Aware Depth Allocation for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: DepthMSA adaptively allocates encoder depth across modalities to substantially reduce MSA computation while preserving sentiment accuracy.

papers.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.

Experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models show effectiveness and scalability; fused Ascend NPU operators reduce execution latency by up to 44.8%.

papers.abstract: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic. The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.

papers.abstract: Single-modality action-expert pretraining controls competition from visual shortcuts before vision--language--action (VLA) adaptation. Yet single-modality pretraining can impair the vision--language interactions needed for subsequent joint prediction. We construct a diagnostic model in which VA or LA pretraining can disable an initially active pathway for joint vision--language modeling. In this model, subsequent training with complete visual and language inputs cannot restore the pathway, even with unlimited adaptation. We therefore introduce Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP), a new action-expert pretraining stage that precedes full-input training. During this stage, visual and text tokens are randomly masked before entering the VLM. In this unified diagnostic model, SCAP can preserve the joint vision--language modeling pathway during pretraining and subsequent full-input training. Compared with direct full-input training, it can also reduce reliance on visual shortcuts and increase reliance on language instructions. SCAP consistently improves performance across four different VLA architectures. In real-robot experiments, it achieves 76.67% average success across three instruction-conditioned manipulation tasks, outperforming full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.
authors: Xiao Lin, Yaoxu Lyu, Ronghao Dang, Zhili Liu, Kaijing Ma, Yang Zhou, Dingning Liu, Runzhe Teng, Jun Cen, Shanghang Zhang, Chengju Liu, Qijun Chen
bullets: Single-modality pretraining can disable pathways needed for later joint vision–language prediction, and full-input adaptation may not recover them.
SCAP randomly masks visual and text tokens before they enter the vision–language model during pretraining.
The method preserves joint modeling while encouraging greater reliance on language instructions instead of visual shortcuts.
SCAP improves performance across four VLA architectures and reaches 76.67% average success on three real-robot manipulation tasks.
Its reported success is 25 percentage points higher than full-input pretraining in those experiments.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.
authors: Sunli Chen, Yun Zong, Qinhong Zhou, Xiaowen Qiu, Jiaben Chen, Zeyuan Yang, Chuang Gan
bullets: Addresses the blind interval in turn-based agent harnesses, where humans can disrupt robot actions before the agent can reassess.
Uses training-free, stateful Python tripwires that monitor policy execution, optionally query a compact VLM, and return control when conditions are met.
Evaluated with three VLAs and one WAM on 168 RoboCasa365 disturbance scenes in RoboHD, plus real-robot manipulation tasks.
With the strongest policy, TRIP improved safety from 61.3% to 81.3% and task success from 31.0% to 38.7% versus the same turn-based harness.
Real-robot tests showed successful completion of two manipulation tasks under human interference, where baseline approaches largely failed.

papers.title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
papers.tldr: TRIP lets robot agents program event-driven interrupts so they can react to human disturbances during policy execution instead of waiting for the action to finish.

papers.abstract: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.

Shows strong articulation and 3D pose recovery on Humanoids and DHRP-H1, including zero-shot transfer to real-world evaluation.
Public release of the dataset and code is planned to support further research.

papers.abstract: Vision-model-based robotic navigation has gained increasing popularity, yet existing approaches still struggle to deliver effective and efficient navigation performance, \textit{e.g.}, diffusion-based policies that require costly iterative denoising. In this work, we propose three improvements to bridge these gaps. First, we adopt a rectified flow framework to reduce the required inference steps to one while achieving comparable or even superior performance. Second, we leverage a bidirectional Mamba-based visual encoder that employs selective state-space modeling to more effectively capture bidirectional temporal dependencies across observation frames, even with longer input sequences. Most importantly, we find that na\"{i}vely combining these two components to balance accuracy with inference speed yields no further performance gains or even produces inferior results. Upon extensive analysis, we realized that the root cause lies in the fact that the Hydra-derived temporal context is shared unchanged across all flow timesteps, and timestep information is introduced only within the velocity network. This weak coupling limits the model's ability to adaptively exploit temporal visual features at different flow states. To address this, we propose a feature-wise timestep conditioning design that explicitly conditions the visual embedding on the flow timestep, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation, thereby restoring a meaningful gradient pathway and enabling coherent interaction between the rectified flow and the temporal encoder. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms both baseline and competitive methods.
authors: Xiaogang Wang, Debasish Mishra, Jia Hao Toh, Wangsheng Liu, Yash Shah
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of diffusion-based robotic navigation policies that require iterative denoising.
Uses rectified flow to reduce inference to one step and a bidirectional Mamba-based encoder to capture temporal dependencies across observations.
Finds that simply combining these components can hurt performance because temporal features are shared unchanged across flow timesteps.
Introduces feature-wise timestep conditioning of visual embeddings, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation and stronger interaction between the encoder and flow model.
Experiments across multiple datasets show consistent gains over baseline and competing methods, though specific metrics are not reported.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
authors: Zhikang Shi, Yuk Tung Samuel Fang, Hongyu Ding, Zixuan Chen, Yujin Wang, Junhui Guo, You Wu, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
bullets: Organizes 2,071 episodes into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, with later instructions referring to earlier objects or routes.
Evaluates three capabilities: historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization with route reproduction.
The latter two levels require agents to align historical memory with current episode frames without cross-episode frame transformations.
Introduces MemBridge, combining semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval.
Experiments show MemBridge benefits existing VLN agents, while memory-dependent navigation remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model's internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.
authors: Xuancheng Xu, Xiaofeng Wang, Yue Ma, Zheng Zhu, Bing-Kun Bao
bullets: Addresses motion-prior bias, poor localization of force-induced changes, and limited force-annotated data.

Uses a Physics Attribution Network to link force interventions to localized latent-state changes.
Applies self-supervised, physics-aware reinforcement learning on out-of-distribution videos to improve consistency and generalization.
Experiments report improved force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization.

papers.abstract: Successful agent interactions provide training data, but success alone does not determine which records a student should learn from. We examine experience selection for a 4B language agent as a component of continual agent learning. Nine selectors are compared across two fixed experience pools, eight initialization seeds, and two sampling seeds, yielding 288 trained students. Each student is evaluated on 128 development task groups with a common executor. With equal global selection freedom, 256 distinct contents, and 768 training presentations, optimizer-aware gradient selection reaches 81.45\% and 73.19\% success in the two pools. Its gains over global random selection are 8.25 and 5.96 percentage points; gains over global high-NLL selection are 4.10 and 4.05 points. All eight initialization-level contrasts are positive against both baselines in each pool. Relaxing coverage constraints improves gradient selection but reduces random-selection performance, showing that the ranking rule and selection space must be considered together. A separately frozen replication on 128 reserved task groups is complete; its equal-source gradient-minus-random and gradient-minus-high-NLL differences are +7.03 and +5.03 points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Reward models and LLM judges are routinely quantized to 4 bits so that scoring many candidates stays affordable, and the usual check is that benchmark accuracy barely moves. That check is close to blind. Across eight reward models from two families (0.6B-8B), three generative judges and four 4-bit quantizers, quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on RewardBench while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points (p = 1.00), because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to the quantization noise scale sigma: a Gaussian approximation Phi(-|m|/sigma) describes the aggregate rate, over-predicting it in all 30 scalar settings and failing for generative judges, and occupancy of the resulting vulnerability window falls from 25% to 7% with model size, which is what makes small judges fragile. The churn stays within noise under benign best-of-16 and becomes clear under adversarial pressure for some quantizers (146:54 harmful:helpful flips on one family, reversing sign on another). Downstream it changes what ships: across six (model, quantizer) pairs from two families, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection while only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, with selections changing 5-8x more often than answers in every pair, and the pair the benchmark calls identical (0.03 points, p = 1.00) still changes 34.5% of them. Benchmark churn ranks that downstream change (rho = 0.89); benchmark accuracy does not order it reliably. Held-out audits then locate the useful diagnostic in the margin rather than the Gaussian: every margin-based predictor orders flips identically (AUC 0.927), and on the level a directly measured churn rate wins in-distribution. As a routing signal it is matched by plain top-k. The contribution is the characterization, not the model.
authors: Omkar Shewale, Deepak Kumar, Divakar Kumar Yadav
bullets: Across eight reward models, three generative judges, and four quantizers, quantization changed 1.1–12.3% of RewardBench pairwise preferences while aggregate accuracy sometimes shifted by only 0.03 points.

Downstream, 14.6–65.7% of best-of-64 selections changed, versus 2.6–9.6% of final answers; benchmark churn tracked this change better than benchmark accuracy.
Margin-based predictors identified flips well (AUC 0.927), but directly measured churn was most useful in-distribution and was matched by plain top-k routing.

papers.abstract: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.
authors: Saurabh Chopra
bullets: Repository histories contain roughly 19 copies of current code typically, rising to 89 in mature projects; nine in ten tokens of a changed file already existed before the edit.
Exact-match deduplication removes none of these non-identical historical versions.
Near-duplicate file grouping reduces repetition to about two copies, but version-selection rules may retain old files when dates are ignored.
Sorting versions newest first fixes stale-version selection at minimal cost.
Benchmark fixes can persist through many later versions, requiring a separate all-version scan to remove them from training data.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models learn to forecast observations, but accurate short-term predictions do not necessarily produce physically coherent behavior over longer horizons. We investigate how incorporating physical structure can strengthen world models while retaining their underlying predictive objectives. Across token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems, we study conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics. In planetary motion, angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, while the benefits of temporal regularization depend on the accompanying physical objective and representation. In visual models, generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads produces more faithful trajectories and phase-space evolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of how physical structure participates in prediction: improvements in an auxiliary physical readout or a local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon behavior. Evaluations across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts further reveal where these benefits persist and where generalization remains limited. Our study supports physical structure as a practical means of improving predictive world models and provides a unified framework for understanding its effects on representations, learned transitions, and autonomous rollouts. The central lesson is that effective physical inductive biases should help models both represent physical regularities and use them to generate future states.
authors: Panayiotis Christou, Satyapragnya Kar, Flavjo Xhelollari, Parijat Dube, Rajarshi Das
bullets: Accurate short-term prediction alone may fail to produce physically coherent long-horizon behavior.
The study examines conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and structured dynamics in token-based and visual world models.
Angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous forecasting for planetary motion, while temporal regularization depends on the associated physical objective and representation.
Energy-based dynamics heads generate more faithful visual trajectories and phase-space evolution for mechanical systems.
Benefits vary across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts, showing that generalization remains limited.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates physical structure in predictive world models and long-horizon rollouts; directly fits world-model prediction.
papers.title: Where Structure Enters a World Model: From Predictive Fit to Physical Rollout
papers.tldr: Physical structure can improve world-model rollouts, but only when it directly shapes how future states are generated—not merely how they are represented or evaluated.

papers.abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.
authors: Tengfei Shao, Asma Rezaei, Ali Reza Kamali
bullets: Treating reports from shared sources as independent can double count evidence; instruction value depends on the receiver’s baseline.
The study constructs an exact reference over binary worlds with 0.65 single-report reliability and four dependence levels, then evaluates raw versus instructed answers on 2,976 worlds.
Agreement with the exact rule and improvement from instruction were distinct: some models already agreed nearly perfectly, while others gained modestly.
The prespecified dependence-level gain contrast was 0.0342 (95% interval 0.0303–0.0382); the grouping endpoint difference was not detected and was bounded within ±0.0031.
The authors recommend estimating paired Brier-score gain on labelled deployment items before adopting the instruction for a given receiver and prompt.

papers.abstract: General-purpose point tracking requires large-scale training data with diverse dynamics, yet existing datasets struggle to combine rich dynamic content, accurate scene geometry, and sufficient scale. We introduce TrajRealm, the first public synthetic point-tracking dataset to reach the ten-million-frame scale, constructed from games and embodied simulations. TrajRealm uses the rich environments and motion systems of modern games to capture diverse targets, activities, and interactions across diverse worlds, while embodied simulations add robot manipulation and indoor navigation data. The dataset provides RGB observations, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. These annotations provide precise, geometrically consistent supervision across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. We also build TrajRealm-Bench with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across diverse scenes. Benchmark evaluations reveal the strengths and limitations of existing trackers in handling complex motion and maintaining long-term point correspondences. Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
authors: Ni Yang, Weiguang Zhao, Jiafei Cao, Yankai Jiang, Haoyu Guo, Tao Yang, Chunhua Shen, Junting Dong
bullets: Combines game environments with embodied simulations to cover varied targets, interactions, robot manipulation, and indoor navigation.
Provides RGB, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D/3D point trajectories with geometrically consistent annotations.
Introduces TrajRealm-Bench, spanning eight Interaction and Locomotion categories for evaluating diverse tracking scenarios.
Benchmark results expose strengths and limitations of existing trackers, especially for complex motion and long-term correspondences.
Training on TrajRealm improves existing trackers on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-generated descriptions enrich zero-shot skeleton-based action recognition but repeat cues shared by confusable actions. Their contextual semantics also lack explicit links to skeleton features. To address these challenges, we propose CRAFT, which couples Concept Refinement and Feature-grounded Tokens. Hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring identify concepts that distinguish each action from its closest rivals. Unique-QDPP selects complementary descriptions within each semantic slot and prevents their reuse across slots. This bank supervises learnable concept tokens that read motion and context cues from each skeleton. On fixed NTU-60 and NTU-120 splits, CRAFT improves five baselines spanning four recognition paradigms. ZSL accuracy and GZSL harmonic mean increase on every baseline-split pair, by 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on average. Random-split experiments extend these gains to three datasets, including PKU-MMD. Code will be released after acceptance.
authors: Siyu Zhu, Feng Ding, Zixiao Jin, Kaizhi Li, Xin Dong, Haisheng Fu, Yuchen Zou, Guohe Zhang, Jie Liang
bullets: Targets redundant LLM-generated descriptions and weak links between semantics and skeleton motion.
Uses hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring to find concepts that distinguish confusable actions.
Selects complementary descriptions with Unique-QDPP and assigns them to separate semantic slots.
Learns concept tokens that extract motion and contextual cues from skeletons.
Improves ZSL and GZSL performance across five baselines and multiple splits, with average gains of 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on fixed NTU splits.

papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.

bullets: Targets the unresolved conflicts that arise when LLMs must satisfy competing values.
Decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.
authors: Xingyue Zhang, Yuxuan Bao, Jeffrey Keck, Erkan Istanbulluoglu, J. Nathan Kutz
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring transient landslide dynamics from post-event deposits or very short monitoring windows.
Uses latent-space temporal inference with shallow recurrent decoders trained on physics-based simulation ensembles.
Supports backward reconstruction from a single frame and forward prediction from a short initial sequence across runout regimes.
With 32 single-timepoint sensor observations, reconstruction NRMSE was below 5.8%.
Validation against observed deposits produced spatial correlation r = 0.843, compared with r = 0.853 for the calibrated simulator.

Stage 2 (Temporal Model): A separate network learns to map the terminal latent 𝐳𝑇 (augmented with positional encodings) to the complete preceding latent sequence ?̂?0,… , ?̂?𝑇 . Stage 3 (LAPIS Inference): At test time, only the terminal observation 𝐬obs 𝑇 is available. papers.title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains a student to match a teacher's output distribution. However, full-vocabulary KD requires costly output-head backpropagation. To reduce this cost, we introduce Distillation with Errors (DWE). Our key insight is that minibatch training already approximates the training gradient, so per-position backpropagation does not need to be exact. DWE therefore exploits the zero-sum structure of logit gradients to construct sparse paired gradient estimates whose expectation matches the full-vocabulary gradient. It then uses geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling to further reduce estimation variance. We prove that the estimator is unbiased and evaluate DWE's gradient estimation accuracy and training efficiency. At the same sampling budget, DWE reduces hidden-state and output-weight gradient MSE by 63.5% and 57.9%, respectively, compared with importance sampling. In off-policy KD, it achieves up to a $1.95\times$ output-head speedup and reduces training time by 10.4-15.7% relative to full-vocabulary KD. In on-policy distillation (OPD), it achieves up to a $2.20\times$ output-head speedup. DWE maintains competitive downstream performance in both settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/dwe-lab/DWE.
authors: Yuyang Zhang, Yuxin Li
bullets: Targets the high cost of backpropagating through the full vocabulary during knowledge distillation.
Builds sparse paired gradient estimates using the zero-sum structure of logit gradients, with geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling.
Proves the resulting gradient estimator is unbiased.
Reduces gradient-estimation MSE versus importance sampling and speeds up the output head in off-policy and on-policy distillation while maintaining competitive downstream performance.

This estimate enables backpropagation through only the selected output rows, at most 2K per token (d). The illustration uses K = 2.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we analyze multi-layer visual representations in large vision-language models (LVLMs) and examine the effectiveness of layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection. Representative LVLMs connect visual encoder features to a language model through a projector. In this design, deep visual encoder features carry high-level semantics and alignment with text representations, whereas shallow and intermediate layers retain information relevant to vision-centric tasks, such as local appearance and fine-grained shape. It is therefore important to choose layer representations and fusion methods according to the nature of the downstream task. Focusing on anomaly detection, we compare layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion across multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers, and examine from several perspectives how multi-layer visual representations affect downstream performance. By analyzing the resulting performance differences, we further discuss the contribution of each layer representation to anomaly detection and provide empirical insights into representation selection for vision-centric tasks.
authors: Satoshi Hashimoto, Hitoshi Nishimura, Mori Kurokawa
bullets: Deep layers provide semantic, text-aligned features, while shallow and intermediate layers preserve local appearance and fine-grained shape information.
The study compares individual layer features with multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection.
Experiments cover multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers.
Layer contributions are analyzed to provide guidance for selecting representations in vision-centric tasks.
The abstract reports empirical comparisons but does not specify datasets or numerical results.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.
authors: Xinnan Zhang, Zeyi Liao, Siliang Zeng, Zhongruo Wang, Jiaxiang Li, Xinyan Zhao, Huan Sun, Mingyi Hong
bullets: OPD failures include excessive length, repetition, performance degradation, and spurious agreement with the teacher.
The analysis identifies mismatched states where sampled-token updates fail to correct the teacher–student gap, characterized by the student’s probability mass on the teacher’s top-p tokens.
Gradients from mismatched states can interfere with learning at other tokens, making teacher imitation difficult.
A termination-token mismatch can suppress the student’s existing generation modes and steer sampling toward states where the teacher is unreliable.
The findings support SFT initialization and targeted correction of student–teacher mismatch states.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes learning dynamics of on-policy distillation for LLM post-training; relevant to LLM training and behavior.
papers.title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: This paper explains why on-policy distillation can destabilize language-model training by reinforcing student–teacher mismatches that distort future generations.

papers.abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.
authors: Huiyuan Tian, Chih-Yung Wen, Shijian Li
bullets: More CEM iterations can reduce predicted cost while causing planners to lose up to half of previously solved problems.
The world model’s predictions alone fail to reveal these planning failures.
The proposed check executes plans after each iteration and compares predicted actions with actions read back from predicted states.
It improves CEM and MPPI across three released world models with only 0.2%–3.1% additional planning time.
Reported success increases from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall, 0.56 to 0.94 on JEPA-WM, and 0.70 to 0.81 with MPC on Cube.

papers.abstract: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.
authors: Jinyuan Zhang, Shengshuo Jiao
bullets: Position-dependent dark zones require active probing, unlike timed outages where hovering is effective; the two appear identical when vision is first lost.

The module interfaces with an unchanged host controller and combines loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height correction, and an optional prior-map branch.
On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark with 1,920 flights, the full configuration achieved 88.5% worst-condition completion and outperformed the reported baselines.
Attached to SimpleFlight without retraining, it improved worst-condition completion to 86.5% and achieved 90% completion across tested speed conditions with no hard failures.
Diagnostics indicate that recovery depends primarily on asymmetric visual-inertial re-acquisition at vision return, with a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on held-out EuRoC windows.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
authors: Ruijia Yang, Ruikai Li, Zeyi Wen
bullets: Addresses inefficiency from either serial GPU time-sharing or inflexible whole-GPU partitioning.
Co-resides a persistent rollout engine with a learner on each GPU using CUDA MPS.
Uses host-memory optimizer state and layer-wise weight streaming to fit the learner beside rollouts.
A publication gate and step-time bound control policy staleness and compute sharing.
Across reported platforms and workloads, CTRL delivers 1.11–2.24× the throughput of stronger asynchronous baselines and consistently outperforms time-sharing and measured GPU splits.

papers.abstract: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.
authors: Shengxiang Xu, Liang Yao, Shuyi Chen, Yishu Wang, Shimin Di, Fan Liu, Bishun Yao, Hanghui Guo, Xinyu Liu, Chengye Liang, Yuyu Luo, Min-Ling Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed toolsets and task-specific experience accumulation in agentic remote sensing systems.
Uses execution feedback to evolve persistent tools and workflow knowledge while keeping the base model parameters fixed.
Acquires specialized tools on demand and distills successful executions into reusable agent skills.
Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench report substantial accuracy gains from the initial system and improvements over existing methods.
Scope: improvements depend on the availability of execution feedback and the harness’s ability to acquire and verify tools and skills.

papers.abstract: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.
authors: Haozhe Wang
bullets: Shows a periodic sequence where every transition has spectral radius below one, yet the period product is expansive.
Extends the construction to sufficient conditions for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling.
Derives a necessary-and-sufficient spectral-norm criterion for channel-wise-decay rank-one erasure, computable in O(d) time.
The criterion matched direct SVD on all 1,800 tested operators.
In a Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base replay, terminal gain rose from 0.99938 to 1.3977 under repeated text with feature and gate trajectories fixed.

papers.abstract: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io
authors: Ankit Pal, Guillaume Kugener, Sofia Volpi, Joshua Schwartz, Alex Idarraga, Pranav Rajpurkar, Gabriel A. Brat
bullets: Provides 41,909 training hand instances and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows from 68 procedure recordings, covering 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees.
Includes multi-sensor imagery metadata, hand landmarks and confidence, timestamps, eye gaze, and SLAM extrinsics when available.
Uses procedure-disjoint and leave-one-wearer-out evaluation with sensor-fused, human-reviewed, surgeon-adjudicated, and multi-view reference labels.
Across eight zero-shot methods, JointTransformer performed best at 14.95 mm PA-MPJPE; ego-pretrained methods transferred better to held-out wearers.
MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1% of evaluation rows, and a substantial surgical domain gap remains; the dataset and benchmark code are released publicly.

figures.caption: Figure 6: JRN architecture. The frozen backbone f (any of the eight evaluated methods) maps the input image I to a 21-joint prediction x ∈ R21×3 in camera frame. JRN is a 58,306-parameter two-headed MLP residual corrector. The pose head (blue, 32,831 params) consumes the root-relative pose x− x0 ∈ R63 and emits a 21× 3 root-relative residual δp. The translation head (orange, 25,475 params) consumes the root-relative pose concatenated with the raw wrist xyz, [x− x0, x0 ] ∈ R66, and emits a 3-D wrist correction δt broadcast to all 21 joints via 121. The corrected output is x̂ = x+ δp + δt · 121. Both heads are zero-initialized, so JRN equals the identity at t=0. The training loss panel reproduces the formal definition; targets are computed from the training partition only. Pose head and translation head are orthogonal on four of the five reported metrics (Appx. A.4): the pose head drives PA-MPJPE / MPJPE-RR / PA-P2D (translation-invariant under Procrustes), while the translation head drives Root err. MPJPE-abs depends on both heads; the full JRN trains them jointly.

Figure 4: Benchmark: zero-shot error with 95% PR-bootstrap CIs, and the effect of JRN. Ego-pretrained backbones (green) have the lowest zero-shot error among single-hand methods, 40% (JointTransformer) and 18% (WildHands) below the non-egocentric reference HaMeR. Left: PA-MPJPE (mm, vs Aria MPS). Right: PA-P2D (px); protocol as in Tab. 2. Circles: zero-shot, colored by model family, with CI bars; diamonds: +JRN.
