papers.title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
papers.tldr: EgoSurgHands introduces a real egocentric 3D hand-pose dataset and benchmark for open-surgery training, showing that egocentric pretraining improves transfer to unseen trainees while substantial domain gaps remain.

papers.abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.
authors: Faraz Tahmasebi, Michael Pellauer, Hyoukjun Kwon, Sitao Huang
bullets: Addresses prompt-specific dominant activation directions that fixed, offline-calibrated subspaces may miss.
Extracts dominant components during prefill, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer’s GEMM.
Reuses each prompt’s low-rank basis throughout decoding, avoiding weight modifications.
At comparable mixed-precision bit width, outperforms the referenced state of the art across six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters.
Recovers up to 46% of perplexity lost by 4-bit activations, with 4% prefill and 8% decoding overhead on Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PLoQ at one layer input, on an activation example (6 tokens, 12 channels; color: magnitude). Steps 1–3 and the INT8 GEMM are the offline mixed-precision method: a calibrated basis U , folded into the weights, gathers the directions that are large in every prompt into a block kept at 8 bits. PLoQ (dashed box) handles the remaining 4-bit part Xc, whose dominant direction depends on the prompt. Once per prompt, during prefill, it estimates that direction V from a sample of the prompt’s tokens (4). Each token’s component along it, C = XcV ⊤, is subtracted (5, 6); the remainder R has a smaller range and is quantized to 4 bits with clipping, and C to 4 bits on its own scale (7). C is restored through k extra rows VW⊤ c of the 4-bit GEMM (8). V and VW⊤ c are kept for decoding.

Figure 4. Activation magnitudes |X| over tokens and channels (max-pooled to a 128× 128 grid) for one WikiText-2 prompt on Llama3.2-1B, layer 15. From left to right: the original input; after QuaRot’s Hadamard rotation, all at 4 bits; what a calibrated 8-bit block leaves at 4 bits; and what PLoQ leaves at 4 bits after subtracting the prompt’s own 32 leading directions. The last two share one scale. Each title gives the mean per-token range, which sets the token’s 4-bit step. PLoQ narrows the calibrated block’s range by 12% at the attention input and by 47% at the down-projection input, where a few tokens carry very large values; averaged over all 16 layers, by 10% and 27%.

Figure 1. Four ways to treat the dominant activation directions, Llama-3.1-8B, W4A4KV4, 8k tokens. QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024b): a rotation, all activations at 4 bits. ResQ (Saxena et al., 2025): a calibrated eighth of the directions at 8 bits and the rest at 4. Per-prompt: each prompt’s own leading eighth at 8 bits instead, mapped into the 8-bit channels by a per-prompt block reflection. PLoQ: a calibrated block of 224 directions plus a per-prompt rank32 component with 4-bit coefficients. All but QuaRot at equal bits. (a) WikiText-2 perplexity. (b) Prefill time relative to ResQ on an RTX 4090, batch 1. Per-prompt is unfused: ResQ’s time plus its measured extra work; dotted: lower bound, at the GPU’s peak fp16 rate.

Figure 5. Per-prompt rank k at equal bits: 512 − k calibrated directions and k per-prompt ones (k = 0 is ResQ), Llama-3.1-8B, WikiText-2 at 8k tokens. Prefill time relative to ResQ (RTX 4090, batch 1); kernels are tuned for k = 32 (star) only. Hollow: whole 8-bit block per prompt (Fig. 1).

Figure 3. Energy of each input’s 4-bit part captured by k directions on held-out tokens: PLoQ’s, fitted on the prompt’s fit sample (solid); the calibrated ones (dotted); and the best for the scored tokens themselves (dashed, in-sample, not deployable). Vertical line: the rank PLoQ uses, which reaches 84–98% of the largest gap to the calibrated directions at a small overhead (Fig. 5). Llama3.2-1B, eight 8k-token WikiText-2 prompts; held-out tokens are outside the fit sample and after the first quarter; averaged over layers. The 4-bit part is everything outside the calibrated 8-bit block; at the down-projection input, which has none, the whole input.

papers.selection_reason: Prompt-adaptive low-bit quantization of LLM activations and KV cache for memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
papers.tldr: PLoQ improves 4-bit LLM activation quantization by adapting a low-rank protection subspace to each prompt without changing model weights.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.
authors: Yalin Yang, Xiao Huang, Yanan Wu, Hao Yang, Ryan Zhenqi Zhou
bullets: Weight-space programming improved reference-frame accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% and StepGame accuracy from 19.2% to 33.7%; permuting the edit removed the gain.
A rank-1 LoRA trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8% on the two target tasks using 0.09% trainable parameters.
Without worked-solution supervision, the adapter failed the learning gate; generalization was partial across templates, difficulty levels, and heading-answer combinations.
Adaptation reduced distance-task accuracy from 94% and 92% to 0–2% and caused outputs to apply the StepGame solution pattern to distance questions.
The comparison exposes a trade-off between larger target-task gains and preservation of neighboring skills.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Accuracy of the base model, the weight-space-programming patch p50c and its variants, prompting baselines and LoRA adapters on the original reference-frame (128 items) and StepGame (200 items) benchmarks. Bars show the mean over seeds and dots the individual seeds; the dashed line marks the threeseed mean of p50c. Randomly permuting the elements of p50c’s weight change within each tensor returns accuracy to the base level, prompting does not improve on p50c, and LoRA adapters trained on worked solutions approach ceiling on both tasks even at rank 1, provided the supervision includes the intermediate steps.

Figure 2: Accuracy of rank-16 LoRA adapters trained with step-by-step supervision on 448, 1,792 and 7,168 examples (reference-frame scenes plus StepGame problems in a fixed 2:5 ratio), evaluated on the original benchmark items with three seeds (dots) and their mean (line). The dashed line is the three-seed mean of the weight-space-programming patch p50c. Accuracy is already far above p50c with 448 examples and saturates by 1,792.

Figure 3: Generalisation of LoRA adapters to parts of the input space removed from training, measured on the corresponding subsets of the original benchmark items (three-seed means). (a) Accuracy of p50c, the adapter trained without the held-out part, and the adapter trained on everything. (b) StepGame accuracy by dataset difficulty level for p50c, an adapter trained on all levels, and an adapter trained on levels 1–5 only; the shaded region contains levels absent from that adapter’s training data. Accuracy is highest on unseen sentence templates and lower on held-out difficulty levels and heading–answer combinations.

Figure 4: Effect of training on two tasks outside the training data: comparing straight-line distances between points on a map, and the same comparison phrased in terms of product price and weight (128 original items each, three seeds). (a) Accuracy, with seed values as dots and the mean printed above each bar. (b) Percentage of outputs that contain the StepGame worked-solution template. The weight-spaceprogramming patch p50c answers more than 90% correctly and never uses the template; every LoRA adapter applies the StepGame template to almost every item and answers with a direction label, so its accuracy falls to between 0% and 2%.

Table 2: Accuracy on the original benchmark items (correct items per seed and mean). Changed or trainable parameters are given as a fraction of the language-model parameters. p50c is the published weightspace-programming patch; “further closed-form edit” is the best submitted candidate of Section 4 (one seed). The shuffled-delta rows are two independent permutations, each evaluated with seed 0. An asterisk marks conditions that meet the improvement criterion of Equation 2 on that task.

papers.selection_reason: Spatial reasoning via weight-space programming and LoRA, relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.tldr: Supervised rank-1 LoRA adaptation dramatically improved spatial reasoning but caused severe interference on related distance-comparison tasks, while weight-space programming delivered smaller gains with better skill preservation.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.
authors: Sibi Gokul, Jyoti Prakash Meher
bullets: Targets two failure modes: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep reasoning steps.
Uses auxiliary heads to supervise exact canonical execution states and keep latent trajectories on valid computational manifolds.
Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, RoPE primarily recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%).
Combining RoPE and ORION yields complementary additive gains on joint length-depth extrapolation.
Negative controls show that exact canonical alignment is necessary; hashed state statistics do not constrain depth extrapolation.

figures.caption: Figure 7: The ORION architecture on both domains. An exact simulator emits the canonical state Φ(S) = (µ, ν, ω, T, ans) at every execution step; five read-out heads decode it from one shared latent, and their losses are added to the language-modelling objective. The answer head is one probe among several rather than the privileged output. The identical wiring runs on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT, which is what lets the contrastive term act across domains.

Figure 3: Canonical-state pretraining transfers across domains. Exact match during adaptation to the other domain under an equal 800-step budget, using five seeds. Models are initialized from scratch, from a Transformer pretrained on the source domain, or from an ORION model pretrained on the source domain. The ORION initialization improves target-domain held-out performance over Transformer pretraining by +0.085 ± 0.041 for FOLDING→GRIDSHIFT and +0.035 ± 0.013 for GRIDSHIFT→FOLDING. The improvement is positive in every seed in both directions.

Figure 2: ORION composes with RoPE on depth extrapolation. (a,b) Exact match at execution depths 5–8, after training at depths 1–4, for RoPE alone and ORION + RoPE on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. Bands show ± one standard deviation over three seeds. Printed values give the pairedby-example difference at each depth; stars indicate p < 0.05. Across all held-out depths, ORION + RoPE improves over RoPE by +0.016 on FOLDING (p = 0.036) and +0.024 on GRIDSHIFT (p = 0.002). (c) The corresponding difference across model widths in the five-seed scaling ladder. The gains are +0.000, +0.004, and +0.082 at 3.5M, 11M, and 26M parameters, respectively; the largest model favors the combined condition in all five seeds.

Figure 1: ORION + RoPE keeps computing the canonical state beyond the training depth. Exact accuracy of the canonical-state read-outs by execution depth (seed 0; shaded region: training depths). (a, b) The answer set read directly from the latent at the decision position, without autoregressive decoding, on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. (c) The occupancy map on FOLDING. With absolute positions the read-outs collapse at the first unseen depth (0.04, 0.19, 0.06); with RoPE they remain at 0.63, 0.67 and 0.85 at depth 5 and decay gradually, so the state is still being tracked where it was never supervised.

Figure 4: Canonical supervision confines the latent trajectory. The final-layer hidden state at each executed operation is one point per step, projected on the two leading principal components of the in-distribution states and expressed in units of their spread. Arrows: mean step-to-step displacement of 800 paths through each cell; bold path: mean position from step 1 (square) to step 8. The baseline moves 1.18 spreads per step with no coherent direction; ORION + RoPE moves 0.44 along a coherent field. The effect comes from the supervision, not the positional encoding (0.45 for ORION without RoPE, 1.36 for RoPE alone).

Figure 9: Layer-to-layer linear CKA within each model on FOLDING (seed 0, 384 in-distribution prompts). Both models show the same smooth block structure, with adjacent layers above 0.97 and the embedding layer the most distinct. Canonical supervision does not reorganise the layer hierarchy. Note the colour scale starts at 0.90; on an absolute scale the two panels are nearly identical, which is the point.

Figure 5: An execution trace in the FOLDING domain. Each operation reflects part of the sheet onto the rest and concatenates the stacks, so layer count grows with depth while the footprint shrinks. The canonical state Φ(St) is the stack-valued geometry at each step; the query is a punch through the final stack, scored by exact set match over the original cells it perforates.

Figure 6: An execution trace in the GRIDSHIFT domain. Cyclic row and column shifts permute origin labels over a grid whose extent never changes, so unlike FOLDING the state size is independent of program length. The canonical state is the origin-per-cell permutation and the query asks which positions hold marked origins after execution.

Figure 10: Degradation on FOLDING, from the reduced-budget surface sweep. (a) Exact match against execution depth at the training state sizes; the shaded band is the trained range and the printed values are the endpoints at 2×. The rotary conditions degrade gradually while the two absolute-position conditions fall off a cliff at the first unseen depth. (b) The joint surface for ORION + RoPE over both axes, every cell labelled with exact match; red lines mark the edges of the training region and n/a marks a combination the generator cannot produce. Reading up the left columns shows depth costing accuracy gradually; reading across to the right column shows the size axis costing all of it at once, at every depth. The size axis is not drawn as a separate curve because all four conditions coincide on it (0.195, 0.190, 0.169 and 0.170 at S/Strain = 1.33).

Figure 11: Per-algorithm exact match on the CLRS pilot (single seed). (a) In-distribution (n = 16). (b) The preregistered out-of-distribution endpoint, the mean of the length and structural axes. papers.selection_reason: Improves transformer length/depth extrapolation via canonical-state supervision and RoPE, relevant to LLM architecture and long-context research.
papers.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
papers.tldr: ORION improves Transformers’ systematic generalization by supervising exact canonical execution states, addressing depth-related state drift alongside RoPE’s handling of long-sequence positional corruption.

papers.abstract: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.
authors: Niccol\`o Ronchetti
bullets: Long-context degradation stems from hidden-state drift, MiniLM’s 256-token truncation, and final-token signal dilution.
Length-routed dual banks and strided window pooling improve long-context Content Harm Moderation LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 and fused FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886.
Bank routing adds no latency overhead, while a long-context embedding model is evaluated as another training-free adaptation.
Sentence-embedding kNN stays near random for RAG hallucination detection; length-matched hidden states recover medium-length performance but remain weak beyond 1,000 tokens.
The study evaluates training-free adaptations using small reference banks across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-context prompt processing and hidden-state drift in LLM guardrails, fitting long-context model research.
papers.title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
papers.tldr: kNNGuard degrades sharply on long prompts, but length-aware banks and strided pooling substantially restore harmful-content detection while hallucination detection remains difficult at extreme lengths.

papers.abstract: Language models assign different probabilities to token sequences that decode to the same string. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), a trainer that re-encodes sampled text may train on a different token sequence with the same reward. We ask how far this moves a training update, and whether the movement has a consistent direction. From one checkpoint, we compare updates on the same rollouts, canonical and with selected tokens split into two pieces, against an update on a different batch. On Qwen2.5-0.5B with three-digit addition, splitting about one token in 25 moves the update 0.556 times as far as replacing the batch. The ratio rises with the fraction split in four models and depends on which tokens are split; within a checkpoint, the displacements share a direction across batches. In a tabular model with one table per tokenization and a single sampled string, we prove that whenever two strings below an unsampled prefix differ in probability, only the zero full-gradient step agrees across tokenizations, however it is weighted. In an audit that decodes and re-encodes resampled rollouts, re-encoding touches up to 5.2% of rollouts but at most 0.08% of tokens, far below the split fractions we test. Training on fixed rollouts, the canonical arm finishes ahead in 14 of 18 pre-registered pairs; the interval for the mean accuracy difference includes zero over all pairs and excludes it only under the registered exclusion rule, which favours the canonical arm.
authors: Zhe Dong, Fang Qin
bullets: Re-encoding the same text changes token-level probabilities and therefore the RLVR training update despite leaving rewards unchanged.
On Qwen2.5-0.5B, splitting roughly 1 in 25 tokens moved the update 0.556 as far as using a different batch; the effect increased with split frequency and varied by token.
Update displacements tended to share a direction across batches within a checkpoint.
A tabular analysis proves that, when tokenization-dependent probabilities differ, only a zero full-gradient step is guaranteed to agree across tokenizations.

In an audit, re-encoding affected up to 5.2% of rollouts but no more than 0.08% of tokens; canonical training finished ahead in 14 of 18 pairs, though overall accuracy evidence was inconclusive under the stated analysis.

papers.title: How Far Does Lossless Re-tokenization Move an RLVR Update?

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.
authors: Ran Zou, Yang Liu
bullets: Across models, draws, and paraphrases, prediction errors are strongly shared; averaging 20 draws adds no accuracy and can cause overconfidence if treated as independent.
A major error source is describing each feature’s effect in isolation rather than conditional on the other features.
Compared with the best classical prior, LLM centers clearly help on 1 of 4 benchmarks, marginally help on 2, and worsen mean RMSE on 1.
LLM-reported uncertainty is unreliable; estimating prior scale from data reduces the harm of an incorrect center four-fold versus a unit-variance prior.
An external test found mixed outcomes: the center helped on 6 of 18 problems and hurt on 4; evidence-weighted mixtures were safer than a hard trust gate.

(3) The priors are compared with zero-centered adaptive priors on 100 paired small-sample splits, with memorization controls, an error-dependence measurement and a pre-specified external test.

papers.selection_reason: Audits the use of LLMs as priors for small-sample Bayesian regression, evaluating their accuracy and uncertainty reliability.
papers.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
papers.tldr: LLM-elicited Bayesian regression priors are highly correlated, often miscalibrated, and provide inconsistent benefits, so data-adaptive safeguards are needed.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables real-time streaming generation, with each generated chunk serving as historical context for subsequent generation. To avoid the memory explosion of backpropagation through time, previous self-rollout methods typically truncate cross-chunk gradients or detach historical latents. As a result, earlier denoising computations receive no downstream feedback through the generated history on how to synthesize frames that facilitate subsequent generation, leading to visual drift and structural collapse as rollouts extend. To address this limitation, we propose Hindsight Forcing, which allows historical chunks to learn directly from future outcomes by decoupling forward generation from backward credit assignment via a latent straight-through bridge. In the forward pass, each chunk completes a full multi-step rollout to update the KV cache. In the backward pass, the bridge routes gradients from future losses back to a single selected denoising step per historical chunk, training both the context writer and historical denoiser on shared parameters without retaining the full trajectory graph. Remarkably, Hindsight Forcing requires no additional model parameters, architecture modifications, or separate trajectory replay. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that Hindsight Forcing outperforms existing baselines in overall visual quality and dynamic motion, while ablation studies validate the benefit of supervising historical denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/haonanAN309/Hindsight-Forcing.
authors: Haonan An, Yihang Tao, Yu Guo, Renlong Chen, Jiasheng Zhang, Yuguang Fang
bullets: Addresses visual drift and structural collapse caused by detached or truncated gradients across generated video chunks.
Uses a latent straight-through bridge to separate full forward rollout from efficient backward credit assignment.
Routes future gradients to one selected denoising step in each historical chunk, jointly training context writing and historical denoising.
Requires no extra parameters, architectural changes, or separate trajectory replay.
Experiments on VBench report better overall visual quality and dynamic motion than existing baselines; ablations support historical-denoising supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Hindsight Forcing. (a,b) In the illustrated training pipelines, downstream gradients stop at the historical KV cache or latent inputs, respectively. (c) Hindsight Forcing extends downstream supervision to both history encoding and generation. papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that visual tools can improve multimodal reasoning. However, the effects of tools vary substantially across samples, and benchmark accuracy alone does not reveal whether tool interactions are beneficial or redundant. We present $R^2$, a framework that recognizes and reduces redundant visual tool use in vision-language models. We first introduce a sample-level Category Analysis of Tool Utility (CAT), which categorizes samples according to whether a model can benefit from tools. This analysis reveals that benchmark scores may obscure a model's tool-use ability. Across seven benchmarks, samples benefiting from tools account for at most 12.44% of each benchmark, while the majority gain little from tool interaction or are even harmed by it. To assess individual calls, we propose the Visual Feedback Dependency (VFD) metric, which compares the likelihood of the same subsequent reasoning under actual and alternative visual feedback without an external evaluator or trajectory regeneration. Redundancy-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO) combines this dependency signal with a category-conditioned base call cost to assign relative efficiency advantages among correct trajectories, supplementing outcome-based supervision. Across the seven benchmarks, RA-GRPO reduces the mean number of tool calls by 12.39% relative to Vanilla GRPO at comparable benchmark accuracy. Evaluated by tool-utility category, RA-GRPO improves category macro-average accuracy over Vanilla GRPO by 3.35 percentage points.
authors: Yilin Zhao, Jinyu Wang, Wenming Yang
bullets: CAT classifies samples by whether visual tools help, revealing that tool-benefiting samples comprise at most 12.44% of each of seven benchmarks.
VFD measures whether a tool call affects subsequent reasoning by comparing actual versus alternative visual feedback, without external evaluation or trajectory regeneration.
RA-GRPO uses VFD and category-conditioned call costs to reward efficient, nonredundant tool use alongside outcome correctness.
RA-GRPO reduces mean tool calls by 12.39% at comparable accuracy and raises category macro-average accuracy by 3.35 percentage points over Vanilla GRPO.

The two calls receive VFD scores of −0.0183 and −0.0048. papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.
authors: Chris Gu, Marco Andono Sie, Nathan Zhou, Christopher Potts, Julie Kallini
bullets: VLMs often process hundreds of visual tokens, creating unnecessary inference cost when only part of an image matters.
DTM uses a lightweight delete gate to score contextualized tokens, trains deletion differentiably, and physically removes tokens during inference.
The framework is extended to bidirectional multimodal encoders and decoder-only models, producing V-MrT5Gemma2 and V-MrGemma3.
With 80% visual-token deletion—about 60% fewer FLOPs—DTM outperforms FastV on ChartQA and TextVQA while retaining 90–96% of unpruned performance.
Benefits increase at higher deletion rates and are strongest for document, chart, and scene-text reading tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dynamic Token Merging (DTM) in encoder–decoder and decoder-only VLMs. (a) V-MrT5Gemma2 deletes selected visual tokens before encoder layer k, retaining all text tokens. The shortened encoder output feeds the decoder’s merged self- and cross-attention. (b) V-MrGemma3’s prefill uses bidirectional attention within images and causal attention for text, caching the full prompt before the gate and the compacted prompt after it; decoding reuses these caches and appends generated K/V without further deletion. Both diagrams show hard deletion at inference. The gate and deletion rule are the same in both architectures; only where the gate takes effect differs.

Figure 2: One 60%-trained T5Gemma 2 1B–1B checkpoint (V-MrT5Gemma2) across inference budgets, deletion after layer 5. Each curve holds one task- and method-specific checkpoint fixed and evaluates it at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate, 60%, is highlighted. DTM’s advantage widens as the inference budget tightens beyond the training target.

Figure 6: T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 language-backbone architectures. Visual tokens enter after SigLIP encoding, pooling, and image projection. (a) T5Gemma 2 uses a bidirectional encoder and a decoder with merged self- and cross-attention. Each decoder block projects the final normalized encoder states H into its own keys and values. (b) Gemma 3 uses a decoder-only backbone. Here Le and Ld denote encoder and decoder depths: both are 26 for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B and 18 for 270M–270M; Gemma 3 4B has L = 34 decoder blocks.

Figure 7: Matched-rate evaluation on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (V-MrT5Gemma2), deletion after layer 5. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 60% and 80% deletion; at 20–40%, the methods are close.

Figure 8: Matched-rate evaluation on Gemma 3 4B (V-MrGemma3), deletion after five decoder layers during prompt prefill. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. DTM leads on nine benchmarks at 80% and six at 60%; at 20–40%, the methods are close.

Figure 4: Spatial evidence retention at matched 80% visual token deletion after layer 5. Bars show the mean percentage of evidence patches retained on the same eligible questions for each model–dataset pair; dashed lines mark the expected retention of random deletion. T5 1B, T5 270M, and G3 4B denote T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, and Gemma 3 4B. DTM retains the most evidence in 22 of 24 comparisons.

Figure 3: One 60%-trained Gemma 3 4B checkpoint (V-MrGemma3) decoder-only across inference budgets, deletion after five decoder layers during prefill. Each curve holds one checkpoint fixed across deletion rates from 10% to 90%, with 60% highlighted. V-MrGemma3 shows the same widening advantage at 80–90% deletion.

Figure 5: Soft and hard visual token deletion in DTM. Vision and text tokens, denoted as svi and sti , are processed normally from layers 1 through k − 1. The hidden states before layer k are entered into the deletion gate, producing a score for each token. During hard deletion, hidden states with gate scores less than τ are pruned; the gate scores are applied as biases to only the remaining pre-softmax attention scores. Soft deletion adds gate scores to key columns; hard deletion removes sv1 and sv3 and retains the text tokens.

Figure 22: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for Gemma 3 4B on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%); shading marks L5. The attention-based selectors improve with later deletion on this backbone, while DTM stays nearly constant and is highest at 40–80%.

Figure 23: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for T5Gemma 2 270M–270M on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%); shading marks L5. The smallest backbone benefits most from later deletion, especially at 80%.

Figure 21: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched training and evaluation deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%). The horizontal axis gives the number of layers before deletion; shading marks L5. DTM is nearly flat across depth, whereas FastV and φ-R peak at L5 and fall at L6 at every rate.

Figure 16: Checkpoint reuse across deletion budgets at L5. Rows specify training targets; grouped columns specify inference deletion. Gray diagonal cells show matched scores, with the strongest method in bold and underlined. Off-diagonal cells show St(e) − Se(e); negative values favor training at the evaluation rate. All cells average the same ten benchmarks equally. Red shading deepens with the size of the penalty. A 60%-trained DTM checkpoint used at 80% costs at most 0.6 points on average, and on Gemma 3 even a 20%-trained DTM checkpoint loses less at 80% than any baseline.

Figure 9: Matched-rate evaluation on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, deletion after layer 5. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. The advantage emerges at higher deletion rates on the smallest backbone: DTM leads on 1, 3, 7, and 8 benchmarks at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%.

Figure 27: Randomly sampled ChartQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (1 of 2). Each row shows the input with its question and gold answer, then the 52 of 256 visual tokens kept by each method in full contrast (outlined), with deleted patches washed out. Below each panel: the prediction and its relaxed-accuracy score. Blue: DTM; gold: FastV; magenta: φ-R; green: Random. DTM concentrates its budget on labels, tick values, and bar ends.

Blue: DTM; gold: FastV; magenta: φ-R; green: Random. All three informed selectors keep much of the scene text; they differ in which words remain.

Figure 26 shows one way the attention-based selectors spend budget that DTM does not. On Gemma 3, FastV and φ-R keep the four corner patches of the image at median rates of 0.50 and 0.42, above the uniform rate of 0.20 on nine of ten benchmarks, whereas DTM keeps them at 0.02–0.12 on every model and benchmark. The two attention-based selectors also agree with each other far more than either agrees with DTM (median Cohen’s κ of 0.59, against 0.29 and 0.30), while DTM’s keep-sets agree across the three separately trained backbones (median κ 0.63, against 0.34 for FastV and 0.29 for φ-R). Gates trained on different models thus converge on similar selections.

Figure 20: Sensitivity to deletion depth on DocVQA. Models are separately trained and evaluated at 40% (dotted) or 80% (solid) deletion with the gate after each layer. The horizontal axis gives the number of layers before deletion; shading marks L5, the setting used in our main experiments. On T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, the attention-based selectors drop when they read the first global-attention layer (L6), whereas DTM does not.

Table 2: Matched-rate evaluation at 40% and 80% visual token deletion for T5Gemma 2 (1B– 1B) and Gemma 3 (4B), deletion after layer 5. Each score comes from a model trained and evaluated at the given deletion rate δ; Base is the unpruned model fine-tuned in the same way. Bold marks the best method per column within each model; each task uses its own metric (Section 5). The gray row gives the percentage of language-model FLOPs saved, which is the same for every method. Figures 2 and 3 include 60%, and Figures 7–9 (appendix) show 20–80%. DTM’s lead grows with the deletion rate on both architectures and is largest on DocVQA, ChartQA, and TextVQA.

Figure 10: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. papers.abstract: Video fusion integrates complementary information in multiple source video streams into a single sequence for complete scene perception. Existing methods perform frame-wise fusion and lack unified spatio-temporal modeling across sequences, damaging temporal coherence across sequences. When dealing with degradations, they also ignore temporal dynamics and overload a single network with diverse degradations, leading to limited and imbalanced degradation suppression. To address these issues, we propose V2VFusion, the first unified video-to-video fusion framework that directly generates temporally coherent, high-quality fused videos from degraded multi-source inputs. By reformulating video fusion as a video-to-video conditional generation problem in latent diffusion space, our approach holistically models spatio-temporal dependencies across entire sequences and intrinsically ensures sequence-level consistency. On this basis, a text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet bridges high-level textual degradation descriptions with low-level visual priors, enabling interpretable and controllable guidance for structure-preserving fusion beyond purely data-driven conditioning. To handle heterogeneous and compound degradations, a state-modulated degradation-aware hierarchical mixture-of-experts module decouples expert selection into diffusion-state-aware filtering and degradation-aware routing. It prevents unreliable routing and fosters expert specialization to mitigate representation conflicts among diverse degradations. Experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus video fusion tasks and complex degradations validate that V2VFusion surpasses existing methods in fusion quality and temporal stability. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenDoubleJ/V2VFusion.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Han Xu, Yunfei Huang, Zhuoya Zhang, Guangcan Liu, Jiayi Ma
bullets: Targets frame-wise fusion methods that fail to model sequence-level spatio-temporal dependencies and diverse degradations effectively.
Reformulates video fusion as conditional video-to-video generation in latent diffusion space for improved temporal consistency.
Uses text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet to provide interpretable, controllable structure-preserving guidance.
Introduces a diffusion-state-aware, degradation-aware mixture-of-experts module for heterogeneous and compound degradations.
Experiments across infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus fusion report improved fusion quality and temporal stability over existing methods.

papers.abstract: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.

Expands evaluation beyond speech-focused discourse forms.

Covers English-language fictional texts; broader generalization is not established.

papers.abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.
authors: Kartikeya Bhardwaj, Mohammed Almousa, Chaitanya Mullapudi, Ananth Balasubramanian, Nithin Ramesan, Tuc Nguyen, Harris Teague
bullets: Targets flat quantization loss surfaces and optimization difficulties in 2-bit and sub-2-bit channelwise quantization.
Introduces a continuous relaxation of the quantization-aware training process with dynamically changing bitwidth.
Provides theoretical and empirical insights into why gradual bitwidth changes can improve QAT.
Reports up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision tasks and 7.7% on natural language tasks versus leading QAT methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) An example of our proposed RelaxQAT bitwidth schedule which gradually and smoothly reduces the bitwidth. The gradient of the schedule 0 whenever it is approaches 2-bits; this helps to ease into the 2-bit precision instead of an abrupt change. (b) Prior progressive quantization methods reduce the bitwidth suddenly during training like UPQ, or (c) keep it the same throughout.

Figure 7. (a) ParetoQ SEQ simulation for a 1-d optimization problem. QAT gets stuck near the minimum point around step 2000 and stays there until the end of training (10000 steps). (b) RelaxQAT (with just a half cycle bit schedule) converges within the first 2000 steps.

Figure 6. (a-d) Clip-then-Round operation in the existing SEQ (Eq. (2)) creates integers at the extremes (see vertical red dotted lines) since the round operation follows the clip. As the bitwidth reduces, the extreme integers are suddenly lost (e.g., from {−15, 15} to {−13, 13} and so on). This means that a training assumes that the previous range of integers (say {−15, 15}) was available until k = 2b−1 reduces sufficiently; once k is sufficiently small, the round abruptly moves on to the new range of integers (i.e., {−13, 13}). The sudden change in integer ranges can cause loss spikes (similar to UPQ (Lee et al., 2025)) and unstable training behavior. (e-h) RelaxSEQ employs the Round-then-Clip operation (Eq. (3)) which keeps the extremes in floating point as the k reduces. The range of the distribution changes slowly and the extremes stay floating point until the end of the schedule. This causes the loss to change smoothly as the bitwidth shrinks.

Figure 3. (a) A simple 1-d function to minimize. (b) The 1-d function above results in a highly complex 2-d, 2-bit quantization loss surface (generated using LSQ) where the width of the hyperplanes (defined as the flat regions between integer changes) increases with larger scales. Red line shows the QAT trajectory.

Figure 2. ParetoQ SEQ with a bitwidth schedule loses extreme integers as k = 2bt−1 decreases with a shrinking bitwidth. RelaxSEQ shows a smooth change in extreme values which results in a smoothly changing loss.

Figure 5. Existing SEQ (Clip-then-Round) with a bitwidth schedule shows an unstable training behavior with sudden loss spikes as predicted by Fig. 2. The new RelaxSEQ with Round-the-Clip has a smooth transition in loss with changing bitwidth. Although, the final loss after the end of schedule was similar for both Clip-thenRound vs. Round-then-Clip, we found that RelaxSEQ resulted in better benchmark scores (see Table 10).

papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.
authors: Jie Gui, Hang Tu, Wen Sha, Xiuquan Du
bullets: Addresses text-mask conflicts caused by repetitive clinical language and vision-dominated cross-attention, especially for multi-site or multi-lesion descriptions.
Uses Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning with soft text-similarity labels to reduce false negatives during pretraining.
Introduces Bidirectional Complementary Attention so visual and textual modalities each guide their own interaction pathway.
Adds KAN-based Attention Gating to strengthen multimodal feature representations without updating the language encoder.
Reports improved text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets.

papers.abstract: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.
authors: Yutong Xia, Yangyou Liu, Yuxuan Liang, Yuankai Wu, See-Kiong Ng, Roger Zimmermann
bullets: PairST provides six datasets with paired reference and intervened futures across traffic, power transmission, and water distribution.
The benchmark separately evaluates accuracy in affected regions and response error in quiet regions.
ActionST writes an action response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast using node-time addressing, state-conditioned response generation, and graph-aware locality gating.
It achieves the lowest mean absolute error on five of six datasets and the best average rank, including at new action targets.

papers.abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
authors: Weikang Qiu, Zheng Huang, Tinglin Huang, Yujun Yan, Rex Ying
bullets: Addresses the limited transferability of EEG motor representations learned from cue-based trials, coarse labels, or movement-agnostic objectives.
Learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations by treating current EEG as a latent action that predicts future visual representations.
Introduces a Lateralization-Aware Transformer to model shared bilateral and side-specific hemispheric features.
Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% over task-family baselines.
The world model has lower prediction error than an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline and benefits more from matched real actions, including on held-out subjects.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Existing approaches (top) versus MWM (bottom) on the three challenges of motor EEG representation learning. (1) Cue-based trials are costly to scale, and categorical labels give one class to movements that unfold differently (Tangermann et al., 2012; Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018). (2) General-purpose EEG foundation models (FMs) pretrain with EEG-only objectives (Kostas et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). MWM answers both with one mechanism: it treats the EEG recorded up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model that predicts the next visual state. It therefore learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations, and its target is the visual consequence of behavior rather than the EEG itself. (3) Existing methods do not explicitly separate bilateral from lateral activity (Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025a); MWM does, and pairs each horizontal video mirror with an exchange of only the lateral component Hlat.

Figure 2: The Mind World Model. (a) A frozen encoder g maps the current frame to patch features that a residual predictor advances; the same frozen g builds the target from the next frame. (b) The mind model encodes the EEG window, which ends on the current frame; its LAT encoder is detailed in Figure 3. The EEG reaches the predictor only as AdaLN modulation, never as an input token: it occupies the slot a recorded action would.

Figure 3: The Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) for EEG encoding. (a) Patch embedding, applied within each channel, (b) the learned gate G ∈ [0, 1]C×N×De and the electrode permutation Π ∈ {0, 1}C×C , which act on the embedded tokens before any Transformer block; the mirror acts on the decomposed pair and is an involution, (c) a criss-cross block, (d) a shared Transformer with invariant and equivariant readout heads; under the mirror, Hbi is unchanged and Hlat flips sign after aligning homologous channels, and (e) the paired EEG–video mirror. Only the learned lateral component is exchanged across hemispheres; the raw signal is never permuted.

Figure 4: Lateralization analysis. (a,b) Hand-motion correlations with 95% confidence intervals estimated by bootstrap resampling, using participants as the resampling unit. (c–e) Participantaveraged motor-imagery feature-energy contrasts, normalized by channel-wise mean energy; left– right contrasts share a color scale. Control features h(1) and h(2) are equal-sized halves of h.

papers.abstract: The world evolves through the dynamics of its constituent entities and their interactions, with changes in one entity influencing the behavior of others. To simulate this evolution under different actions, interactive world models need to capture the resulting agent responses as part of the world's own dynamics. In autonomous driving, errors in modeling these responses can misrepresent maneuver safety and undermine the reliability of generated videos used for policy evaluation and learning. To formalize this intrinsic requirement for driving world model, we define self-reactivity as the capability to model agent responses from observed history and a specified ego action, and generate visual futures that reflect those responses without prescribed future agent trajectories. To realize this capability, we introduce ReactDrive, a driving world model that jointly learns agent dynamics and visual generation through a shared agent state representation. Within this framework, dynamics supervision grounds a reactive dynamics prior in observed agent states, while the video objective jointly optimizes the self-reactivity and visual realism. Experiments show improved agent responses, ego controllability, and video quality, a 96.0% preference for agent reactivity in human comparisons across five baselines, and better downstream planning through augmentation with generated videos. We hope this work encourages the community to recognize self-reactivityas a foundational capability for developing and evaluating interactive world models. Project page: https://reactdrive.github.io/ .
authors: Yifan Wang, Xiaoqi Wang, Cho-Ying Wu, Wenbin He, Chenyu You, Liu Ren
bullets: Motivation: Accurate modeling of other agents’ responses is essential for reliable safety evaluation and policy learning in autonomous driving.
Method: Jointly learns agent dynamics and video generation through a shared agent-state representation, using dynamics supervision and a video objective.
Contribution: Formalizes self-reactivity as a core capability for interactive driving world models without requiring future agent trajectories.
Results: Reports improved agent responses, ego controllability, video quality, and downstream planning; human evaluators preferred its agent reactivity in 96.0% of comparisons across five baselines.
Scope: Evaluations focus on generated-video quality, reactive behavior, controllability, and planning augmentation in autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Moving objects introduce cross-frame inconsistencies that complicate camera estimation and static geometry recovery in driving scenes. Recent feed-forward Gaussian methods explicitly separate static and dynamic primitives, but often estimate camera parameters and geometry from shared features that jointly encode both components, leaving static reconstruction susceptible to dynamic interference. To address this challenge, we propose S2D-Splat, a feed-forward framework for static-first Gaussian reconstruction with layer-wise feature guidance. Our framework separates static and dynamic features before camera and geometry estimation, enabling the static branch to recover camera parameters and static 3D Gaussians with reduced dynamic interference. Intermediate static features are cached at each layer and reused as fixed conditioning at corresponding layers of the dynamic branch. This asymmetric information flow preserves the established static representations while providing stable geometric context for reconstructing dynamic 3D Gaussians. An instance-level motion decoder further queries the fused static and dynamic representations to estimate object trajectories, supporting motion-aligned Gaussian fusion and temporal interpolation. Experiments on Waymo and zero-shot evaluations on nuScenes and the MM-AU accident dataset demonstrate that S2D-Splat outperforms existing approaches on most evaluated metrics and generalizes to highly dynamic, pre-collision driving scenarios.
authors: Jinheng Li, Tianchen Deng, Bufan Zhang, Qu Chen, Jianwu Fang
bullets: Addresses camera and geometry errors caused by moving objects interfering with static-scene estimation.
Separates static and dynamic features before estimating camera parameters and 3D Gaussians.
Caches intermediate static features to condition the dynamic branch while preserving stable static representations.
Uses an instance-level motion decoder for object trajectories, motion-aligned Gaussian fusion, and temporal interpolation.
Outperforms existing methods on most evaluated metrics on Waymo and transfers zero-shot to nuScenes and MM-AU accident scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of S2D-Splat. Given unposed images, we encode each frame into patchified features and use SAM2 to classify tokens as static or dynamic, which a Motion-Static Separator then refines into clean static and dynamic tokens (camera in , static in , dynamic in , suppressed dynamic in ). The static tokens pass through alternating attention and are decoded by heads into camera parameters and a static Gaussian field, with each layer’s camera and static tokens cached in a Tokens Bank. The dynamic reconstruction mirrors this but takes the fused static and dynamic tokens as input, re-fusing the extracted dynamic tokens with the Tokens Bank after each layer to yield global tokens and a dynamic Gaussian field. From the global tokens, instance-specific queries retrieve each instance’s motion, and all components merge to form the full scene reconstruction.

Figure 1: We propose S2D-Splat, a feedforward Gaussian reconstruction framework that achieves precise dynamic-static decoupling and instance-level motion prediction for complex driving scenes. It disentangles multi-frame input into static and dynamic representations, reconstructs each representation independently, and fuses them into a global representation that guides a motion decoder to recover accurate and temporally consistent per-instance 3D trajectories (e.g., Query 1, Query 2).

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on Waymo. Compared to AnySplat, DGGT, and StreetForward, our method produces sharper structures and more accurate geometry around dynamic objects, consistent with its lower D-RMSE and higher PSNR/SSIM in Table 1.

papers.abstract: Many questions about videos ask for a number, such as how tall a person is, how far a cart travels, or how fast a ball leaves a ramp. We study this task, quantitative physical reasoning from video, where the inputs are a video, a question, and a prior of known facts such as object sizes, speeds, and distances from the camera to named objects. End-to-end video-language models lack an explicit metric scale and physical consistency, and their errors cannot be inspected. We present SceneRuler, which instead recovers a measurable physical scene and answers with that scene as evidence. Its central principle, Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction, builds, for each question, only the smallest scene that suffices to measure the asked quantity, and tests sufficiency on measurements rather than assuming it. The scene is written as a program whose structure a vision-language model writes and whose magnitudes are left to measurement. Physics-guided Fitting measures them through physical motion laws, so that gravity itself can anchor the metric scale, and marks every parameter, and the read-out of the asked quantity, as determined or undetermined. Each question receives a read-out and an answer. The read-out is the asked quantity evaluated on the scene, and it is empty when the scene does not fix that quantity. The answer is always given by a model that takes the scene as evidence. We evaluate on QuantiPhy and also apply the method to 27 in-the-wild videos that we collected, which have no ground-truth answers. On its validation split, the final answer reaches a mean relative accuracy of 0.709 against 0.624 for the strongest baseline, and the reconstruction determines the asked quantity on 47 of 158 questions, where the final answer reaches 0.781. Because every intermediate quantity is explicit, each answer can be traced to the objects, scale, and motion behind it.
authors: Yumeng He, Gezheng Kang, Fanlian Zeng, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
bullets: Targets questions requiring physical quantities such as height, distance, and speed from video plus known prior facts.
Uses Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction to build the smallest question-specific scene that can determine the requested measurement.
Represents scene structure as a program, estimates magnitudes with physics-guided fitting, and can use gravity to establish metric scale.
Marks parameters and outputs as determined or undetermined; answers are generated with the reconstructed scene as evidence.
On QuantiPhy validation, achieves 0.709 mean relative accuracy versus 0.624 for the strongest baseline; fully determined cases reach 0.781 on 47 of 158 questions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.
authors: Haoyang Xu, Christian Iha, Colbren Fujimoto, Yingfei Dong, Rui Ning, Liuwan Zhu
bullets: Addresses location leakage from ordinary images even when GPS metadata is removed.

Open challenges include deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and evaluation against adaptive attackers.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.
authors: Ye Mao, Jinhui Xiong, Egor Larionov, Shiyang Lu, Krystian Mikolajczyk, Wei Ye
bullets: Addresses the limitation of models tied to fixed camera counts, placements, or layouts.
Disentangles per-view generation from cross-view interaction using shared slot tokens.
Uses curriculum training and Cross-View Slot Agreement to align geometrically and semantically similar regions.
Achieves the best evaluated generation quality on RoboView-Bench and improves cross-view consistency over independent view generation.
Transfers gains to world-action models, robot benchmarks, and a real Franka robot, including better generalization across camera settings and scenes.

papers.abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
authors: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
bullets: Agent execution histories grow over time, driving shared GPU KV-cache demand and limiting throughput.
Tool-operation provenance identifies earlier outputs and turns superseded by later operations; 64% of final-history tokens are removal candidates.
Contexture separates the complete harness history from the model’s execution context and evicts context based on supersession, cache residency, and GPU pressure.
Across two models, harnesses, and benchmarks, it improves SLO-constrained throughput by 20–73% versus the strongest baseline and reduces GPU energy per session by up to 11%.
Live-agent accuracy improves by 1.4 percentage points on average versus unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points.

papers.abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with llama.cpp Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than llama.cpp's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.
authors: Vinnam Kim, Seong Hoon Seo, Junhan Kim, Jaeseong You, An Chen
bullets: Addresses the gap between sub-4-bit memory savings and decoding speed on mobile NPUs, where unsupported formats may require costly conversion.
Executes 3-bit and symmetric 2-bit weights directly with native integer operations, avoiding wider weight expansion during decoding.
Assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-grained mixed precision without disrupting execution.
On a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 Hexagon NPU across Qwen3 models, it matches or exceeds llama.cpp sub-4-bit accuracy at equal bits per weight.
Reports 1.16–1.41× faster decoding and 1.5–4.3× higher tokens per joule than the llama.cpp Hexagon backend.

papers.abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.
authors: Soheil Zibakhsh, Pedram Aghazadeh, Farinaz Koushanfar
bullets: Local LLM decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, leaving compute capacity unused for safety checks.

It detects 11.8 percentage points more unsafe responses than a cheap hidden-state probe at similar cost.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.
authors: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Jinli Ou, Yuhua Zheng, Jianqiang Huang
bullets: Introduces Cognitive Inertia and Perceptual Inertia as two opposing failure modes of multimodal integration.
Presents TheaterBench, a benchmark featuring counter-intuitive videos that violate physical laws or common sense.
Finds severe Modal Polarization across current state-of-the-art video understanding models.
Reports that existing de-hallucination methods often shift the balance between the two inertias rather than resolve the conflict.
Positions perceptual-cognitive equilibrium as an important direction for future model evaluation and improvement.
