papers.title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
papers.tldr: The paper identifies Modal Polarization in video MLLMs: models either cling to prior knowledge or blindly trust perception when visual evidence conflicts with common sense.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/
authors: Zhiyuan Li, Charles Eret, Dingsheng Liu, Xuan Zhao, Joshua Choi, Yangzheng Wu, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Covers 80 bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished environments, with 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K language instructions.
Varies distractor density from clean scenes to dense visual and operational clutter.
Introduces safety-aware metrics for collisions with the environment and non-target objects, beyond task success rate.
Evaluates visual, linguistic, and object-level perturbations through per-factor analysis.
Experiments show clutter reduces success and increases non-target collisions, while perturbation type and training-data composition affect performance.

papers.abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
authors: Anika Misra, Chimaobi Okite, Rada Mihalcea
bullets: Existing evaluations may overestimate child-safety alignment by focusing on prompts that name predefined harm categories.
Across six models, uncued requests produced higher misalignment than cued requests, with large model-specific gaps.
Adding one harm-associated word reduced misalignment across most models.
Behavioral and mechanistic analyses suggest lexical and semantic prompt associations partly drive safety reasoning.
The study supports context-dependent evaluations that extend beyond fixed harm categories.

papers.abstract: Existing game super-resolution methods typically operate at moderate upscaling factors, struggling to recover fine visual details from extremely low-resolution inputs (e.g., 120p). At such resolutions, super-resolution shifts from reconstructing existing information toward synthesizing missing visual details. While video diffusion models offer powerful generative priors for this challenging task, their dependence on future frames limits their applicability to interactive games. We present CIDER, a causal diffusion framework for extreme game super-resolution that synthesizes high-frequency details from current and past low-resolution frames, guided by G-buffers (depth and motion vectors) to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency. We collect data from two AAA games (Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong). To reduce inference load, we develop a lightweight latent projection encoder tailored to ultra-low-resolution inputs, fine-tune a decoder (TAE) on our high-resolution outputs, and distill the diffusion model to reach interactive frame rates. Our experiments demonstrate high-fidelity 8$\times$ upscaling from 120p to 960p at around 13 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art game upscalers in visual quality and showing potential for 16$\times$ magnification.
authors: Christina Zhang, Jenna Kang, Colin Groth, Akshay Jindal, Stavros Diolatzis, Qi Sun
bullets: Targets extreme upscaling, where ultra-low-resolution inputs lack recoverable visual detail.
Uses current and past frames plus depth and motion-vector G-buffers to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency.
Combines a lightweight latent projection encoder, a high-resolution-trained decoder, and diffusion distillation to reduce inference cost.
Evaluated on Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong, achieving about 13 FPS for 8× upscaling and showing potential for 16× magnification.
Scope: designed for interactive games and relies on temporal context and G-buffer guidance.

papers.abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.
authors: Zijia Cao, Hanqing Dou
bullets: Studies how unsupported claims evolve as they pass between agents.
Compares homogeneous pipelines using one model with heterogeneous pipelines using different models.
Attaches each claim’s support status, source, evidence, and transmission history; no new evidence is added during transmission.
Evaluates meaning changes, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation.
Tests whether provenance tracking reduces unsupported changes relative to a baseline.

papers.abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/
authors: Jingchen Sun, Jiaxing Zhang, Qingqiao Hu, Dingqiang Ye, Yuqi Jia, Yijun Liang, Di Fu, Yunjie Tian, Dongdi Zhao, Changyou Chen
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of annotated or externally supervised video foresight training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation over past–future video pairs as a natural self-supervised signal.
Introduces a foresight score and contrastive privilege advantage to emphasize informative future content over irrelevant context.
Optimizes a tractable lower-bound surrogate combining true-versus-random future comparison with teacher–student distillation.
Improves base models by up to 14.2 points on open-ended prediction and 15.9 points on closed-ended planning, without harming general video understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Future-OPSD and comparison with other training paradigms. (a) SFT learns annotated future descriptions y⋆ from past observations x using cross-entropy. (b) Naive OPSD uses a frozen future-aware teacher π0 to score the student’s own response ŷ, converting the teacher–student log-probability gap into token advantages for PPO. (c) Future-OPSD (ours) has a frozen teacher score the same response under the true future z (blue) and a reference future z̃ from another video (orange). The contrastive privilege advantage ℓzt −ℓz̃t compares the two futures, and the teacher–student distillation advantage ℓzt −ℓSt compares the true-future teacher with the past-only student. Their interpolation at down-weights context tokens supported by both futures (next / chop / the) while keeping content tokens specific to the true future (cilantro), helping the student focus on the most valuable future information. The advantages are clipped and centered into At for PPO, and inference uses only the student.

Figure 4. Case study: why Future-OPSD improves video foresight reasoning. On an EgoPlan-IT example with Qwen3-VL-8B, we compare the initial token advantages and trained predictions of Naive OPSD and Future-OPSD. A frozen teacher scores the same initial rollout under the paired future z and a reference future z̃ from another video, giving token log-probabilities ℓzt and ℓz̃t ; ℓSt is the past-only student’s log-probability. The context and content components are Ct = ℓz̃t − ℓSt and It = ℓzt − ℓz̃t . Before clipping and centering, Naive OPSD uses at = It + Ct, while Future-OPSD uses at = It + (1 − λ)Ct with λ = 0.75. Plotted values are initial advantages, with Ct and It below each token. Future-OPSD suppresses context information and amplifies decision-relevant content information, yielding the correct next-action prediction.

Figure 1. Not all of the future is equally important. To answer what will I do next? from what is seen now, only a small part of the future clip carries content information (rinse the knife); most of it is context information (tap, dish rack, sink, sponge) that neither answers the question nor reflects the expected action and trajectory of the ongoing event.

Figure 3. Data scaling on EgoPlan-IT (Qwen3-VL-2B). We compare SFT and GRPO trained with answer labels against Naive OPSD, Future-OPSD, and its stronger-teacher variant (frozen Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct). Future-OPSD scales better than naive distillation and surpasses SFT and GRPO at larger data scales, with further gains from a stronger teacher.

Figure 5. Search over the mixing weight λ. We sweep λ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} for Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B on both tasks: (a) EgoPlan-IT training with SEED-Bench-R1 evaluation; (b) Future-L1 training with TwiFF-Bench evaluation. Among the tested values, λ = 0.75 achieves the best overall performance, balancing contrastive learning and distillation.
Figure 6. Teacher weights and vision encoder (Qwen3.5-2B, EgoPlan-IT). Each variant changes one setting of the default (frozen teacher, trained ViT).

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.
authors: Stefan de Lasa, Mohammadreza Mofayezi, Gennady Pekhimenko, Nandita Vijaykumar
bullets: VLAs support generalizable robot control but can leave serving hardware under-utilized.
Multi-client serving may improve hardware utilization by processing requests concurrently.
The study evaluates batching and co-execution across latency, throughput, power, and utilization.
Results highlight trade-offs and challenges for designing future multi-VLA serving systems.

papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.
authors: Bonny Banerjee, Geetha Raju
bullets: Addresses the gap between AI risk governance frameworks and implementable, lifelong risk-monitoring methods.
Decomposes risk into dataset, hardware, and model/algorithm components, represented as slowly evolving latent states.
Separates fast interaction dynamics from slower component-risk states in a structured latent-variable model.
Learns latent risks by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally using evidence-supported behavior–cause records rather than risk labels at every step.

Under stated assumptions, provides guarantees for risk-budget compliance, adaptive-regulation regret and convergence, risk-rating identifiability, detection and containment, and computational complexity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Block diagram of the proposed CENTRY framework. The SELP (Surprise→Explain→Learn→ Predict) cycle (in blue) continually monitors a given AI system’s interactions with its environment (in red) and updates the model and policy parameters and risk rating of the different components in the monitored system’s pipeline throughout its lifecycle. The monitored system’s behavior is regulated using the risk ratings to minimize risk in its behavior (in black). Best viewed in color.

Figure 3: Simplified dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) representation of CENTRY, showing three consecutive time slices. The DBN encodes the first-order Markov assumption: each variable at time t depends only on variables at times t and t − 1. Observations yt = (xt, at) are generated from the latent state
Figure 1: Block diagram depicting the AI risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation problem.
Table 1: Key symbols and notations used in this paper.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a probabilistic framework for continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of AI systems, modeling latent risk states over time.
papers.title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
papers.tldr: CENTRY is a probabilistic latent-state framework for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating AI risk from system–environment interactions throughout deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language agents can reconstruct rooms from video as editable 3D scenes, but convincing renders do not establish geometric accuracy. We introduce a scan-referenced evaluation and use controlled experiments to study reconstruction accuracy, the role of geometric inputs, and agents' ability to verify and correct their scenes. Our geometric score measures surface, depth, and furniture placement agreement with laser scans of 30 real rooms on a 0-100 scale. The strongest tested agent, GPT-6 Astra, scores 51.4 from video alone, while a dense reconstruction from the same video scores 75.9. Given the point cloud used for that reconstruction, Astra produces an editable scene that scores within three points of it. Agents also inherit input errors: rescaling the supplied geometry changes scene scale almost proportionally. During revision, viewing renders improves appearance more consistently than geometry. Logs of their tool calls show that agents repeatedly measure their inputs but rarely compare them with the scenes they build. To provide this missing check, we introduce a geometric error report that compares each saved scene with the agent's input points and lists the largest discrepancies. Without new geometric evidence, the report raises the revision gains of GPT-6.1 Terra and Sol by 3.9 and 5.5 points over concurrent controls.
authors: Ziyang Long, Yen-Liang Lin, Shifan Zhu, Allen Tu, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Srikumar Sastry, Sarosij Bose, Mellon M. Zhang, Hsin-Jung Yang
bullets: Evaluates reconstructed rooms against laser scans using surface, depth, and furniture-placement agreement across 30 real rooms.
The strongest video-only agent scores 51.4/100, versus 75.9 for dense reconstruction from the same video.
Providing the reconstruction point cloud brings the agent’s editable scene within three points of the dense reconstruction.
Agents inherit geometric input errors, while render-based revision improves appearance more reliably than geometry.
A geometric error report improves revision gains by 3.9 and 5.5 points for two tested agents without adding geometric evidence.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and improves geometric accuracy of vision-language agents' 3D scene reconstructions.
papers.title: Looking Right Is Not Being Right: Evaluating the Geometry of Agent-Built 3D Scenes
papers.tldr: Agent-built 3D scenes can look convincing while remaining geometrically inaccurate, but scan-based evaluation and targeted error reports substantially improve revision quality.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.
authors: Minda Zhao, Yue Zhang, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Targets privacy leakage from images, including geolocation, PII, facial attributes, and medical information.
Agents identify visual evidence exposing sensitive content and iteratively adapt invisible perturbations based on VLM responses and an appearance reviewer.
SecretAgent-Gradient uses six surrogate encoders for cross-model transfer; SecretAgent-Tool is gradient-free and uses procedural noise.
Evaluated across four applications, five datasets, and six VLMs, it improves perceptual quality over prior methods while providing state-of-the-art privacy protection.
Protection transfers across different VLMs, though the abstract does not specify detailed quantitative results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SecretAgent. (a) Given an image x and its private queries Q, the Privacy Assessor (A1) first queries the target VLM on x (t = 0). The tabs mark the four privacy tasks across five datasets, with a street-view image as the running example. The history Ht records the outcomes of every round and the latest and best candidates. In round t, the Planner (A2) reads Ht−1 and outputs a plan pt of where and how to perturb, including the regions Rt; the Configurator (A3) sets its numerical parameters θt; and noise injection produces the candidate x̃t = x+ δt with ∥δt∥∞ ≤ ϵ. The Appearance Reviewer (A4) rejects candidates with visible artifacts and returns their appearance reports to Ht, and passes the others to A1. After T rounds, SecretAgent outputs the most protective passing candidate. (b) In SecretAgent-Gradient, A3 weights six frozen surrogate encoders by at,k, and each round takes a sign-gradient step inside the mask Mt that pushes the features of x̃t away from those of x on the full image and the planned regions. In SecretAgent-Tool, A2 assigns noise families to the regions as components, A3 sets their parameters, and the masked components are summed and clipped to ϵ.

papers.selection_reason: A multi-agent framework for privacy protection against VLMs using invisible perturbations. While relevant to VLMs, it focuses on security rather than the core embodied or generative research interests.
papers.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
papers.tldr: SecretAgent uses collaborating LLM agents to hide private information from vision-language models while keeping protected images visually natural.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
authors: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong
bullets: Long-video token pruning and merging can lose accuracy because sparse frames may span unrelated scenes, causing 3D patch tokenizers to blend them before token selection.
The method analyzes frame similarity and tokenizer behavior across 16 open models to guide budget allocation.
A closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and tokenizer class to choose token grids and the reduction dimension before encoding.
Across five accelerators and three video LLMs, ESSENCE is more accurate in 58 of 60 matched-TTFT comparisons.
Using 80% of tokens, it matches full Qwen-model accuracy with 1.6× faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it improves accuracy by up to 3.4 points.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free method to accelerate video LLMs by tokenizing 'moments' (segments of frame similarity) rather than individual frames, addressing tokenization inefficiencies.
papers.title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
papers.tldr: ESSENCE accelerates video LLMs without training by allocating tokens to temporally coherent moments instead of uniformly sampled frames.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.
authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Ferdinando D'Elia, Greta Tuckute, Evelina Fedorenko, Meenakshi Khosla
bullets: Tests 12 LLMs spanning six model families against randomly rotated representations with identical geometry.
Native axes align more reliably with other models, human language-related brain responses, and interpretable linguistic features.
The findings challenge the assumption that meaning exists only in directions rather than individual coordinates.
Native-coordinate alignment remains below the best achievable level, indicating incomplete canonicality.
A complete theory must explain both shared representation geometry and recurring unit response patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Axis-by-axis alignment under rotation of the coordinates. A. Schematic of the unit matching procedure. Each coordinate axis of an LLM hidden representation X (one axis per unit) generates a response profile across the input stimuli. Each unit of a target representation Y (a unit of another LLM, a voxel in the brain, or an interpretable linguistic feature) is matched to its most correlated axis in X on a training split; the alignment score is the correlation r between matched pairs on held-out stimuli, averaged over target units in Y . B. The stimuli in X are represented as a point cloud in three coordinate frames (with all pairwise distances fully preserved). Left: a random orthogonal rotation (α = 1) moves away from the native axes but keeps the geometry intact. Middle: the native basis (α = 0), where each axis corresponds to one model unit. Right: the optimal rotation Q∗, learned by gradient descent on SO(n) to maximize the pairwise alignment with the target. If the native axes were arbitrary, the matching in A would give identical alignment scores in the left and middle panel; if they were fully canonical, it would give identical scores in the middle and right panels.

Figure 2. Three settings for probing the LLM representation basis. In each setting an LLM’s hidden representation (X) is aligned to a target representation (Y ) via axis-by-axis matching. For each basis of X (native or rotated), we match each target dimension to the single axis of X with which it has the highest absolute correlation on training stimuli and evaluate that match on held-out stimuli. Top: Model-to-model, where Y is the hidden representation of another LLM elicited by the same set of 627 naturalistic sentences (the 384 sentences of Pereira Experiment 2 combined with the 243 sentences of Pereira Experiment 3). Middle: Model-to-brain, where Y is human fMRI responses recorded in the language network while participants read the same 627 sentences across two experiments. Bottom: Model-to-feature, where Y is an interpretable linguistic feature, either a binary well-formedness label from a minimal-pair task (Y ∈ {0, 1}; morphology, syntax, hypernymy) or a multi-dimensional rating vector (Y ∈ Rk; perceptual and affective ratings).

Figure 4. Model-to-feature alignment as a function of rotation. Pairwise alignment of each LLM against five interpretable feature targets that span morphology (Wug), syntax (BLiMP, averaged across 12 sub-tasks) and lexical semantics (hypernymy minimal pairs; perceptual sensorimotor norms; affective valence/arousal/dominance norms). Each curve is the mean over layers; the same decline with α appears in all panels.

Figure 5. Random, native and optimal alignment. From left to right: model-to-model alignment (with Pythia-160M as the reference); model-to-brain alignment (Pereira Experiments 2 and 3); and model-to-feature alignment (grouped by morphology, syntax, and lexical semantics). Each box shows the distribution across models of the alignment under a full random rotation (α = 1, gray), the native basis (α = 0, light blue), and the optimal axis alignment (Q∗, dark blue); thin lines connect the three values of one model. Across all alignment targets, the pattern is random < native ≪ optimal.

Figure 3. Model-to-model and model-to-brain alignment as a function of rotation. A. Pairwise alignment between Pythia-160M and every other model in the set, as a function of the rotation fraction α. The light-blue dashed line is the comparison with an identical model trained with a different seed. B, C. Pairwise alignment of each LLM with human fMRI responses in the language network, separately for Experiment 2 (B) and Experiment 3 (C) of Pereira et al. (2018). Each curve is the mean over layers (and participants); alignment decreases with α in most models and in every panel on average.

Figure 6. Readout sparsity and training dynamics. A. Kurtosis of the ridge readout weights across hidden units in the native basis, for the discrete features (left; Wug, BLiMP and hypernymy labels) and the continuous features (right; perceptual and affective norms). For each model, the line shows the distribution over layers of the native kurtosis (median over tasks); the small dots are the individual layers (darker = deeper; gray if within the null of that layer), and the vertical square is the median over tasks and layers. The gray band is the 95% interval of this median under a full random rotation of the basis (α = 1, 10 rotation samples) using the widest interval across models. B. Basis privilege across training. The difference between native and random alignment across 29 log-spaced Pythia training checkpoints, for five model sizes. The thick line indicates the mean across sizes; the shaded band around it, the SEM across sizes. The basis privilege is positive but small at random initialization and increases with training.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the internal representations of LLMs, finding that coordinate axes are partially canonical rather than arbitrary, providing insights into LLM geometry and interpretability.
papers.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
papers.tldr: LLM representation axes are neither arbitrary nor fully standardized: native coordinates show meaningful cross-model, brain, and linguistic alignment, but remain only partially canonical.

papers.abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.
authors: Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon
bullets: Addresses the costly need to re-embed an entire corpus when changing embedding models, without query logs.
Selects informative anchors using Cosine Farthest Point Sampling from the existing target index.
Trains a lightweight adapter with Manifold Alignment Loss and orthogonal regularization to align representations without collapse.
Uses a deterministic router to escalate rare, difficult queries that most affect retrieval quality.
Across five BEIR datasets, achieves up to 35% relative nDCG@10 improvement on Arguana and reduces latency from roughly 160 ms to 38–86 ms at a 20% nominal escalation budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overview of the ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt) architecture for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval.
Figure 2 | Effect of Cosine FPS anchor count 𝑁 on retrieval fidelity. Performance generally improves with more anchors, with diminishing returns on most datasets.

Table 4 | Escalation rate by query disagreement gap (target nDCG minus projected nDCG) at a 20% budget across all five BEIR datasets. Agnostic is a single uniformly random escalation draw at the same routed count as ERA. Because hard-query buckets are small (e.g., 𝑛=8 on SciFact), a random policy’s capture of them varies widely from draw to draw, whereas ERA’s escalation is deterministic (see text for exact miss probabilities). Here ERA escalates the 20% of test queries with the lowest router scores (text-embedding-004 → gemini-embedding-001, Foundation phase).

LEAF minimizes the ℓ2 error between unit-normalized embeddings, which coincides with cosine regression up to scale, and thus closely corresponds to ERA without LGOR. ERA+ denotes a four-term variant that additionally includes a listwise KL distillation term over the target’s top-100 documents and a signed bilinear alignment term; its leave-one-out rows isolate each ERA term within the richer objective.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval using lightweight adapters and routing, addressing test-time adaptation and memory efficiency in retrieval systems.
papers.title: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
papers.tldr: ERA enables cold-start retrieval with a new encoder by adapting embeddings from a small informative anchor set and routing only difficult queries for re-encoding.

papers.abstract: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. Visual information gain (VIG) is the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one. It splits exactly into global information, carried by image statistics, and layout information, which shuffling the patches within the image destroys. We apply it to decoders with 158M to 1.04B parameters that read pixel patches through a linear embedding, evaluated every billion tokens up to 40B, and to 19 public checkpoints. In our decoders the image lowers the loss by 3% to 46%, depending on the image type. Global information is present after the first billion tokens. Layout information starts near zero, grows slowly with training and does not grow with model size on five of six image types, and a larger batch reaches the same loss with less of it. With a frozen SigLIP 2 encoder in front of the same decoder the loss is lower only when the arrangement of the image is intact. On shuffled images the losses with and without the encoder agree to within 0.04 nats on five of six image types, so the net advantage of the encoder in the loss is layout information, above all the ability to read text in images. Public encoder-free models at production scale (Gemma 4 12B, NEO, Mono-InternVL) do acquire layout information. On the same documents they have 0.53 to 0.76 nats of it, against 0.65 to 0.82 for recent encoder-based models and 0.04 to 0.07 for our decoders, and their released training stages show it rising. These results agree with the reported parity of the two families when both are trained from scratch and place the reported advantage of a pretrained encoder in layout information.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Wei Qiu
bullets: Visual information gain (VIG) measures how much an image reduces loss versus a uniform replacement and separates global statistics from spatial layout.
In 158M–1.04B encoder-free decoders, global information appears early, while layout information grows slowly and is largely insensitive to model size.
A frozen SigLIP 2 encoder helps only when image arrangement is preserved; on shuffled images, its loss is nearly identical to the encoder-free setup.
Production-scale encoder-free models acquire substantial layout information, approaching recent encoder-based models on documents.
The findings support parity between model families trained from scratch and attribute pretrained-encoder benefits primarily to layout information.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces visual information gain to analyze encoder-free vs encoder-based multimodal pretraining.
papers.title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
papers.tldr: Visual encoders mainly improve multimodal pretraining by providing layout-sensitive information—especially text-reading ability—rather than simply lowering text loss.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video is the most scalable source of manipulation data for robot learning, but its difficulty lies in producing high-quality supervision. Existing large corpora lack metric 3D labels or rely on heterogeneous devices, motion-capture labs, or a headset's built-in real-time tracker, whose accuracy is not reported for the released data. We introduce RoboCap-10k: 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation recorded during workers' paid shifts in 11 countries, spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks. Every hour is captured on one device, the RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Online calibration brings every device below 1 px of epipolar error, visual-inertial SLAM yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories, and a multi-view hand tracker yields metric cm-precise hand poses. Each episode is annotated with task and sub-task language captions. Project page: https://robocap10k.com
authors: Kheri Hughes, Qasim Ali, Nikash Bhardwaj, Owen Akhibi, Niresh Dravin, Vivek Sharma, Sam Cho, Ethan Lee, Paul Luo, Sunny Yu, Jonathan Victor, Amanda Young, Michael Cho, Ademi Adeniji, Vincent Liu
bullets: Contains 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation across 11 countries, 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks.
Uses a lightweight 250 g hat equipped with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs.
Provides gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories and centimeter-precise metric hand poses.
Includes task- and sub-task-level language captions for each episode.
Scope: recordings are collected during workers’ paid shifts using a single device per hour.

papers.abstract: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).
authors: Yang Liu, Shengbo Tong, Xiyuan Chen, Shiwei Hou, Sen Yuan, Hao Wang, Yanfeng Li, Hongwen Li, Yiming Zhu, Zhuolun He, Wenjian Yu

Enhances the ZhuLong harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, sandboxed execution, and static checking.
Stores distilled experience in a three-tier memory with ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval.
Achieves 92.4% pass@1 on the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark without self-evolution, outperforming ZhuLong across five LLM backbones.
On an instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution reaches 80.0% pass@1 versus 77.5% for human-crafted experience.

papers.selection_reason: LLM agent with governed cross-task self-evolution and a persistent three-tier memory store distilled from execution traces.
papers.title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting
papers.tldr: ZhuLong-SE improves EDA scripting by grounding an LLM agent in execution feedback and safely evolving reusable knowledge from past task traces.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.
authors: Congyuan Yu, Runping Tian
bullets: Addresses the limitation of judging self-improvement using only task progress, QA accuracy, or episodic memory.
Evaluates agents in Outer Wilds, where each 22-minute episode resets the world but preserves the agent’s knowledge.
Measures reached locations, revealed rumor facts, correctness on 164 world-knowledge questions, and whether answers are supported by cited frames and positions.
In eight-episode baselines, the three measures did not consistently improve together; GPT-6.1 Sol’s correct answers rose from 14.6% to 26.8%, but only 59–68% were evidence-supported by episode 8.
After episode 3, GPT-6.1 Sol revealed no new rumor facts while exploration and memory continued growing; over half of later newly correct answers cited earlier-episode evidence.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for embodied agent self-improvement across episodes measuring knowledge, evidence, and progress; fits test-time learning, embodied memory, and embodied AI.
papers.title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
papers.tldr: AstronautBench evaluates agent self-improvement across episodes by jointly measuring knowledge, evidence grounding, and world progress, showing these dimensions can diverge substantially.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.
authors: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets the trade-off between expensive, capable solvers and cheaper, weaker solvers in multi-subgoal theorem proving.
Uses a cross-solver predictor to select solvers and revise computation allocation as proof attempts and verification feedback accumulate.
Trains with class-weighted cross-entropy for early solver assignment and plain cross-entropy for calibrated later-stage allocation.
Evaluated on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench across progressively broader solver configurations.
Uses less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation for solving the same number of subgoals; savings increase as cheaper solvers are added.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of BudgetPV. A theorem p is decomposed into a proof sketch, and standard proof-assistant procedures first process all subgoals. At each decision step, BudgetPV predicts the success probability of each available LLM solver for each unresolved subgoal and selects a subgoal–solver action based on predicted success, computation cost, and the remaining allowed proof attempts. The selected subgoal is processed using the corresponding solver and verified by the proof assistant. The outcome is used to update the predictions for the next allocation decision.

Table 2: Controlled replay generation GPU-seconds required to reach the corresponding solving-rate target. BudgetPV results are mean ± standard deviation over five runs. Uniform and Statistics Oracle are deterministic for a fixed proof-attempt pool. Lower is better.

papers.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
papers.tldr: BudgetPV reduces theorem-proving computation by dynamically assigning heterogeneous LLM solvers to subgoals based on predictions and verification feedback.

papers.abstract: Zooming into a region often turns a wrong answer from a vision-language model (VLM) into a right one, and a growing literature takes this as evidence that the model lacked the pixels. But a zoom changes several things at once. It removes the surrounding context, re-tokenizes, at a higher density, pixels the model has already seen, and, if the first pass was downsampled, exposes detail the model never received. We separate these factors for each failure. Holding the first pass fixed, we vary only the second look and assign every failure to the cheapest one that fixes it: reusing cached tokens, isolating the region, re-tokenizing the seen pixels, or acquiring new ones. The study covers 2,753 zoom-rescued failures of Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3 on V*, ZoomBench and TextVQA, at first-pass budgets from 17x fewer pixels than the source to native resolution. First, most rescued failures did not lack the pixels: upsampling the pixels the model had already seen fixes 47-73% of them even at 17x downsampling, against 1-3% for a random region. Second, the first-pass budget decides how often new pixels are needed: depending on the benchmark, new pixels are required for 23-50% of the rescues at 17x and for 12-23% at 4x. The missing-pixel reading and the accounts that dispute it thus hold at different budgets. Third, the useful magnification is large and differs between objects and text: seen pixels fix more failures up to 6-12x their first-pass size per side on objects and saturate by 4x on text, and even native pixels gain from being rendered beyond native resolution. Allowing any magnification, 68-94% of the failures at 17x need no new pixels. These models more often need a better rendering of evidence they already have than new pixels, which motivates re-tokenizing a region before acquiring it.
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Kexin Geng, Wei Qiu
bullets: The study decomposes zoom benefits into cached-token reuse, region isolation, re-tokenization of seen pixels, and acquisition of new pixels.
Across 2,753 zoom-rescued failures in three VLMs and three benchmarks, upsampling previously seen pixels fixed 47–73% of failures, versus 1–3% for random regions, even under heavy downsampling.
New pixels were needed for 23–50% of rescues at 17× downsampling and 12–23% at 4×, showing that the initial pixel budget changes the interpretation of zoom success.
Useful magnification differs by content: seen pixels help up to 6–12× per side for objects and saturate around 4× for text; even native pixels can benefit from further enlargement.
With unrestricted magnification, 68–94% of failures at 17× downsampling required no new pixels, motivating re-tokenization before acquiring additional image content.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Strict regime partition of zoom-rescued failures. Panel rows are benchmarks and panel columns are models. Within a panel, rows are regimes and columns first-pass budgets (coarse to fine), and the area of each dot is the share of that budget’s rescued failures assigned to the regime (number in %, n under each column). This is the strict partition: a condition counts only if it fixes the sample while its sham does not. Reading down a column gives the partition at one budget, and reading along a row shows how a regime grows or shrinks as the first pass gets finer: R4 empties, down to zero for InternVL3 on V∗ at 2.8×, and R1/ R2 fill. The dotted line marks the native crop’s own magnification (≈ 4× at a 17× first pass), and the dashed marker the magnification at which the seen-pixel curve reaches 90% of its plateau. Objects gain up to about 8×, native pixels included, and then plateau. Seen-pixel text saturates by 4× and then declines.

Zoom rescues a large, budget-dependent slice, and on V∗ it is near ceiling everywhere.

Dashed hollow markers are the shams, shaded areas the effect beyond the sham. Upsampling already-seen pixels fixes most rescues even at 17×, and reuse and isolation become competitive only near native resolution, where the seen and native crops coincide.

papers.selection_reason: Decomposes zoom-rescue failures in VLMs, clarifying when re-tokenization vs new pixels are needed.
papers.title: What Does a Zoom Actually Add? Decomposing Fine-Grained Perception Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Zooming often fixes VLM errors by rendering already-seen pixels better—not by revealing new visual information—and the balance depends on the initial image resolution.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
authors: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of re-encoding long video histories when escalating from a continuously running small VLM to a large VLM.
Distills a label-free, per-layer linear map from the large model’s answers, using only the current frame to transform the small model’s KV cache.
The useful transfer is concentrated in one direction across the middle third of the large model’s layers; faithfully reproducing the large model’s cache does not improve performance.
On RoboMME, Baton outperforms the small model alone, pruned or shortened re-watching, and text memory, while matching re-watching with 28–47% less compute.
The approach transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA and scales with the large model’s capability across eight model pairs from four families.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Two ways to train the same handoff map, and what they give (2B→8B, RoboMME choice). (a) The small model’s KV memory is mapped into a memory the large model reads while it encodes the present itself. Translation fits it to the large model’s own cache; BATON distills the large model’s answer through the deployed path. (b) The translation maps are eleven times closer to the large model’s cache than BATON and gain nothing; BATON carries the gain in each of four runs (dots; bars: mean, 95% interval).

When it is unsure, the decision is escalated: instead of re-encoding the whole history, the large VLM reads the small model’s memory through BATON, a per-layer linear map, and encodes only the current view itself. (b) Reader compute per escalation on 16-frame histories. (c) At a 25% escalation budget the memory cascade is within 0.7 points of re-watching for both readers.

(b) Top: read-out error per layer of the 8B: BATON departs from the reader’s own cache everywhere, but least in the middle third. Table 2. Alternatives to the memory handoff (2B→8B, RoboMME test, 16-frame histories; TFLOP per escalation). Every other way of seeing the history costs more and loses on choice or point; text memory loses on both, even with a trained reader.

papers.selection_reason: Hands off visual KV memory between VLMs for embodied agents; fits KV-cache efficiency and embodied memory.
papers.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
papers.tldr: Baton lets a large VLM reuse a small VLM’s visual KV memory during escalation, preserving re-watching quality while substantially reducing compute.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for embodied perception and reasoning, yet their physical understanding is largely evaluated on questions answerable from images. Many properties critical to manipulation, such as an opaque bottle's fill level or an object's compliance, may only be revealed through touch. We introduce TouchBench, an egocentric vision-language-tactile benchmark that distinguishes visually answerable questions (Tier A) from those involving properties hidden from the camera (Tier B). It pairs head-mounted video with synchronized 137-channel whole-hand tactile sensing, comprising 900 clips from five participants across 11 tasks, with 900 absolute and 4,102 relative questions. Four state-of-the-art VLMs average 66.4% accuracy on Tier A relative questions but only 49.8% on Tier B, near chance (50%). To bridge this gap, we propose Tactile-as-Prompt (TaP), which presents 34 interpretable tactile statistics as text, enabling VLMs to reason with touch without a learned tactile encoder. TaP raises zero-shot Tier B relative accuracy to 62.9% and reaches 73.1% after leave-one-user-out fine-tuning, outperforming video alone (67.4%) and a learned tactile-token encoder (67.3%). The gains extend to unseen objects and users. On a separate 20-hour in-the-wild corpus, tactile text improves fine-tuned contact-question accuracy from 67.1% to 75.5%. These results highlight the limits of vision-only physical reasoning and establish language as an effective interface for tactile perception.
authors: Ziyao Zeng, Ziyi Kou, Chuan Qin, Mia Huang, Roger Boldu, Zhiwen Fan, Daniel Rakita, Eric Whitmire, Li Guan
bullets: Introduces an egocentric vision-language-tactile benchmark separating visually answerable questions from camera-hidden physical properties.
Combines head-mounted video with synchronized 137-channel whole-hand tactile sensing across 900 clips, 11 tasks, and five participants.
Four VLMs achieve 66.4% on visually answerable relative questions but only 49.8% on touch-dependent questions, near chance.
Tactile-as-Prompt (TaP) represents 34 tactile statistics as text, raising Tier B zero-shot accuracy to 62.9% and leave-one-user-out accuracy to 73.1%.
Tactile text also improves contact-question accuracy on a separate in-the-wild corpus from 67.1% to 75.5%.

figures.caption: Figure 3. The Tactile-as-Prompt interface can turn the input whole-hand touch into a prompt for VLM inference. The glove stream is summarized by 34 interpretable statistics in four groups (ϕ) and serialized as text into the prompt (σ). For illustration, each card and prompt shows a few of its group’s statistics with their values for this clip. The video frames, this line, and the question form a prompt for VLM inference. No training is needed so the same prompt can be sent to an open-weight or a proprietary model.

Figure 2. The six attribute dimensions and eleven tasks of TouchBench. Each task leaves the queried property visually ambiguous over at least part of its range: the fill level behind an opaque wall, the inflation of a ball that looks the same until squeezed, a surface covered by the hand, vibration with no visible motion, the tightness of a cap and the strength of wind or elastic tension. The touch-target task asks whether the hand presses a gloved or a bare hand, and the occluded-texture task is listed as its two material pairs. Clip counts per task and tier are in Fig. A2.

papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-tactile benchmark and tactile-as-prompt method extend VLMs to physical property reasoning.
papers.title: TouchBench: Can Vision-Language Models Feel Invisible Physical Properties?
papers.tldr: TouchBench shows that vision-language models struggle with physically hidden properties, while converting tactile signals into text substantially improves their tactile reasoning.

papers.abstract: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.
authors: Ashish Molakalapalli, Kangda Wei, Haonan Duan, Alex Carter, Ruihong Huang
bullets: Targets runtime prediction for shared-GPU scheduling, hardware selection, and compute budgeting.
Provides 801 training records, 1,884 inference records, and 64 standardized text-generation configurations with repeated launches.
Compares three LLMs with regression baselines and analytical estimates on a forward-pass subset.
On 16 held-out generation configurations, open-weight LLMs underestimated latency by 90–99% on average without examples.
Five labeled examples substantially improved Claude’s generation predictions, with benefits varying by timing target.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PreRun, a benchmark for predicting LLM runtime on GPU clusters, directly relevant to LLM behavior and resource estimation.
papers.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
papers.tldr: PreRun benchmarks how well LLMs can predict deep-learning training and inference runtimes before execution, finding that zero-shot estimates are often highly inaccurate but improve with labeled examples.

papers.abstract: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.
authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Mailhe, Hang Yu, Yikang Liu, Xiao Chen, Ankush Mukherjee, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, safe interactive environments for robotic ultrasound learning.
Conditions a causal ultrasound generator on CT-derived anatomy and probe-controlled anatomical and acoustic visibility.
Combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion, and long-rollout alignment; inference reaches 81.2 FPS.
Introduces the Action-Following Index to evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity.
On 40 held-out volumes, it improves liver and macro-organ AFI, reduces long-rollout brightness drift, and raises simulated key-plane success from 48.2% to 81.2%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SonoAtlasWorld. (a) Five rendered poses illustrate interaction with one persistent scene. The final pose, anatomical rendering and generated observation share the same saved time step. The current pose provides anatomy and visibility conditions; generated history provides temporal context for causal ultrasound generation. Persistent anatomy supports consistent modeling under challenging bone-induced occlusion. (b) Training proceeds from anatomy-conditioned pretraining to causal few-step distillation and long-rollout alignment. The final stage applies DMD to a teacher-length window after a no-gradient generated prefix.

Figure 4. Long-rollout alignment mitigates accumulated drift. Compared with the short-rollout model (S), the aligned model (L) better preserves ultrasound appearance and anatomy over 40 repeated scan cycles, reducing cycle-40 brightness drift by 3.46×. Top: drift and anatomical agreement across cycles; shaded bands denote 95% confidence intervals. Bottom: generated frames at the same return pose for two cases. Early appearances are similar, but S progressively darkens and loses visible structures, while L maintains clearer boundaries.

Figure 3. Anatomical consistency across controlled scans. For each of two initial observations, slide, fan and wide-scan trajectories produce distinct ultrasound sequences. Right: liver reconstructions from generated frames along the executed poses, overlaid on the reference 3D anatomy. The shared anatomical state grounds each scan in the same spatial reference.

Figure 5. World-model data scaling improves downstream policy learning. (a) More training volumes and generated trajectories improve closed-loop key-plane acquisition on unseen volumes. (b) Lower offline action-prediction error is associated with higher closed-loop success across the displayed checkpoints.

Table 1. Patient-specific anatomical fidelity, action following and temporal continuity. Given anatomical inputs, SonoAtlasWorld’s benefits extend beyond gross liver structure to finer anatomical recovery and temporal continuity. Vascular distance: median 2D error from projected reference branch points to the predicted vessel skeleton, conditional on detection within 10 mm. Warping errors: 8-bit gray levels; prefix-only (–) omitted for nearly static output. Bold/italic: best/second-best excluding prefix-only and teacher. Real/sim: real/generated training data. †Adapted re-implementations; real action/geometry baselines use EM tracking.

papers.selection_reason: Anatomy-grounded interactive ultrasound world model for scalable robotic policy learning and evaluation.
papers.title: SonoAtlasWorld: Anatomy-Grounded Ultrasound World Models for Wide-Range Scanning
papers.tldr: SonoAtlasWorld uses persistent 3D anatomy to generate fast, anatomically consistent ultrasound scans for robotic policy training and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for surgical robots is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. Meanwhile, many robot-assisted procedures are recorded as stereo video, yet policies cannot learn from them directly; clinical video carries no action labels. We present FlowScope, which pretrains a surgical policy network on unlabeled clinical video by forecasting scene flow, the metric 3D motion of scene points, with labels computed by off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models. We pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) on a dataset of 1,149 clinical procedures (1.35M clips) and discard the flow head afterward, so the deployed policy is a standard ACT with no added inference cost. On a real surgical robotic system, FlowScope raises needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and first-handover success on needle regrasp from 4% to 52% (full task: 2% to 14%) over training from scratch (n=50 trials each), and retains its gains with a generative flow-matching action head. Ablations indicate that metric 3D motion is the strongest pretraining signal among those tested; kinematics, 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow, each paired with kinematics, yield smaller or no gains. Representation analyses suggest that scene-flow pretraining encodes metric needle depth more accurately, that kinematics pretraining increases reliance on the robot state, and that needle-depth probes follow the ordering of real-robot success where offline validation error does not.
authors: John J. Han, Adam Schmidt, Jingpei Lu, Zooey He, Muhammad Abdullah Jamal, Jie Ying Wu, Omid Mohareri
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of labeled robot demonstrations by learning from action-free stereo surgical video.
Pretrains an Action Chunking Transformer trunk to forecast metric 3D scene motion, using pseudo-labels from stereo depth and optical flow.
Uses 1,149 procedures and 1.35M clips; the auxiliary flow head is discarded before deployment.
Improves needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and full needle-regrasp success from 2% to 14% in 50-trial evaluations.
Metric 3D motion outperforms the other tested pretraining signals; analyses link gains to more accurate needle-depth representations.

figures.caption: Figure 1. FlowScope. Each image is encoded by a frozen DINOv2 pretrained on surgical images. Pretraining (top): point queries read the image features at their pixels, and the flow head predicts each point’s metric 3D position and future trajectory, supervised with an L1 loss on scene flow pseudo-labeled by off-the-shelf stereo and optical-flow models. The robot state is set to zero. Fine-tuning (bottom): the point queries and flow head are discarded, and the pretrained trunk is trained on robot demonstrations to predict action chunks with either the ACT or a flow-matching (FM) action head, giving a standard ACT policy. The CVAE (encoder not shown) is used only during training; z = 0 at test, similar to standard ACT rollout.

Figure 2. Scene-flow pseudo-labels on clinical video. Each track shows where a point on the anchor frame moves over the next 10 keyframes (1.7 s), computed from stereo depth and optical flow and kept only where both pass consistency checks. More visualizations can be seen in Figure S2.

Figure 3. Data efficiency. Real-robot performance with 50% and 100% of the demonstrations (ACT head, 50 trials per point). With half the demonstrations, FlowScope matches the pickup success of a policy trained from scratch on all of them and far exceeds it on regrasp, while kinematics pretraining is no better than training from scratch.

papers.abstract: Language models may enable general autonomy in robot planning, but onboard their reasoning can run for most of a minute while the robot and nearby pedestrians keep moving. The robot must then decide how long to follow a plan that the pending answer may overturn. Here we present staleness deadlines, which hand that decision to the robot's clock. Calibrated prediction regions for pedestrians and deviation tubes for the robot set the deadline. When the language model answers, a graph planner rebuilds the route, which the robot adopts only after it passes the same clearance check against walls and predicted pedestrians. Exact binomial tests determine which prespecified budget-selection policies keep close calls, wrong decisions and late arrivals below their targets at each inference profile. Candidate policies either fix one budget or set each query's budget from how long the robot can continue its plan before it must brake. We study corridor signs that close routes and delivery requests whose destination the language model must infer. In 81,000 simulated missions with recorded Qwen3-4B answers, full reasoning cuts wrong decisions about twentyfold, and tracking until the deadline cuts late arrivals by up to 64%. The robot never collides while it moves, although pedestrians who never yield still walk into the stopped robot in 23% of offline and 32% of live missions. On a Jetson AGX Orin under perception load, short budgets fail the wrong-decision target, and full reasoning the lateness target. Between these extremes, a fixed-budget policy passes for corridor signs and per-query policies pass for deliveries. Live Orin runs match offline replay on all three losses in 24 of the 32 missions where either run records a loss. The deadline turns slower reasoning into measurable mission outcomes, which let designers test how much reasoning each inference profile can support.
authors: Hassan Iqbal
bullets: The problem is that onboard language-model inference can take nearly a minute while the robot and pedestrians continue moving.
Calibrated pedestrian prediction regions and robot deviation tubes define when the current plan becomes unsafe to keep following.
After the model responds, a graph planner rebuilds the route and accepts it only after checking clearance from walls and predicted pedestrians.
Across 81,000 simulated missions, full reasoning reduced wrong decisions about twentyfold, while deadline-based tracking reduced late arrivals by up to 64%.
Fixed budgets worked for corridor-sign tasks, whereas per-query budgets worked for delivery tasks; stopped robots were still entered by non-yielding pedestrians in some missions.
