papers.abstract: Flow matching policies underpin the state-of-the-art in robot learning, with impressive results ranging from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, they provide no measure of whether their predicted commands can be trusted, particularly in novel situations outside their training set. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the model's weights and quantifies this ignorance, but calculating it at inference time from a flow matching policy is not trivial. Actions are produced by an ODE solver, requiring uncertainty to be propagated through the entire integration process. BayesDiff addresses this problem for diffusion models by propagating the mean and variance of the state through the denoising chain under a last-layer Laplace posterior approximation, but it severely underestimates the epistemic uncertainty. In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff's total variance decays at rate $O(1/T)$ as the number of Euler steps $T$ used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff's variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.
authors: Miguel Saavedra-Ruiz, Anqi Li, Claudia D'Arpino, Alperen Degirmenci, Tucker Hermans, Fabio Ramos
bullets: Targets unreliable confidence estimates for pre-trained policies in novel situations.
Proves BayesDiff’s propagated variance decays as O(1/T) with more Euler solver steps.
Introduces two extended/unscented-Kalman-inspired recursions that propagate state–weight cross-covariance.
Improves last-layer uncertainty estimates using observation embeddings already computed by the policy, without retraining.
On three manipulation benchmarks, supports failure detection and demonstration selection while matching or outperforming several estimators.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Variance collapse in moment propagation. (c) Our estimators CoMP-EKF and CoMP-UKF carry the cross-covariance between the state and the weights and recover the reference to within 1%. (d) The total variance trPT at the same seed for every estimator re-run on each grid from T = 10 to 400 Euler steps. BayesDiff halves with every doubling of T , while our methods track the reference regardless of the number of Euler steps.

papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty estimation for flow-matching robot policies; directly relevant to learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: Coherent Moment Propagation: Epistemic Uncertainty for Pre-trained Robot Policies
papers.tldr: Coherent Moment Propagation estimates epistemic uncertainty in flow-matching robot policies by preserving state–weight dependencies during ODE integration, avoiding BayesDiff’s variance collapse.

papers.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
authors: Sheng Cheng, Deqian Kong
bullets: Uses newly observed frames for label-free test-time training while preserving a short input history.
Accumulates updates within an episode and resets them between episodes, retaining information beyond the observation window.
Improves task success across four simulation benchmarks and two world-action models.
On RoboCasa GR-1, 2.4 seconds of history matches a 9.6-second model; 4.8 seconds exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Adaptation improves predicted future frames and increasingly influences actions as episodes progress.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context. We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task. First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method. We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate rich textual captions for each of these proposals. These captions are integrated into the training objective to directly align the 3D features with these rich semantics, creating a composite loss that combines direct feature distillation with caption-based semantic enrichment. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, establishing a new state of the art in 3D open-vocabulary detection on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.
authors: Thomas E. Huang, Alex Zihao Zhu, Hao Xiang, Tianyi Cai, Jingwei Ji, Yuliang Zou, Jiafan Yu, Xin Huang, Mingxing Tan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of transferring rich 2D VLM knowledge to outdoor 3D object detection.
Uses class-agnostic 3D proposals and spatially aware VLM embeddings from projected 2D regions for object-level distillation.
Generates proposal-level captions with an MLLM to add domain-specific semantic information and improve zero-shot capability.
Trains with a composite objective combining direct feature distillation and caption-based semantic alignment.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Data Generation Pipeline. (a) Generic Objects Extraction: We use RANSAC and DBSCAN on the raw point cloud to generate class-agnostic 3D proposals across the entire scene, which are then projected to all 2D camera views. (b) Visual Feature Extraction: The proposals are used to RoI pool features from the VLM vision encoder, creating the visual distillation targets f vis. (c) Language Feature Extraction: The proposals are used to crop and mask the images and then sent to a MLLM for captioning, which are then encoded by the VLM text encoder to create the language distillation targets etext.

Fig. 2. Overall Pipeline. During (a) training, our detector is supervised with three losses: class-agnostic bounding box loss Ldet along with two distillation losses, Visual Alignment loss Lvis and Language Alignment loss Llang, for feature alignment. During (b) inference, we directly use the trained detector to predict boxes and open-vocabulary embeddings. Text-based queries are encoded by the VLM text encoder, and cosine similarity between the embeddings and queries are used to assign the final class label.

Fig. 1. 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection Results. Given text prompts for each class, our detector can retrieve corresponding objects in 3D, without using any ground-truth data during training. Our detector can even generalize to novel object classes like TVs.
Fig. 4. TIPS Features. Comparison of visual features from TIPS [26] (middle) and CLIP [7] (right). TIPS produce features that are higher resolution and more spatially aligned.
Fig. 5. Example Captions. We obtain detailed descriptions of rare objects in the Waymo Open Dataset.

TABLE II. Open-vocabulary 3D object detection on WOD (standard range) (UP-VL [33] setting). No ground-truth labels are used during training. VRU combines pedestrians and cyclists into a single class. AP is computed with IoU=0.4 at difficulty level L2. * indicates class-agnostic AP is used.

papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary 3D detection via VLM distillation and generative captions, advancing generalist 3D perception.
papers.title: 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection via Visual Alignment and Generative Captions
papers.tldr: A two-part framework transfers 2D vision-language semantics to 3D proposals through visual embedding distillation and MLLM-generated captions, achieving state-of-the-art open-vocabulary 3D detection on Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the few-shot minus zero-shot residual is measured at the final prompt token, the ICL task vector, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and of fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.
authors: Konstantinos Skianis, Aristidis Likas
bullets: The study examines six tasks, four frontier editors, and three families of weaker language models.
Editors convert few-shot-minus-zero-shot behavior into a task vector and write it into model weights.
The sparsest updates target near-silent MLP units associated with prompt format.
Performance usually matches in-context learning and fine-tuning, including LoRA, while leaving perplexity largely unchanged.
Performance worsens with wording changes; one editor underperforms fine-tuning, and comparable results on unseen items are limited mainly to the strongest editor.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Writes In-Context Learning and Matches Fine-Tuning in Language Models

papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets
authors: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair
bullets: Targets parameter-efficient continued-fraction channel mixing for language models.
Introduces a non-expanding gated component compatible with MLPs, GLUs, and MoE experts.
Reformulates division using logarithms and exponentials to simplify and stabilize training.
Across GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2, and Llama-MoE variants, performance is similar or better than prior continued-fraction designs with higher throughput.
Eliminates the need for prior incremental-training procedures for stable deeper CoFrGeNets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Above we see our continued fraction inspired architecture that can replace feedforward layers in dense as well as MoE architectures. Our architecture performs a non-expansive gating of the input that then passes through an (ensemble of) continued fraction ladders. The fact that we do not expand the hidden representation and each layer of our ladders requires only a linear number of parameters we obtain significant parameter savings over typical (gated and vanilla) feedforward layers leading to dense models that are ≈ 2 3 the size and MoEs that are ≈ 1 2 the size. In our implementations we create a different class for CoFrGeNet that has the same api as the FFN class, that is, same parameters are passed and the same size output tensor (equal to embedding size) is returned. The depth and width parameters for CoFrGeNet could be additionally passed or just set in the CoFrGeNet class itself. Hence, no changes are made to the residual stream or other aspects of the original architecture. The input x1, ..., xp in the figure is thus simply the output of the attention or SSM layer where the residual stream is added and the representation normalized in the particular block. In other words, nothing else in the model architectures changes and the input and output tensors are both size embedding dimension.

Figure 3: CoFrNet architecture from [14] to simulate FFNs. Two ensembles are used each consisting of specified number of p-variate ladders. Element wise multiplication is done between the representations coming out of the linear layer of each ensemble for higher expressivity.

papers.abstract: World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one. However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian, while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model's training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills. Across three JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% with raw actions to 62%; the gains grow with goal distance and hold across four planners. On AntMaze, a quadruped locomotion task, success on goals two maze cells away rises from 0.4% to 38%. This suggests that part of the difficulty of reaching distant goals lies in the action space, and can be removed without changing the planner.
authors: Tom\'as Couso Coddou, Christ Devia, Rex G. Liu, Rodrigo Toro Icarte
bullets: Standard Gaussian action sampling produces candidates unlike the structured actions seen during training, making distant-goal planning unreliable.
A state-conditioned VAE encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a Gaussian prior and decodes them back into actions.
The world model predicts skill effects, while the unchanged planner searches over skills sampled from the same Gaussian distribution.
Across three JEPA models and four benchmarks, average success for goals 80 steps away increased from 42% to 62%.
AntMaze success for goals two cells away rose from 0.4% to 38%, with improvements growing for more distant goals.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. (b) Inference: the action encoder is replaced by a sampling-based planner initialized at the skill prior, π0 = p(l), which searches over skill sequences with the predictor and decodes the selected plan into actions (Sec. 3.2).

papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
authors: Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi
bullets: Motivation: Search is often added only after static-text pretraining, potentially limiting foundational search ability.
Method: Augment ordinary text corpora with web-search queries and responses retrieved from a local index, then train models on the resulting data.
Result: QueryLM models improve knowledge-intensive task performance and follow retrieved evidence more effectively across tested model scales and corpora.
The gains persist after supervised fine-tuning, suggesting the tested post-training methods do not fully recover capabilities learned through search-pretraining.
A 1.4B QueryLM consistently matches or outperforms a FLOP-matched 3.3B conventional baseline on the reported knowledge-intensive tasks.

papers.abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.
authors: Ziqing Wang, Hamid Palangi, Lili Zhao, Kaize Ding
bullets: Addresses recurring errors in deployed medical agents that do not learn effectively from experience.
Uses a Solver agent and an Improver strategy that writes medical harnesses based on Solver failures.
Rewards harnesses by their performance gain over acting without one, training both roles together.
Evaluated across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, with transfer to unseen workflows, new models, and new databases.
The framework targets continual improvement but depends on harnesses generated without a fixed clinical reference harness.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of MedicalRSI. One model plays both the Improver and the Solver. In each round, ❶ the Solver first attempts the tasks of a workflow with H0, and ❷ a few of its failed and successful attempts form the workflow evidence 𝑃𝜏. ❸ The Improver reads 𝑃𝜏 with its outcome feedback and writes 𝐺 candidate harnesses H1, . . . ,H𝐺 without seeing reference answers. ❹ The Solver then attempts the tasks with each of them. ❺ The Solver is rewarded for solving a task, and each harness by how much it raises the Solver’s score over H0, as in Eq. (5). ❻ One loss over both roles updates the shared weights, as in Eq. (7), and both roles use the new weights in the next round. Memory keeps the better harness for each workflow, and the Improver revises it in later rounds.

Figure 1 | MedicalRSI Outperforms Existing Methods and Keeps Improving over Training. Left: tasks solved on MedAgentBench with Qwen3.5-9B, with the methods grouped by what they change: the harness only (context-level: an RL-trained improver, GRASP, or a frontier LLM writing the harness), the model only (weight-level), or neither (a frontier LLM solving the tasks itself, or the Base Agent, whose score the dashed line marks). Right: MedicalRSI keeps improving over the training rounds. It also improves faster: after two rounds, it already passes the final scores of the two strongest trained baselines.

Figure 6 | Analysis of Transfer Beyond Training. (a) The Improver of MedicalRSI helps every solver, even frontier models, and RL training adds much of this gain. Each solver runs alone, with the harness that this Improver writes before RL training, and with the one it writes after. Total gives the gain over the solver alone, and From Training the part that RL training adds. (b) The Solver of MedicalRSI makes strong use of a harness from another model. Each solver runs alone and with the harness that GPT-6.1-Sol writes from its failures. (c) MedicalRSI carries over to a new database. The methods are trained on MedAgentGym over MIMIC-III and tested on eICU without further weight updates. The dashed line marks the Base Agent, and error bars show the bootstrap standard deviation over test tasks.

Figure 9 | Case Study on an Unseen Workflow. Without a harness, the Solver misses the 24-hour window and places neither order. From these failures, the same model writes a harness that fixes the window, the decision rule and both orders, and the Solver then passes every check. papers.abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).
authors: Yixuan Duan, Kexin Geng, Hanwen Xu, Wei Qiu
bullets: Addresses two gaps: H&E-only pathology models lack mIF-derived cell phenotypes, and final-answer rewards do not verify intermediate reasoning.
Uses paired same-section H&E and mIF to supervise guideline-based steps, including compartment delineation, cell counting, and marker normalization.
A process reward checks each stated quantity against cell-level mIF ground truth during R1-style reinforcement learning.
Across four colorectal cancer TIME tasks, HERMES achieves 84.5% average accuracy, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline at 74.7%.
Maintains strong performance without retraining on CODEX images and on head and neck cancer, though its scope is evaluated on field-level tasks and specific cohorts.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain unreliable on spatial reasoning problems that require composing grounded relations across multiple objects. Yet, scaling reasoning supervision is challenging since human-annotated visual datasets often rely on fixed relational annotations and coarse object localization, making it difficult to obtain precise intermediate reasoning states across diverse spatial configurations and complexities. We introduce FARON (Fully Automated Reasoning Over spatial relatioNs), a framework that executes spatial queries to provide both execution-grounded reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards. Rather than relying on existing annotated data, FARON constructs synthetic 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries, enabling configurable object arrangements, spatial relations, and multi-step compositions. Deterministic query execution yields intermediate sets and final answers, providing precise supervision without manual relation annotation. Our pipeline converts intermediate states into natural-language reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the execution-derived answers provide verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Controlled experiments show that trace-based SFT improves multi-step spatial reasoning over final-answer supervision and that subsequent group relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides further gains. The resulting models also demonstrate transfer across external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning. These results show the potential of using spatial query execution as a unified, flexible source of reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards for multimodal spatial reasoning.
authors: Jiyoon Pyo, Dongwon Jung, Zekun Li, Nayeon Kim, Muhao Chen, Yao-Yi Chiang
bullets: Targets LVLM unreliability when composing grounded spatial relations across multiple objects.
Builds configurable 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries and executes spatial queries deterministically.
Provides intermediate execution states for supervised fine-tuning and final answers as rewards for reinforcement learning.
Controlled experiments find trace-based SFT improves over final-answer supervision, with GRPO providing further gains.
Shows transfer to external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.
authors: Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke
bullets: Compared fixed perception agents and a common reasoning model using agent messages, a tool-explored evidence graph, flat text, or a single audio-visual model.
On 799 XD-Violence clips, flat text nearly matched the single model (F1 0.967 vs. 0.968), while graph and message interfaces were less accurate.
Sound events improved F1, consistent with annotators relying on sound or speech for most violent clips.
Stored-observation citations were generally faithful, but graphs did not improve faithfulness over flat text; the agent pipeline used about 3× the GPU time.
Results were broadly robust to prompt rewording and a larger reasoning model, though model scale changed the relative ranking of message passing and graph use.

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer a scalable source of human demonstrations for robot learning. However, recovering metric object geometry and motion from monocular video is hindered by scale-depth ambiguity and hand-induced occlusion, while image-derived contact and shape priors alone cannot uniquely determine metric scale. We introduce TacHOI, a training-free framework that integrates tactile contact with monocular vision for joint hand-object reconstruction and tracking, without requiring object templates or depth sensors. Starting from pretrained visual estimates, TacHOI uses tactile contact to constrain object depth relative to the estimated hand, while spatially separated contacts on a metrically calibrated hand provide a physical ruler for object extent. It incorporates these constraints into a joint optimization of hand poses, object trajectories, and anisotropic object scale alongside visual alignment. Across 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, TacHOI achieves the lowest median ADD-S* among the evaluated baselines, reducing error from 15.6 to 3.6 cm on ARCTIC and achieving 2.8 cm on HO3D. Additional experiments on OpenTouch demonstrate its applicability to measured tactile observations.
authors: Jackson Codd, Haoyu Li, Xianyi Cheng
bullets: Addresses scale–depth ambiguity and hand occlusion in egocentric monocular videos.
Uses tactile contacts to constrain object depth and a calibrated hand as a physical ruler for object extent.
Jointly optimizes hand poses, object trajectories, anisotropic scale, and visual alignment.
On 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, reports median ADD-S* errors of 3.6 cm and 2.8 cm, respectively.
OpenTouch experiments show applicability to measured tactile observations; scope includes tactile sensing and relies on pretrained visual estimates.

papers.abstract: Kinodynamic motion planning in large-scale, cluttered environments remains challenging, as dynamically feasible, collision-free trajectories must be computed efficiently over long horizons. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) can strategically explore long-horizon alternatives but faces large branching factors in continuous control spaces and often relies on random default-policy rollouts, whereas Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) efficiently optimizes local trajectories yet remains susceptible to obstacle-induced local minima. To overcome these challenges, we propose Search-Informed MPPI (SI-MPPI), a unified framework that embeds MPPI trajectory optimization within MCTS-based tree search. The core concept is to fuse the expansion and default-policy simulation stages of MCTS into a single MPPI expansion stage guided by structured intermediate targets, termed baits. During each expansion, an adaptive bait-handling rule retains geometrically valid baits as local targets for GPU-batched MPPI optimizations that generate dynamically feasible candidate motion segments. Feasibility gating then checks these candidates for collision safety and sufficient progress, and top-$k$ selection admits the lowest-cost accepted candidates as tree edges, yielding sparse, directed tree growth; thereafter, effective sample size (ESS)-guided adaptation warm-starts subsequent expansions, while cost-based backpropagation updates tree statistics. Extensive simulations across four large-scale, cluttered 2D occupancy-grid maps demonstrate that SI-MPPI consistently produces the smallest search trees and smoothest angular control profiles compared with three kinodynamic baselines, while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths. Ablation results further highlight the importance of GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and retaining multiple expansion candidates for planning efficiency and robustness.
authors: Ihab S. Mohamed, Lantao Liu
bullets: Addresses MCTS’s continuous-control branching and random rollouts alongside MPPI’s vulnerability to obstacle-induced local minima.
Uses structured intermediate targets (“baits”) to guide GPU-batched MPPI expansions within an MCTS tree.
Applies feasibility gating and top-k selection to create sparse, directed tree growth, with ESS-guided warm starts and cost-based backpropagation.
Across four large 2D occupancy-grid maps, it produced smaller trees and smoother angular controls than three kinodynamic baselines while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths.
Ablations identified GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and multiple retained candidates as important for efficiency and robustness.

papers.abstract: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).
authors: Anika Misra, Shreyas Vinod, Huteng Dai
bullets: Evaluated 361 corruption settings on GSM8K, including errors in locations, trace–answer consistency, and corruption rates up to 100%.
SFT-only accuracy fell from 43.61% to 13.80% as corruption increased.
GRPO generally restored performance to roughly gold-baseline levels (~60%) despite corrupted initialization.
Initializing with just 8 incorrect three-line form-only traces reached 69.30%, versus 60.71% with gold SFT and 35.00% without SFT.
SFT accuracy was nearly uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r≈0), indicating distinct roles for structural form and functional reasoning.

papers.abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.
authors: Jiangfan Zhang, Wentao Bao, Xian Wu, Xiangjun Fan, Jianpeng Cheng, Jun Xiao
bullets: Targets the latency of iterative transformer architectures and the redundancy and limited refinement of standard learnable tokens.
Appends K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are progressively coupled through a residual recurrence in one pre-filling pass.
Provides theoretical guarantees of expanded geometric directional reachability and a one-step descent advantage over standard tokens.
Consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense and sparse MoE backbones.
Reports up to 11.9× faster training and 4.3× faster inference than looped architectures.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
authors: Guangyu Zhao, Yongchang Zhang, Ruizhang Jiang, Zhihong Yu, Yuhao Zhang, Tao Wu, Qimin Zhou, Kunsong Shi, Haoran Wen, Zeyu Zhang, Yin Li, Kun Zhan, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Introduces VMBench, a benchmark for manipulation tasks requiring memory of locations, appearances, and their associations.
Uses a hierarchical design: a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes, while an executor predicts actions from selected memories.
Achieves 49.9% average success on VMBench, 31.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
Transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances and reaches 43.7% success on an unseen task with a few memory annotations, near 44.3% with full supervision.
Also reports competitive RMBench results and improvements in real-robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.
authors: Junde Li, Wei-Han Yu, Xiangyi Chu, Yaoxin Li, Jiawei Xu, Ka-Fai Un, Pui-In Mak
bullets: Addresses three grounding failures: lost contact geometry, misaligned token-level gradients, and optimization collapse from discrete indicators.
Uses a forward-only tactile encoder, token-parallel zeroth-order activation updates, and SlipGuard for continuous incipient-slip verification.
On an elasto-plastic shell, its closed-loop gate reached 29× lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp and avoided permanent deformation.
Achieved 97.6% average success across three evaluated LIBERO suites while reducing peak activation memory 7.12× versus a backpropagated step.
Scope is limited to the reported structural-shell and LIBERO evaluations.

papers.abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers the promise of bypassing this high cost by segmenting a target video using a few annotated references, which are the sole source of surgical knowledge for a frozen model. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). To address these challenges, we propose INCISE, a training-free ICS framework for surgical videos. INCISE selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos that jointly cover the local appearances of a target video, and then segments the target video using these references. With only 1.7% of training frames selected and annotated as references and no target video frame labeled, INCISE obtains 67.2% mean mIoU and outperforms the best SOTA fine-tuned method by 9.2 points. We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.
authors: Yifan Xu, Bofang Zheng, Guangyu Meng, Nishchal Sapkota, Xianshi Ma, Xu Cao, Tianjiao Yu, Danny Z Chen
bullets: Addresses the high expert-labeling cost of fine-tuning-based video object segmentation.
Selects unlabeled frames across multiple surgical videos to cover the target video's local appearances.
Uses the selected frames as the sole references for a frozen model, with no target-frame annotations.
Using annotations for only 1.7% of training frames, achieves 67.2% mean mIoU.

papers.abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath, Anindita Ghosh, Uttaran Bhattacharya, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of long-horizon planning, where sampling methods struggle and gradient methods can get trapped in local minima.
Uses Sequential Monte Carlo to evolve action-sequence populations through intermediate target distributions with importance weighting and resampling.
Combines SMC population updates with gradient-based plan optimization in learned latent world models.
Introduces a PDE-derived cost-to-go to guide sampling using latent-state-space structure.
On visual and proprioceptive navigation/manipulation tasks, improves average success rates over gradient-based, sampling-based, and MPPI planners, with competitive iteration counts.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient prompt learning has become a cornerstone for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), yet it remains highly vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval scenarios. Existing noise robust methods typically rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction, which discard valuable semantic ambiguity and overlook how observed annotations are actually generated. To bridge this gap, we reformulate noisy prompt learning through the perspective of data generation, proposing SACP, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework. Instead of suppressing noise heuristically, SACP decouples latent clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation. By integrating frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals, SACP constructs a structured annotation channel optimized via generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. Furthermore, a posterior-aware memory is introduced to preserve label uncertainty during test-time inference. Extensive experiments across different synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy Food101N dataset demonstrate that SACP achieves state-of-the-art performance against its counterparts in different label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise.
authors: Zibin Geng, Yitong Bao, Jia Li, Xuefeng Jiang, Sheng Sun, Yuwei Wang, Min Liu
bullets: Targets label noise in few-shot vision-language prompt learning for Web and retrieval settings.
Decouples clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation.
Combines frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals in a structured annotation channel.
Uses generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors and a posterior-aware memory for test-time uncertainty.
Performs strongly across synthetic noise benchmarks and Food101N, particularly under severe asymmetric noise.

papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
authors: Renjia Deng, Yuxi Liu, Yutong He, Xue Wang, Kun Yuan
bullets: Existing gated linear attention uses state-independent gates, which ignore the information currently stored in recurrent memory.
SDG computes element-wise gates from the memory change over each chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary.
The approach preserves parallel within-chunk computation and is implemented with fused kernels for several linear-attention architectures.
Theory connects SDG to improved signal reconstruction and interprets fixed-gate boundary decay as an element-wise ridge proximal step.
Experiments on 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens report improvements across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.

papers.abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model, using 146 training runs across 200 unique languages and more than 10,000 evaluations. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.abstract: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.
authors: Jungjin Lee
Se Jin Kim
Sung Kwon On
Insoon Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting to hidden, changing physical conditions that make identical robot states respond differently to the same action.
Re-infers a latent context from recent interactions and uses it to condition a fixed network modeling inertia and potential energy.
Requires neither retraining nor a hand-specified robot model to adapt to new conditions.
In Isaac Sim experiments with a Franka Panda arm, it predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing unseen-payload error by 1.6–3.8× over baselines.
The learned context captures payload properties and changes, supports counterfactual torque queries, and produces physically valid gravity and inertia components.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. Observations suggest that RCPI provides the closest estimation to the exact solution and has the most stable training curve; however, it is data-intensive and requires the largest volume of data. D-DDPG is the most data-efficient one, but at the price of the training stability. Based on the observations, we provide suggestions for the algorithm selection for AV decision making.
authors: Dechen Xie
Mushuang Liu
bullets: Evaluates FVI, RCPI, DQN, and discrete-action D-DDPG on the same AV decision-making problem.
Compares optimality, safety, training stability, and training and decision costs.
RCPI most closely matches the exact solution and shows the most stable training.
D-DDPG is the most data-efficient but has less stable training.
The findings inform algorithm selection for AV decision-making.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.
authors: Yize Hao
Guangxin Jiang
Shuang Qiu
bullets: Studies offline Q-learning in tabular, finite-horizon MDPs with KL regularization.

Introduces KLPQ, adding pessimism to retain the fast rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence.

papers.abstract: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents must learn to coordinate their actions to achieve shared objectives. A key indicator of effective coordination is behavioral diversity, i.e., the agents' potential to enact distinct yet complementary control policies given the same set of observations. Although behavioral diversity can enable role specialization and richer joint behaviors, its appropriate level is highly context- and task-dependent and often costly to tune. We propose Adaptive Diversity Control (ADiCo), a two-timescale framework that adapts behavioral diversity online during training. On a fast timescale, Diversity Control (DiCo) regulates system diversity toward a target value. On a slower timescale, an Extremum Seeking Controller (ESC) adjusts this target using only mean episodic returns, without requiring an explicit model or analytical gradient of the diversity-performance landscape. We evaluate ADiCo on six configurations across two cooperative MARL tasks, where it maintains task-appropriate diversity levels: low diversity when homogeneous policies are beneficial and higher diversity when heterogeneous policies are required. Through this adaptation, ADiCo matches or exceeds the mean performance of DiCo (best grid-searched diversity target) and Unconstrained DiCo (diversity allowed to emerge without target regulation). These results demonstrate that incorporating classical feedback control into MARL training enables effective coordination by providing a systematic alternative to task-specific manual selection of the diversity target.
authors: Svar Rajankumar Patel
Kshitij Jerath
bullets: Behavioral diversity can support role specialization, but the ideal level depends on the task and is difficult to tune.
ADiCo uses fast-timescale Diversity Control to track a target diversity level and a slower Extremum Seeking Controller to adjust that target from mean episodic returns alone.
Across six configurations and two cooperative MARL tasks, it maintained low diversity when homogeneous behavior helped and higher diversity when heterogeneous behavior was needed.
ADiCo matched or exceeded DiCo with the best grid-searched target and unconstrained DiCo.
The method provides a model-free, gradient-free alternative to manually selecting diversity targets.

papers.abstract: A learned representation is useful beyond its source task only if later tasks can make use of what the encoder has already learned. Source-task performance, however, gives no guarantee that the representation itself will remain useful once the original head is removed. We study representation reuse with respect to a specified family of future tasks. For such a family, we define the task-relevant state as the coarsest deterministic state sufficient for all of its tasks. A larger task family can require a finer state, and losing a required distinction makes at least one future task unrecoverable on a target support containing that conflict. Exact reuse also depends on how the retained information is presented to the downstream rule. We separate this into structural accessibility, which concerns whether the required distinctions remain recoverable, and coordinate consistency, which concerns whether those distinctions can be interpreted by the same downstream rule across samples. Both failure modes appear separately in the experiments. Reuse improves as task-relevant distinctions become more accessible. Reversible sample-dependent coordinate changes can sharply reduce reuse even when the representation remains recoverable, and inverting the applicable coordinate change restores performance. The same accessibility-reuse ordering appears in prospectively specified CIFAR-100 experiments with both ResNet-18 and DenseNet-121. Finally, preserving a candidate state that contains the distinctions needed by the anticipated task family improves reuse on compatible held-out tasks, with the clearest benefit when target supervision is limited. Representation reuse is therefore relative to the tasks that follow source learning: a useful representation must retain the distinctions those tasks need and make them available in a form that a shared downstream rule can use.
authors: Zibo Meng
Andrew C. M. Austin
Alin Achim
bullets: Reuse is defined relative to a specified family of downstream tasks and its task-relevant state.
Two failure modes are identified: inaccessible required distinctions and inconsistent coordinate presentations.
Reversible sample-dependent coordinate changes can hurt reuse despite preserving recoverable information; correcting them restores performance.
Experiments, including CIFAR-100 studies with ResNet-18 and DenseNet-121, show that greater accessibility improves reuse.
Preserving anticipated task-relevant distinctions especially helps on compatible held-out tasks when target supervision is limited.
